I have such mixed feelings about this game. It started out as a 10/10 experience. The character backstories are the best of any game I've played. I LOVE that there is even a mini audiobook for each one. I began this game so invested in my character and in the world.

The mechanics are great - especially the event system that allows you to flip story cards when you get close enough to a POI. The combat is pretty basic, but in the early scenarios it goes faster enough that you don't really mind. There's lots of great gear to pickup and town phase is really interesting and varied.

But then...

... the game just keeps going and going. Every scenario starts to feel like the last and they get longer and longer and it just starts to feel like a grind. We ended up "fast forwarding" the last half dozen or so scenarios by skipping the mechanics and just flipping cards to discover the story so we could figure out what happens to our characters...

... only to discover that the character stories are designed to resolve in a future expansion. This left a very bad taste in my mouth and even now I have a hard time thinking positively about this game.

But those first dozen or so missions when the game was shiny and new and fully of mystery, were some of the best gaming moments of my life.

I wish they had shortened the game significantly by making many branching paths so that you only saw 1/3 of the scenarios each time through. Then I might have been excited to start over again with a different character. As it stands, I have no desire to touch this game ever again.

Agemonia is a huge, story-driven campaign game packed with variety—tons of equipment, consumables, enemies, professions, and a world full of original races and lore. The campaign spans 35 scenarios, and you can really see the effort that went into building a rich and unique fantasy setting.

One of the best parts of the game is how each scenario unfolds as you explore. Every scenario has its own custom deck of cards that you reveal as you move through the map—NPCs, enemies, events, and hidden surprises are gradually discovered, which adds a great sense of immersion and exploration. It really keeps things feeling dynamic and alive.

Combat is dice-based, and while it’s not overly complex, there’s enough strategy thanks to the stamina management system. You have to think carefully about how to spend stamina on actions and movement, and that decision space is satisfying without being a brain-burner.

I played solo, running three characters, and while they are mechanically different, they didn’t always feel drastically unique during gameplay. The city phase between missions starts off as an exciting change of pace, letting you manage upgrades, items, and events—but by the later scenarios, it started to feel a bit too much, especially solo. I think playing with two characters would have helped reduce the mental load.

The story is clearly important to the design, but at some point I found myself losing the thread of it. The reputation system didn’t add much to my experience either. In the end, while I appreciated the variety and innovation, the combination of story fatigue and solo overhead led me to sell the game after 16 scenarios.

Overall, Agemonia is a solid game with some standout mechanics and a lot of ambition. I think it could really shine with the right group, especially if you’re into story-heavy campaigns and exploration mechanics.

I adore this game. It's not perfect, and it's mechanically very simple with low depth. But the kind of experience I get when playing Agemonia is very rare and grand, and it's exactly what I'm looking for when playing these big adventure games. That being said, I think it may be a bit too long, so finishing the game is a major commitment. Espeically since the set up and tear down, while made accessible with scenario pages and booklets, is still quite long.

Unlike others who have complained about the timer in the game, I think it works wonderfully when it is very tight, and feels too loose when you feel like you have a lot of time in a scenario. Especially because the actual actions you take during your turn aren't that mechanically interesting. Therefore it relies even more heavily on the strength of the scenarios and the novelty of the adventure.

And in this aspect, Agemonia is (for the most part) a major hit. Not every scenario is the most innovative, but quite often you stumble across one that just blows your mind. Exploring the different events and arcs of the mission feel so rewarding and exciting. Many pull off clever tricks that I haven't seen in any other games, while also giving you very attractive objectives to go for such as unique loot.

Beyond the scenario design, the city step is also quite fun, although it takes an extremely long time to resolve when you level up and are given hours of things to read and do. But the general system of buying items, crafting, interacting with locals, etc... - while it isnt unique to this game - is done better than many other iterations in other titles.

The characters you play also have their own mini stories and unique mechanics attached to them, making the experience even better. It gives a little nudge of uniqueness and personality to the adventure, which is always awesome.

This game isn't a mechanical masterpiece like Arkham Horror LCG or Gloomhaven. And it's not a grand open-world adventure that you find in Sleeping Gods. But Agemonia is its own thing. It's a game where, although the game is somewhat linear, each adventure in every scenario feel distinct and rewarding. And while your turns aren't filled with combos and extremely hard decisions, the game constantly pulls tricks that will leave you surprised and even inspired. An incredible adventure that's worth the hours and effort.

Agemonia is a fantastic and unique game. It is a fantasy world, but not a traditional fantasy; it is entirely unique. There are nine different classes/races in that universe; no two are similar. Given your initial choice of race, you have various interactions with the world and play style.

There is no linear story; you have many choices, and each one impacts the campaign meaningfully. Each scenario is different and requires a different strategy to succeed. The game is very forgiving, and most scenarios have a fail-forward option. It is an excellent adventure/dungeon-crawler game.

Leveling up is exciting, strengthens each character, and can change the play style. As you advance in the campaign, you get access to better gear and sometimes entirely new ones.

It is a long campaign game and requires a serious commitment. To be clear, I am a solo gamer and played it solo 4-handed. I think the game is better with four characters in your party, and it will become slightly tougher with a lower player count.

Given the asymmetry of characters, there is a potential for replayability. I won’t play the next campaign immediately after the first, but I will definitely do it after six months to a year with a different group of characters.
There are tons of contents in this big box. It is really worth it. Agemonia has its place in my collection, but it won’t replace my other favorites in this overarching genre, such as Oathsworn, Gloomhaven, Frosthaven, Arydia, etc.

Cheers!

Essentially a Gloomhaven-like with more writing and exploration, unfortunately there's more potential than punch here. I totally respect people who rate this game highly, as there is a lot to love, and I think everyone will need to make up their own mind on how the game comes together for them, but for me, it fell flat.

I'll touch on a couple of the main draws, first the scenarios. While most are interestingly designed, they're not well balanced. The game is exceptionally difficult, and I lost almost every scenario. This is largely due to a punishing timer, which I realize has an online errata, but it still doesn't lead to much better gameplay because it stems from another issue: the huge amount of unknown knowledge with almost no hints. You often don't know how to complete a scenario, what you can or cannot touch without a gotcha, or what it takes to achieve an interaction point's test without stumbling into it, so you most often end up flailing around frustratingly. If you played a second time, you could plan and achieve accordingly but while I appreciate the replayability of this idea, I don't plan on playing a second time. These issues are compounded when playing with two characters, as despite a little balancing in the rules, you just don't have the action economy or utility to explore and fight properly. This is a four character game, through and through.

The writing and lore have been praised, and while I certainly appreciated the attempt at crafting a deep world and narrative, I found it shallow. I never felt connected to the characters and I don't feel that the multitude of races, factions and history are fully taken advantage of. It all blends together after a while and comes off as generic 'good and bad', 'magic stuff' or 'wizards and demons', with choices and surface level differences that technically have impact, but only barely. Many of the story entries are redundant fluff, just as Gloomhaven's but more long winded. I'm being overly harsh, as there are standout points to the story, but there's a lot of filler. I found the separate short stories in the lore book better written and more interesting than anything the game, so unfortunately I wasn't drawn in when playing.

Finally, the rulebook needs revising. Even with tutorial scenarios, it was difficult to learn the mechanics, icons, and nuances that need to be remembered. I wish the rules reference was a proper rulebook, as it skirts a weird line where things from the tutorial that I didn't remember I didn't know where to find in the reference. It's all there and can be found, but frustratingly so.

Now for some praise: The combat mechanics are interesting. Simple to learn and play, relying on some randomness but with push your luck mechanics, the stamina/hp system is a good push/pull that I'd like to have seen built on with more interesting character skills. The campaign structure is familiar, yet well built, not too big or too small, unfolding over 5 acts and about 30 quests. You essentially 'level' together, causing the next part of the main and personal stories to unfold as well as unlocking new skills, areas of the city, and quests. While I've been harsh on some parts of the game, the potential is there and I did enjoy most of my time with it, it's just a shame it's shy of the sum that it's part's could have made.

It's a massive box, bigger than Frosthaven, but comes with nice internal storage. The gameplay is classic dungeon crawler where your characters move about the map and battle with skills and items, without the highly constrained action system of the Gloomhaven series or more abstracted gameplay of campaign games like Sleeping Gods or Isofarian Guard.

BUT THE SCENARIO DESIGN. These are just so good, so interactive and interesting compared to anything else I've ever played. As someone who's spent a little time as a dungeon master and game master for other RPG's, I can recognize all the little tricks of the trade used by the masters of the art (even though I am surely not among them). The individual character design is also fantastic, and every one of them has an interesting story to follow.

Update: I'm about 2/3 through the campaign and not sure if/when I will finish. While the early scenarios were fantastic, later on there were a few more cases of them being a little annoying, and you go through more and more of them without any real progression in terms of character abilities so turns start to feel a little too simple. Overall it's a fantastic game and I think still my favorite in the dungeon crawler genre, just not quite in love with it as I was through the first half dozen scenarios.

I'm not sure where I land with this game. When I first started playing, I was completely floored by the scenario variety and the exploration. The more I play it, though, the more frustrated I become by how incessant combat is, which leaves you with little opportunity to explore the rest of the map. This is especially annoying, since combat is rather repetitive. I think this has to do with poor scaling. At two players, you're constantly inundated with enemies that 3 or 4 people would be able to handle much more easily.

While I appreciate the effort at world-building, there are too many factions to keep track of. The game doesn't tell you all that much about each one of them, and it forces you to make choices about who to support when you have little information to go off of about who is who or what their motivations are. I would prefer to have fewer factions with deeper story and quest lines.

Rules wise, the game is rather fiddly for a system that is based around simple skill checks. I could do without the hook and rope rules, which I have to refresh myself on every time a scenario calls for it. I also don't much like how long the city phase can take, especially when you level up. Even just getting to a scenario can take several steps that could have just been one.

Overall, the highs in this game are very high, but these things are really grating on me. I like a lot of what this game is doing, but it is a very strange mix of overwrought and underbaked.

I've only played the game Solo with 3 characters. This is my spoiler free review.

TLDR: 10/10 would recommend to anyone looking for an amazing story driven RPG campaign with character customization and progression. Scenarios are quick and easy to setup thanks to the scenario booklet (think Jaws of the Lion).

I've completed the main tutorial and the first scenario afterwards and so far it is amazing. The tutorial has 3 scenarios that slowly teach you each mechanic in the game without overwhelming you right out of the gate. The rulebook is also easy to navigate and digest. Setup is very straightforward and easy thanks to the insert trays in the box. Characters can be packed up into their own tray and brough back out to pick up where you left off. Scenarios are easy to setup with majority of them being pages in the scenario booklet (like Jaws of the Lion).

The story is amazing and is made even better with the narration app (which is free btw, looking at you Aeon Trespass). Wanting to explore the entire map often clashes with the timer of the current scenario, which is great. Do you go for more rewards but possibly put yourself at a disadvantage in the next scenario? These risk vs reward moments help give weight behind your choices, but don't leave you feeling like you made a bad choice.

The character progress seems good. Your character slowly levels up as you go through the campaign. Before a scenario begins you slot in 2 actions into your character board from your available pool of actions, giving you a total of 4 primary actions. Items are varied and actually have more use than just a stat card. For example, Hook & rope can be used as a melee/ranged weapon, but also events on the map can call out specific items to give you bonuses. Attempting to climb that cliff, have the hook & rope? +2 success to your roll. Characters also have specializations that you can choose later on that change the role of the character. Do you want to be a water mage or support caster? Tanky Brawler or Geomancer? Great choices all around! Each character also has a special book with side quests and events that take place throughout the game.

Combat is fun and straightforward. Roll dice, look at success/modifiers, that is damage/defense. Monster Automa system is easy to follow and manage. Turns are based off an initiative card which determines heroes and monsters turn in the round.

The game has a fail forward system, which I actually prefer. The one thing I did not like about Gloomhaven was having to repeat a scenario you failed after having just spent 2 hours playing that scenario. Often a scenario will have a countdown timer (Fate cards) which determines the outcome. The scenario instructions explain that the outcome is impacted on how fast you complete the level. It does not tell you what the outcome will be, just that your outcome will be better if you are faster.

The replay value of the game is like any other RPG game, the main story does not change but your choices and actions can provide different outcomes than your first time through. As this is my first playthrough I'm exploring every single section, often at the cost of the overall story (not finishing fast enough). My second playthrough would be with different characters and possibly faster completion.

The App is amazing. You can track everything that you need. Reputation, Party Stats, Keywords, Achievements, Missions that have been completed. The narration is on point as well, with multiple voices for different characters. The ambient music they play during the scenario actually helps set the mood.

Overall, I would recommend this game to anyone that is a fan of Gloomhaven but would rather roll dice for combat and immerse themselves in story both during the scenario and campaign.

The only similar games I played to this are Kingdom Death: Monster and Gloomhaven and both we're kind of a mixed bag for me. I bounced from both of these games kinda quickly. Agemonia on the other hand has gotten it's hooks into me. The slightly lighter tone somewhat helps. Also I quite enjoy how story centered the game feels as a whole. Your own character has a private story and like a TTRPG you can choose to divulge as much or as little as you want to your party members. That with the addition of the companian book really fleshes the world out even though the book itself has a slight Young Adult feel to it than what I would read usually in my spare time. It reminds of some of sword and sandal stories that I used to read and that ain't a bad thing.

The biggest time playing you are still doing missions on a very familiar looking D&D map with miniatures and the like although I've very much liked the streamlining of many of the genres staples. That is not to say that Agemonia lacks depth (or heft - the box is like a lead microwave). It gives you opportunities to strategize and scheme but every time your turn rolls around you still feel like the hero. Your teammates might be defending an entryway from rabid demon bugs as you channel your energies into magical spell to release a captured mage and everyone is easily having a fun time.

The companion app is kinda hit and miss most of the time. It's fun that it's there and the audioscapes for most of the locations feel high quality. On the other hand it has some usability problems. Some stuff isn't as intuitive as I would hope and the need to have it running on my phone all the time with the screen on is kinda a pain in the ass (if I wan't the music to play etc.). Narrated audio book stuff about the character backstories is a good but the world is filled with so many unique names that one really needs to see them in written out to even have a chance to recognize them later on.

The tutorial mission (easily your first play session) is gonna have some bumps if you go by the the books assertion that you shouldn't read anything beforehand. I recommend that you at least leaf through the specific mechanical descriptions of the tutorial before playing because it ain't that much fun spending 15 minutes every half an hour to try to decipher basic game rules when you are really just itching to go. It's not game breaking but still a tad annoying.

Lastly I've got to give praise for the art of Petri Hiltunen who has done most of the non key art stuff in the cards and peripheral materials. I've been a fan of his work for quite some time so it was kind of a given that I would love his work here. Have played 7 scenarios so far (all two-handed solo):

Negatives:
- imperfect knowledge of scenario goals leads to inefficient play and frustrating defeats
- fail-forward makes the defeats sting more, in my opinion
- timers deter exploration

Positives:
+ story integrated into gameplay make for the ultimate roleplaying campaign-in-a-box experience
+ versatile adventure system, varied scenarios
+ challenging difficulty makes for important strategic decisions
+ strong character design

Overall, I think it's great. For my campaign though, I am not committing fully to fail-forward and allowing myself to reset if a scenario goes poorly (particularly early), as I had frustrating experiences with some of the early scenarios, even. I understand the benefits of fail-forward for adding tension and consequence to the game, but at the end of the day it IS a game and when things weren't going my way, I wasn't having fun. I won't waste perfectly good cardboard on bad times when there's a more pleasant alternative available to me, and no human opponent I'd be undercutting. I still feel like there's plenty of tension with deciding whether or not to spend consumables, and making an honest effort to win on a first attempt.

Might consider full fail-forward in a replay of the game, if only because hindsight improves strategic choices by a significant margin, allowing for greater success.

I've played all the tutorial missions on TTS - and am surprised at how much I like the game. The feature/flaw of programmed instruction (ie, teaching a bit at a time) is that one's first impression can be underwhelming. Sure, there isn't a lot of complexity to learn, but there isn't a lot of interesting features either.

All that is to say my first impression was much less than my 4th. The game gets more interesting as more rules are introduced, and I'd be very happy my friend Kickstarted it except he moved away, heh. I'm hoping more scenarios will be made available on TTS.

As to the game, it does a very good job of telling a story (at the price of a LOT of cards on the table, but it's either that or a story book). I like the story points on the board and deciding if I want to go trigger or skip them. The skill tests are often a free action and offer fun choices and ways to maximize equipment.

The combat is reasonably interesting. It's not Gloomhaven, of course, but for dice-based combat, it's reasonably good. From what I understand, as you level up not only do you get the choice of new skills, but you can choose a career path for your character and make them more individual. Leveling up is obviously a big draw in an RPGish game like this.

The game is very streamlined with managing enemies - and in this way it's good that it's not GH with all the focus edge cases - and rolling for attacks, defense, and skill checks is streamlined into a single roll each. It's impressive how the board ends up being much bigger than it first appears. It's not easy to get everywhere and do everything. A neat feature is the way some story points reveal a card which is actually an overlay on the board and changes the board in some way.

All in all this game seems like a winner, and I expect it to be very well received.

Branching storylines with variant endings for all forward (no re-play on fails) scenarios and individual character development and goals should add depth and immersion. Professional artwork, miniatures (playtest shapeways made items were already quite convincing) and writing combined with well tested and suitable mechanics. Rather balanced dice rolling, action choices and hidden scenario elements with combined health/action -pool and scenario lasting injuries are simple and intuitive yet leaving much room for player choice. Comes with app bells and whistles but thankfully plays without that as well. Only played three individual scenarios but seen some of the development material. Should defeat Gloomhaven with ease and will likely replace the rather seen Descent on my table. This can only fail if it is stupidly overpriced or the target audience misses it completely. Very impressive.

This is a fun dungeon crawl game with Cthulhu style monsters and a wild west setting. In general the game is all about making your die rolls. There are some luck mitigation tokens which helps a little, and as you level your character more options are available to you. The game is fully co-op, which I love, and the board is built randomly from a deck of tile cards which is an interesting if messy concept. Player turns are quick, and player abilities are different and interesting. I love how the dungeon populates through random card draws as you explore, so you really never know what lurks behind the next corner.

In terms of components this game leaves something to be desired. The minis are creepy looking, but don't hold up in comparison to similar games. This game also doesn't come with alternate gender hero minis even though you can pick the gender of your character. It also doesn't come with tokens for gold or experience, asking you to write that stuff down on a sheet. There aren't many monster types, and in a single scenario, you will likely see all of them. In terms of playing a campaign, players only get exp when they hit something, which means by the end of a level, different characters will level at different rates depending on how effective they are. The game also asks you to write down your new, leveled up abilities rather than give you cards representing those abilities. While the campaign scenarios themselves flow nicely, the book-keeping step at the end of going to town to spend your stuff is a bit over-complicated. It might not sound like it, but I actually like this game a lot. Getting some expansions helps a lot in terms of getting the game the replayability it's clearly built for.

An odd shortcoming of the game appears to be player turn order. Players who go earlier in the turn have a big advantage in terms of getting more exp points and being able to kill monsters with fun moves. Since it's fully co-op this is perhaps forgivable, but it seems a pity to have players with slow characters watch the fast characters pull off incredible feats and then just do a movement action. The bookkeeping phase when getting back to town is where I wound up losing my enthusiasm for the game. The town has lots of steps and places to go with things to do, which is cute, but it takes a long time, and works out being less fun than a map that would take maybe part of that time. It's also a bad feeling way to start or wind down the night of crawling.

Easily one of the best games I've ever played. The amount of variety in this game is nearly endless and is completely dictated by the player and how they want to play it.
There's a ton of classes, not to mention the ability to purchase more, mix from the other core games, etc. And that's really just the tip of the iceberg as each class, already very unique from one another, has several different starting abilities which can drastically change them from the get go, a personal item which also can change things in a big way, and then you continuously augment your character with an open ended skill tree of 16 abilities unique to your class, of which you'll be able to acquire up to 7 in a given playthrough, alongside any number of items and artifacts. It's a mind boggling amount of customization that will see each campaign play out completely differently driven by both randomness and player choice.
For me, character development is at the forefront of what drives this game's draw, but it also goes hand in hand with progression through the game, and the random and open-ended nature of how each mission plays out. While many will see you stay within the confines of the core box's world, you can just as easily step through a portal into any number of other worlds, even into other core box's. That along is an amazing design decision as it makes any core box or other world you purchase immediately increase the value of everything else you own. More on purchases in a minute.
The whole game is very unforgiving. If you like hard, this game is for you. You're constantly driven by important dice rolls which are hard to pass, and can have lasting negative impacts, often permanent ones. Good planning and character development are important, but you are also at the mercy of the events you encounter, and how well the dice treat you. I can see these elements bothering some people, but to me it makes the game come alive and pits you against the board in a desperate way that few other games manage to capture.
In my opinion the story is on the weaker side, with the setting and ambience being much more persuasive than the flavor text. That's fine, as I feel like the game is mostly just dressing to drive the fun combat and character progression. And it's certainly not absent lore and narrative, it's just not the thing that stands out.
Enemy design is also very unique and varied, and continues in the game's tradition of difficulty. Enemies grow in power alongside you, gaining elite abilities and eventually appearing in their "brutal" version as your party gets high enough levelled. Threat cards (Which dictate which enemies you'll be facing in any given attack) are well balanced though, determined by how many characters are in your party, though you'll occasionally be instructed to take threat cards above your level.
As far as ease of learning and player count - for my group, 3-4 characters felt very well balanced versus the amount of enemies you're faced with and good flow of the game once everyone had learned the rules. I think two is probably too few and if only two people were playing I'd likely suggest each person play two characters. Six, likewise, might be too many, especially game length wise. You'd also immediately be facing high threat cards which are very challenging, alongside epic threat cards (I.e. the biggest bosses or largest groups of enemies possible) as early as your first mission. I think this is doable, and probably even fun provided everyone was familiar with the rules, but may well require a very specific party composition to have a fair chance of not being disastrous.
While not strictly related to the quality of the core box itself, it's important to note that there are a huge number of addons that can be bought to add variety and replayability to your game. These range from enemy packs, full-on mission expansions, other worlds, and small things like card packs which provided different mission additions (E.g. the Long Arm of the Law card pack that adds specific law objectives to any law character or additional personal items to draw from when creating a character).
These packs are a double edged sword though, and probably my biggest critique of the game. Yes, most of them are high quality, and fantastic characters, interesting new worlds, or amazing boss fights to the game... But if we're being honest, a LOT of this should have just been included from the get go. The value of the core box is rather less than the price tag compared to other games. The core boxes tend to retail for 100-120 when not on sale, come with the main mission packs plus a few random ones, an anemic 4 heroes, and not a ton of monsters which doesn't even include a really big bad guy. All of them, as far as I know, only come with a Large "mini" boss type creature rather than the big bad XXL models. It's just not what it could be. Is it still a great game? Absolutely. Is it a much better game if you go out and augment what comes with a core box with extra classes, monsters, etc? Yes. Those additions take it from great game to one of the best gaming experiences available. Should a large amount of that extra content have just come included? Yes. And there's little doubt in that. If you compare the core box's content with other similarly priced games, it's hard to arrive at any other conclusion.
So here's my conclusion: For anyone who likes character building dungeon crawling campaign-driven games with coop, this game is very hard to pass up. But beware that if you want to get the most out of your experience, you'll be hunting down and buying several expansions.

Really fun dungeon crawler with a cowboys vs. Cthulhu theme. As for drawbacks - the game is fiddly and needs a large table as well as you have to assemble the minatures. Character advancement adds progression. (I use the fan made Companion app to keep track of purchased items).

From a gameplay standpoint, after playing a lot of the scenarios (in order, not randomly), I felt like I could kick some butt and take names but bad rolls could still doom me. Besides the base game I purchased the Enemies of the Void pack, which adds a tough melee monster and a ranged monster.

I play solo with 2 characters and there's a lot of management of inventory. The number of monsters on the board sometimes borders on silly with 12 spiders, 6 tentacles, etc.

If you like thematic dungeon crawlers, this is a good one. If you're looking for a gateway game, this probably isn't it.

Update: I've moved this to my donate/give away pile as the games are too long and too repetitive for the experience. If you get a lot of the expansions the saminess of the game improves. I'm still glad I bought this and played it.

Update (2025): And I bought it again and it's a fun sandbox game. I'm probably going to end up painting it. I appreciate the gonzo world and that you can tailor the experience to what you want.

Of all the dungeon crawlers I have played, this is definitely one of my favorites. It suffers from the same problem as many of the others though, which is simply an abundance of rules, exceptions, checks, tokens, cards, etc. By the time you have hauled out hundreds of cards, chits, minis, tiles, setup the game, and explained the 35-40 pages of rules, an hour has gone by. For the rest of the session you are constantly checking rules exceptions and trying to track a dozen different exceptions to these rules such as special monster abilities that change based on various factors.

On the plus side it tells a better story than Gloomhaven, which feels far too sterile, or Sword and Sorcery which tries too hard. I would recommend this if you are ready for a strong commitment. Playing it at least weekly, and doing so for months on end (there is plenty of content to support it) would be a worthwhile effort. This would eliminate rules checks after a time and create setup and tear down efficiencies. For me, I prefer to spread my limited gaming time around amongst many good games vs committing to something like this.

Fast becoming one of my favorite games, in tandem with Swamps of Death, Forbidden Fortress, Frontier Town, and a few mission packs. This game is the perfect blend of ongoing rpg/solo dungeon exploration with narrative generation from the various (and rich), card-based elements (geography of the mine, other world, encounters, danger, monsters, gear, artifacts, and events). Character advancement is satisfying and story generation from the game is excellent. I have only played this solo with 2 and 3 characters, and it is at last the answer for my quest to recreate the 1st edition AD&D solo dungeon experience (and surpasses it). There is no game in my collection that is as likely to stay on the basement game table for 4 months at a time as this. The stories from SoB sessions live on in the mind and it's interesting how the open-ended nature of the tables for travel and town expand the sense of possibility in the world beyond the cards and tiles. Another strong aspect of the game is how you can customize your version of a weird-west world (or east meets west) with careful selection of expansion content. It all fits, so it is only a matter of choosing the thematic flavor that you want your characters to inhabit.

This is a high rating from me. Is this a dice chucker, sure. Tactical, not really. But the theme oozes out everywhere, and the leveling aspects are fun.
You can really get into the characters as they grow, mutate, and save one another. I highly suggest playing with four people, although you don't need a steady group. A player group of diverse personalities will make this game great.

Main gripes are that the minis require glue and don't fit quite right in the box. Mechs vs Minions had great minis and a way to box them up quickly and safely.
This game really needs the expansions as well; there aren't enough cards and enemy types to keep the game interesting for long.
Bluntly, SoB requires some house rules and added story elements to keep it alive. You can find fan-made rules and story additions easily on-line. For example, I added complex enemy reactions and lowered enemy health, because otherwise the game was too repetitive. You'll also need to print out player pages like an RPG to monitor stats and equipment. If you're alright with all of that, then this is an excellent Ameritrash experience. If you want a great game out of the box, you may not enjoy this game for long.
Lastly, sessions can go pretty long, so having a game table to walk away from is helpful.

If Wild West gunslingers fighting dimensional monsters feels good to you, then this delivers very nicely. I had to rent this to be sold on it, but now I plan to collect many expansions. This game will either match your personality, or it won't.

Here in City of ancient core set, you have 4 different classes of hero with their own assets and specialties. All classes enable a very interesting game and can be played without being dependent on another one. Another originality is the hero you play can improve with the experience you get from your adventure and becomes stronger with time, but the good point is that characteristics of the enemies evaluate also depending on the level of your hero posse! So you never become too strong and you can also get some injuries or madness that you will keep if you do not heal them between each mission. In fact the system introduces rules for sanity loss if you encounter horrors and your hero may also may suffer of mutations due to corruption damage (I will let you the surprise). A “time counter” is also introduced to keep you hero posse under stress with possible failure if you take too much time to visit and scavenge instead of focusing on your goals! The only problem you may face is that this game need a lot of space to set up an play and it is good to have a dedicated place for playing this game.

All in all, this is of the greatest game I ever played.

Intro: Joel Thomas

Kickstarter Impressions:

I have played Flying Frog Productions games before and even own Last Night on Earth and have not been very impressed. Decent games but I felt their rules and production quality were a bit shoddy.

I went into the Kickstarter skeptical, but in the end the setting really drew me in. So unique and interesting. I backed it and backed enough to get just about everything they offered.

Intial Impressions:

The two starter boxes were huge! Everything seemed fairly good quality and well packaged. No damages and no immediate quality issues.

The Components:

Models - The models were plentiful but a bit low quality compared to what I'm used to. I would say they are higher quality than the average board game but lower quality than the average miniatures game. The decisions for the sprues and how models were cut were pretty amature. Many places are difficult to clean and the models require a lot of extra work as multiple pieces must be glued at the same time because many limbs need to be placed inside the joining torso. The models once built have many gaps that require filling and sometimes don't even fit together right. Very frustrating.

Tokens and map tiles - Excellent! All tiles and tokens feel good in your hand and appear that they can be used without fear of utter destruction.

Cards - A little thin (similiar to their other cards in games) with a coating that leaves a bit of texture, but overall very usable. The art is all nicely done and cards convey theme and information without issue.

Odds and ends - Rulebooks are paper books and work just fine. The dice are very average as well.The character boards are a little lack luster, but they get the job done.

Da Rulez - Pretty good. I would say 90% of the game is accounted for with very little question. A couple clear ups here and there would have been nice and some term consistency would have gone a long way, but I do think the game can be learned, played and taught using only the rulebook.

Gameplay - Very impressive. They managed to create a dungeon crawler that works with the Old American West setting and the Cthulhu Mythos feel. The game is not only about combat (while it is a large component) and a lot of memorable scenes come from the non-combat encounters.

As long as one person has read the rulebook thoroughly, up to five (with both sets) others can sit down fairly ignorant to the game and pick it up fast. A lot of team work is invovled and there is a bit of a learning curve that can punish a team that doesn't take the game at the right pace.

Bottom Line - This is an impressive game that, while not perfect, shows that with a good idea, passionate, skilled people and the drive to make it fun, any idea can be a great board game.

2020 edit: After taking all of my components and putting it all into the game I found the game terribly unwieldy and dull. Some terrible customer service after a kickstarter has made me swear off Shadows and Flying Frog forever.

Without any expansions, the SoB 'system' is a fairly bland set of rules that relies heavily on dice rolls, random events. Heavily thematic, but ultimately a pretty boring design that isn't going to scratch the puzzle-solving itch.

Combat doesn't involve very many tactical decisions - line of sight, facing and terrain don't really exist. Combat is also largely a matter of rolling, rolling, rolling ... The monsters don't really have any interesting attacks, like area of effect, mind control, etc. Basically, they move as close as they can, then swat at you. Most of the scenarios included in the base sets are samey and dull.

Scenarios usually have a built in timer - but that timer may or may not advance, randomly. That means scenarios can easily be too hard or too easy. A pretty lazy design.

I guess the plus side is, that given how loose the system is, you can easily add house-rules and it wont disrupt what is ultimately a pretty unbalanced game system anyhow. Want to make your own equipment? Go for it. Want to make your own monsters? Go for it. Want to trash the "hold back the darkness" rolls and use a deck of cards, go for it ... you get the idea.

The reason I like the game is that developing your characters over the course of several missions is fun and engaging. You level them up, get new abilities and acquire new equipment. There is a sense of adventure always wondering what you are going to come across next.

I also like the various miniatures/monsters - I like to paint them (and even have a couple on display) - and they look cool on the table.

The game is also a good platform for "role-playing", in the traditional sense where you take on a persona and act it out. Lots of strange and wacky things can happen to your character, like growing a tail, so there is plenty of inspiring material to work with.

Expansions also come and help save the day a bit. Expansion monsters like the Void Sorcerers add a spell deck and special abilities not seen before. Some monsters also act in more interesting and tactically challenging ways. The 'other worlds' like Cynder and Treddera add all kinds of other tactical considerations, like terrain and area of effect weapons.

Here is why I should really love Shadows of Brimstone:

Lovecraftian horror + Wild West as an interesting mix of theme, dungeon crawling, different characters with different abilities, characters gaining experience which lets them grow, equipment and loot, the right amount self-aware humour, miniatures, storytelling elements, roleplaying elements and a modular board system for exploration.

Yet, what brings this game so much down from a potential 9 or even 10 is the game's glaring game design imbalances and boring combat system. The combat system is hopelessly outdated and appears amateurish in design, especially when compared to other modern dungeon crawlers like Descent: Journeys in the Dark (Second Edition) or Claustrophobia.

Positioning does not matter most of the time in combat and the heroes are usually trying to make a stand between the narrow part that connects two map tiles to give the enemies less room and opportunities to attack, as most monsters can only attack in melee combat and will directly charge at the players' characters. Outrunning the enemies does not work, as most enemies are equally fast or even faster with a fixed movement value, while all players need to roll for movement with a 6-sided die -- so there is a always a high variance present in movement for the players.

This high variance also applies to wounds caused in combat or by events, which can be extremely frustrating. The randomness of a D6 with results between 1-6 are already swingy enough, but the game often even goes beyond that. One event card even deals D6 (1-6) hits with each of them dealing 3 damage -- that a random variance span of 3-36 potential damage !

The fixed movement and defense values for enemies are beneficial to the flow of the game and a good design decision, as it streamlines the game a lot, but sadly, the good and clever game design decisions for combat already end here. I don't understand why the designers did not implement some custom dice to at least add some interesting layer to the combat system.

Another huge problem is that the damage dealt by the players is again determined by rolling D6s or D8s, which again results in a way too high variance span and dependency on pure luck. In the end, the game boils down to one huge, brainless and boring dice fest.

The roll for movement aspect for the players is a huge step backwards in modern game design. Granted, there is an optional rule which allows players to work with a fixed movement value, but they still need to roll a die to determine if they get 1 Grit (which is one of the game's resources) at the beginning of their turn.

Speaking of optional rules, this game deserves praise for offering a few indeed nice modular optional rules, which can make the game a bit more thematic, complex and difficult.

What is less appealing to most board game players is the fact that this game requires a lot of time for the miniature assembly. Veteran miniature game players won't have any problems with that, as they have the routine, patience and the required tools at hand, but this can be a real problem for pure board game players. In fact, I have heard from many players that they immediately ignored or even resold the game the moment they realised that the miniatures are not preassembled. This is arguably an overreaction, as the miniatures are relatively easy to assemble and the publisher even released miniature assembly tutorial videos for every miniature on YouTube. Still, it requires some tools and quite some time.

Each starter box features 4 different heroes and each of them has 4 unique skill trees with a total of 16 skills. Every hero also starts with one random unique personal item and one out of three unique starting skills, so the replay value and possibilities for character customisations are really great.

Still, it's disappointing that a game for 1-4 players offers exactly 4 characters, which means that all heroes are always present in a game with 4 players without giving the players some freedom to choose. An additional 5th character would have been really great here.

Some players might also have a problem with the necessary book keeping of this game, as every player is required to have a piece of paper and a pencil at hand, writing most of the character's progress down (experience points, gained abilities, collected gold, ect.). The fan community of this game started to solve this problem by creating and printing their own cards for gold values, experience points and abilities, which can be a great addition to this game, but it also results in more costs to an already expensive game.

The game's difficulty scaling is handled very well in a very streamlined way, but the game suffers like most heavily thematic and dice-focused games from an imperfect balance, which players are probably even expecting from a game like this.

The game has without question heart, but sadly no brains. Most artworks are hand-drawn and really great. The miniature quality is...okay. The amount of cards and tokens is great. The adventure book offers enough to keep the players busy for a long time. The soundtrack could have been left out to lower the price of the game.

The components and details for a good game are all present, but they don't connect in an interesting and exciting way which could impress, as the game design is too naive and the rules are too messy.

The most common positive comment about this game by reviewers and player is, that the town visit phase right after the dungeon crawling is the best part -- and this is arguably true, but also a statement which clearly highlights this game's huge problem.
If players are more interested and are having more fun in the game's indeed very nicely detailed shopping phase (which has parallels to pen & paper roleplaying games) instead of actually exploring the mines and other worlds while fighting enemies, then something went wrong during the development of this game, especially because players are of course spending most of their time outside of towns.

I was expecting this game would at least earn an 8/10 from me, but it's sadly just too messy and random -- and as a result: boring and frustrating.

Neutral:
* Sold as a fast-paced game which is not true
* Cards quality is on the low side; sleeves are not an option but a necessity here

Verdict:

If the phrase "Good idea, bad execution" could be a game, it would be Shadows of Brimstone.

The first time I saw this game, I was immediately fascinated with the theme, art and most importantly the idea of the random dungeons, town visits and multiple event types. Unfortunately after a few months of me trying to gaslight myself into liking the game, it's time to admit that the randomness is an illusion, and ends up not mattering, there's almost no real exploration in the dungeons, the combat lacks tactics and boils down to chucking dozens of dice for every single thing and basically every single part of the design has stupid problems.

1 - Box and components - The problems start with the box itself. It's awkward coffin style and huge size make it almost impossible to store easily. It's way too long, so it pops of the edge of almost all furniture, and if you try to store it sideways, you'd need a 47cm high shelf, which is too long for most furniture. FF have also neglected to make a horizontal artwork for sideways storing.
The cardboard of the box itself is way too flimsy for the size, weight and high price of the game. The first time I opened it, the components themselves had damaged the inside of the lid.
They've made a weird choice to leave a whole bunch of space beneath the insert to store the punch boards, which makes storing the tiles and tokens a pain. You can always store them beneath the insert, but pulling it our every time you play is a pain and could damage the weak cardboard.
The insert itself is flimsy and can't hold the components well. There's no specific space for the tiles, no designated place for the minis or the tokens, and while there are 3 spaces for the cards, they've not included separations for the different card types in order to find them easily, which should be expected for the price of the game.
- The minis are a pain. You have to put them together yourself, which some people may like, but there are a few design issues even with them. Like for example, the bases of their feet are too small and often not flat, which makes it a pain to stick the minis to the base. Also for most of them, the connections that you have to cut are right at the bottom of their feet, which leaves a protrusion that you have to peel in order for them to stick right to the base.

2 - Randomness in the dungeon exploration - I just love the idea of having a random deck of tiles, drawing cards, having random exits and events. Unfortunately the way these are implemented in the game only create the illusion of exploration and randomness, while not really mattering. Let me explain.
- When exploring a new tile, you draw a card and it tells you which tile to put which way, and how many exits it has. So far so good. But which tile you put doesn't matter past how many open spaces it has for you to move to exit it (after you level up, you'd probably get more move points, so you end up being able to exit all of them in 1 turn anyways) or combat (which ends up not mattering, as the enemies are so many, and have so much move points, that you almost always end up fighting near the entrance of the tile, as they just swarm you). Every tile offers the same gameplay experience. Some of the tiles have interesting art, like bone piles, books and etc., but unfortunately you can't interact with any of it. You can't even scavenge when you see a barrel or something, going by the rules, none of objects are actually interactive. So the artwork of the tiles is meaningless and their size doesn't matter for combat, as the enemies swarm you and blocking the entrance is the best "tactic" anyways. How about the exits? They're pointless.
Let's say for example that a room has 3 exits. They're randomly determined by the exploration tokens or dice. So what's the difference if I choose to go straight, to the left or right? There is none... As exploration is determined by the tokens and tile cards, and you keep drawing from the same pile no matter which exit you choose, the only difference is which direction the dungeon expands to. This could've been fixed really easily by splitting the exploration tokens and map deck when multiple exits are available, but I'm going by the rulebook, as it's not my job to design the game. The way it is, there's no reason to backtrack or indeed to explore.
- How about the encounters? Well, they are random, but the base game comes with too few of these, so by your second mission, you'll start seeing repeats. That being said, some of them are pretty interesting.
- Threat cards. These decide how many and what kind of enemies you fight. In concept this is an amazing idea, but unfortunately all enemies behave the same. Combat boils down to being rushed by mobs, chucking dice to see if you hit and deal damage or the enemy hits or you defend, while keeping track of multiple enemy skills. Most skills boil down to stuff like "on a 6 deal 3 hits" or "deal 2 hits when starting on the same tile", "get void venom on hit", "get more combat or better to hit ratio". They don't modify the enemy behavior or fights in interesting ways, so they end up just being more stuff to track and keep in mind, while not adding much to the fun or tactics.
Let me ask you this. What's the difference between fighting a spider or a giant monstrosities? NONE. They all just rush you. The only difference is how much damage they deal, their to hit ratios and how many dice you throw.

3 - Combat - I've already talked about this, but I have to say that the combat is absolutely abysmal. There are almost no tactics or in fact point to using a different strategy. Fighting boils down to the enemies spawning, and if they have a higher initiative them surrounding you or staying in front of you, if you've closed the exit with 2 heroes, which you will always do, because if you don't, you'd get surrounded by 5 to 8 enemies at once. Their movement value is so high, that they almost always have enough movement to get to you from the other end of the tile, so you always end up in the same situation. What if you have a higher initiative? Well, then you just stay in the entrance, so that you create a choke point, otherwise you get surrounded. So it ends up not really mattering, past who attacks first. Oh, and the enemies can also ambush you... so they just surround you at the entrance again.
- The enemy AI is... where is it? they all act the same (although there are enemies with ranged attacks, but they just target using range). Firstly each enemy chooses a random target, which is annoying, because you always get swarmed with many of them. Then they rush, or attack if they have a ranged attack. If you're solo and get surround on a 2 space wide entrance by 5 enemies, you can just kill the 3 on the back, and the rest of the enemies will not move behind you again. If the enemy is adjacent and they can target you, they will not move to make way for their buddies, and most models don't move past each other. Anyways, the AI boils down to choosing a random hero and rushing. That's it.
- How about the actual fighting? Is it any good? Well, it goes the following way. The enemies surround you, you throw around 5 to 25 dice to see if they hit you, then you throw 3 to 15 to see if you defend, then you throw additional dice for cover (only in towns and some expansions with ranged enemies) or armor that you have. Then you attack and roll to hit, then roll for damage. Unfortunately character skills and items rarely add interesting elements to combat. They're mostly things like +1 hit per combat, or 1 reroll. Ranged and melee weapons are also fundamentally the same, so no matter what you do, you end up chucking dice with the only thing you can do being choosing which enemy to attack, or if you want to use a side bag token.

4 - Towns, roll charts and travels. I really like the idea of getting travel events between missions and towns and the events you get when going to town locations. They add interesting story elements to a play. I've got nothing bad to say about them.
- Towns. The first issue I have is the Hotel or Camp mechanic. While staying at the camp, you don't pay at all, but can get a bad event. While in the hotel you pay, but it's safe. Sounds interesting, but unfortunately the Hotel is so cheap, you really have no motivation to stay at the camp. This is a small issue, but worth mentioning.
Every town location has stuff to buy. I loved the idea when I first got the game, but there's a pretty big issue with this. FF have decided to not offer cards for the town equipment. Which means you have to write everything you buy down on paper and track it that way. For a game this expensive, some more cards would be welcome. Overall I enjoy the town experience.

5 - Holding back the darkness and tracking skills and gear. The Holding back the darkness mechanic is interesting in concept, but ends up being needlessly limited, random and just adds more stuff to track. Given the random nature of combat, you can end up either quickly wiping off hordes of enemies by hitting and rolling high for damage, or being stuck not being able to kill some spiders for multiple turns in a row. The darkness is set up in such a way, that it will move on most turns, so you may end up not being able to kill weak enemies, and losing do to bad rolls and not bad decisions on your part. It also adds Darkness and growing dread cards to play, which leads me to my next point...

6 - WAY too much to track. Here an example from my current playthrough a few games in, of everything I have too keep track during a dungeon run on a combat.
My character and his innate skills on the sheet, the skill form his starting item, his card skill, the 6 items I've bought from town, which are written down on paper, the 3 items I found from a dungeon and carry with me, the upgrades I've installed, My horse which gives me grit if I have none, the darkness cards that've popped up, the enemy skills and the 2 elite skills they have, which are written down below their sheet and marked with number tokens, Mutations and madness and injury effects, modifiers from the world you are in.
Due to the nature of the modifiers, most of them add to some of the stats, add xp an etc. Given how many things there are to track, what's the chance you'd remember all of them in a fight?

7 - Content in the box. Given that this game is supposed to be an endless random dungeon generator, what comes in the box, that is quite expensive for the content, is not enough at all. The enemies are few and behave the same, the tiles play the same, the events are not enough to create surprises past a few games and the classes are only 4. The gear and artifact cards however are a good quantity. You don't get them that often, so they're enough to be fresh for a long time.
This game is DESIGNED TO NEED EXPANSIONS. It's no surprise there are advertisements for expansions on the game BOX, in a catalog in the box and in the adventure book. The other boxes come with a whole bunch of cool looking stuff, and if you want to have fun with this game, you need them and to spend a whole bunch of money.

8 - Every single thing in the game is decided by chucking dice. From the Hold back the darkness, to choosing a mission, to movement, to attacks, to defense, to how many enemies spawn (on p dice cards), to which hero the enemies target, to which skills enemies have, to which exits are closed, if an enemies goes to cover, if an enemy moves away if he's ranged and adjacent to you, to how much rewards you receive, to events, to travel, town events and etc.
It's no exaggeration to say you'd throw hundreds of dice each combat. 1 of the enemies in the base box attacks with 5x dice per model and on a 6 it counts as 3 hits. So if you're surrounded by 8x of them, you have to throw 40 dice for their attacks on you only, then about an average of 20/25 for defense per turn. The other enemies aren't so bad, but the fact a turn like this could happen is just silly.

9 - Things I enjoy. While I've been incredibly negative about the game, there are some things I really enjoy. The overall art style is great and reminds me somewhat of the fallout video games. The monster models are great. I enjoy visiting towns and the random events I get. I enjoy the mutations system. Some of the missions are pretty interesting. The idea of going to other worlds through portals is generally amazing, and the worlds themselves are visually interesting. HEXCRAWL is an amazing fan expansion, and the people that made it deserve a lot of credit.

In conclusion I have to unfortunately say this game is objectively bad. I really enjoy some of it on a surface emotional level, but when looking at the design itself, almost every single part of it has problems. It almost seem like the game part of the box was an afterthought, like it was fast thrown together without much thought. It gives the illusion of depth and randomness, but in reality it's meaningless. The best example of this is the random exit mechanic. It seems cool, but given the nature of the exploration token stack, it doesn't matter which exit you take. If just a bit more thought was put into the idea, the designer would realize the way he's made it makes it so exploration is meaningless and it could be fixed by something as simple as splitting the tokens in half for every fork in the path.

If you enjoy having a lot of cool stuff, this game is great. If you're fine with designing your own rules, this is a great facilitator for it. If you love chucking dice, this is the game.

If you're looking for a dungeon crawler with tactical combat, deep exploration and meaningful random dungeon generation... This isn't it.

Absolutely nailed the aesthetic of the PC game, but someone else summed it up well: in the end you feel like you're doing a lot of the work that the computer would do for you. (Slay the Spire board game feels like that sometimes, but it did a better job.) It's pretty complicated, and very "weighty." But it was fun, and as a big fan of the PC game, I enjoyed the style and loved that it wasn't QUITE as deadly.
Like Slay the Spire, this was built with a campaign in mind, and the "save" progress works well. It still takes a while to set up / break down each time, which absolutely adds up over many sessions. As mentioned, you're far less likely to die, which is a feature: again, just like StS, the "rouge-like" elements of the board game are much harder to stomach given the exponentially longer time commitment. The style oozes through each element of the game, and you must still be prepared to face one disheartening obstacle after another. Unfortunately, like other "campaign" games, we managed to complete it once and then the weight of having to do that all again had us put it down. (By contrast, StS has us playing again and again.) Also, like soooo many complex games, the instructions left much to be desired. You will also likely house rule it if you get into it. I would have given this an "8" based on the fun factor but had to take a point away just for the miss when it came to design and manual.
If you're a fan of the PC game it's definitely worth a pickup, and you'll definitely get your money's worth from the campaign, but it might not be something you go back to again and again.

Comments: Darkest Dungeon: The Board Game is a thematic cooperative game about dice rolling, scenarios/campaign, storytelling and variable players powers. The ideia is that players will use their characters, items and abilities to complete the goals of the scenarios, gaining loot and improve their skills and increasing their levels along the way.

The game is centered around a fight with the Bosses, and to get to it players must face several dungeons in order to be able to battle the big baddy - and is quite hard to achieve this. Players can end a dungeon early, to prevent deaths, but don't gain the XP, only the loot. Death of a character is final (but players can still use the earned XP to improve the new character). Being deeply thematic, Darkest Dungeon should be difficult, with damaging, stress and conditions staying with the character, even after the end of a dungeon - only by using (and paying) in the village, de mercenaries will be able to recover somewhat after a delve - there is a single chance to rest in the dungeon itself and, of course, some characters are able to heal. A campaign lasts for 11 dungeons - but is normal for players not be able to finish, if going strictly by the rules, with limitation of characters to use.

Darkest Dungeon is first and foremost made to be true to the source material - the video-game from which it came. But this do mean, some odd choices when regarding the medium of a board game: the quite dark components (boards and art, to the point the stress track on the player board to be nearly invisible; or to see what a monster is like and if a enemy should be in the front or back of the line - both are good eye tests). Another feature that doesn't fit my taste is having to set up several battle maps, which does takes away from the pace of the game; at least the maps aren't too complicated to make, but alongside learning the new IA of monsters, features, etc, is a hassle that happens over and over.

Unlike many of its KS ilk, Darkest Dungeon do have players aids, in the form of two cards explaining some icons and dice symbols: but these are very limited, leaving a lot out, which leads to many searches in the manual in order to understand some effects and conditions. Far from ideal, yet, as long as people by KS for pretty miniatures, why waste time and effort planning a good player aid, right? The manual is also lacking in quality, with some elements having no clear explanation, to the point when looking for more information during a boss fight, e reached a place that said to check the Step 3 of monsters actions, but the manual only goes to the Step 2. A conundrum indeed.

Difficulty, at the start, is on par with the digital version: enemies are tough, and just a couple of hits can take a hero down - there are the saving rolls, in order to keep being alive, even as taking new hits; but I saw both people surviving half of a dungeon going by these rolls; while others died in the first opportunity: fate really does not care. Choosing the abilities of the heroes, and a proper group, in order to use the most of the 4 positions, and being able to continue functioning well even when being moved by the monsters also counts a lot in order to explore the dungeons without more issues. Darkest Dungeon avoided what often happens wtih games in which characters can increase in level and abilities: as it is much tougher to keep the balance (is way harder to test variations of skills, teams, etc), and normally things fall off the wagon, usually becoming way too easy. I didn't really feel this in Darkest Dungeon, but what I did was that characters aren't really balanced, with some being way stronger than others, and, of course, a stronger set of heroes will make the play easier than using a weaker one.

In Darkest Dungeon the difficult ramps up when the enemies of level II come, and the same for level III, as while the skills get better, life and dodge increase, they are mostly on par with the increase of the monsters. Darkest Dungeon doesn't really escapes the D&D paradox: if you increase in level but the monster do also in the same rate, are you really getting stronger? There are enemies which can one shot you in the 1st level, and there are those who can do that in the 3rd level. You get more resistences, and but the enemies also deal more effects; and so on.

Luck have a big role, as basically all attacks are rolled, with modifiers from dodge, effects (buffs, marks, etc), darkess, and more. At least most attacks have a much greater chance of hitting, in normal conditions. Yet, rolling 9, 10, in sequence (in a d10), can be frustrating, as the best way to keep the heroes alives, is unliving the monsters as soon as possible. And, going by this, the turn order is also random to a point, as a deck shows if one or another will act; and as it sounds, if a side acts three, four times in a row, well, the other will have a lot of problems to deal with. Furthermore, there are dice rolls for items carried into the dugeon, and also minor encounters in the corridors; plus blind draws from the curious deck (having a torch helps here); and, and, and, as there is a metric ton of random elements built in the mechanics. In spite of this, as mentioned, good battle plan and proper team, will push the group forward even over some twists of fate.

A strange thing that happened was the realization that our characters had more XP then we could spend! As in spite having the XP, you need enough days in the village in order to be able to use the area that uses XP to increase level and upgrade skill cards. By the end, we had plenty of XP, and nothing to do with it, which felt like this part wasn't really well developed enough, as I have never seen something like it in any of the dozen campaigns played: the standard is to create a compleated path, from start to finish, to allow the players to develop their characters by the use of the hard earned XPs. For instance, if by mere random chance, players aren't at a point they should when entering level III, it would be placed a check that would allow spending XP without the need of using a particular building, or that more than one person could use it per day, etc. What as a designer you really should not want is to give the players the frustrating feel of wasted opportunity: is like giving the players the most awesome weapons, but no way to use them.

I could add that money was close to have the same issue, yet, it was easy to see that, for money, we were simply very, very lucky: high rolls on chests allowed for an early development of the village, which, in turn, allowed us to better put the money to use; and with the destiny still smilling upon us, we did got to a point we had money to place into retirement funds, as we just couldn't use it all on the trips to the village. Still, as I said, with chests that only give white dies, and bad rolls, the lack of money could be a major issue throughout the campaign,

Was also not expected that the corridors were way tougher for us to handle: the constant increase in stress and lost of life was harder to deal than a room with combat. We welcome a battle as a way to heal and get rid of stress. Don't know if this is the proper idea, but it was what happened. I am also not aware of many situations in which one would prefer to roll the two black dice (for corridor events) instead of gaining 1 stress and rolling just 1; but I guess it doesn't hurt to have the option.

Overall, Darkest Dungeon: The Board Game was a very mixed bag. It has some good elements that we enjoyed - the effective need for cooperation and coordination; the variation on heroes, and their skills and builds; etc -; coupled with many others that do lead to believe 1 year or so for more development and tests, from the production to the gameplay, would serve well - I know that the delivery was already very late, but can't shake the feel that, at a point there was a meeting in which someone said: "We do need some months more to iron out some of the issues I said in the report I sent last week." With the reply: "No, we can't. We are already way overdue. It is playable? Yes? Well, so give the call to print, and lets move on." While is possible to have fun with it (and we did, to a level), I can't really recommend it.

Initial thoughts after learning the tutorial setup:

------------------------------------------

I'm still digging into this one but have some thoughts based around components and play so far. My first (and probably biggest) criticism are the terrible player boards, specifically the stress tracker. What a terrible design choice as you have a tiny, fiddly, cardboard piece to keep track of your ever changing stress. For one, this thing is gonna get knocked so many times and you will lose track of how much stress you have. Secondly, you can BARELY see the different spots to place it as the board is extremely dark; make sure you play in a very well lit area. This really needed to either be double layered or at the very least, the spaces need to be highlighted. OR, another option would be to include clips to keep track. You could easily clip something to the top of the board to make this better and that would actually be cost efficient as well.

Beyond that, so far I am liking most of the rest of the components. The minis look great and the cards are nice. The tiles are huge and have good color and designs that are reminiscent of the video game. Overall, the components are excellent with the notable exception of the stress tracker.

The gameplay is...interesting. Although there are a couple things that I'm struggling to see the point of, so far. The initial roll for resources seems kinda silly as each player rolls 2 dice to add to the initial pool of team resources to start the dungeon. Why not just have one person roll all the dice? It seems like added steps to make the game feel more involved than it really is. That point is minor and can easily be adjusted as noted.

However, when you start exploring each player will be rolling these dungeon dice that mostly have negative effects, and you will be doing that quite often as you explore each room. This is where you will discard those resource dice to negate the nasty stuff from the dungeon dice. This part seems silly to me as well since you basically will discard the majority of the dice right at the beginning (because, why wait?) and then after that just have to take the nastiness. I might be missing something here strategy-wise (and probably am since it's my first learning game) but that just stuck out to me.

The battles are pretty cool though! I love how you have a board to show position kinda like the videogame but also have a dungeon tile to show the 3D representation of it. Placement and abilities are very position restricted which makes the battles pretty strategic. The enemies have a simple, random "roll a d10" AI system which seems to work well. The way damage works is pretty confusing at first but once you sit and think it over for a few minutes it becomes clearer. Overall, I had a fun learning experience with the combat.

The tutorial itself is decent. It skips over some bits and pieces of the gameplay to try and make it clearer but also did forget to explain some things as well such as the "resting" and how it works. It basically just tells you to spend extra resources to heal up but doesn't go into detail on exactly HOW, like how much for each etc. It also needs better structure and formatting. For example, the paragraphs listing how many dice you roll for exploring vs scouting. It has bolded that you only roll ONE dice if you already scouted the area BUT it puts that part AFTER the paragraph that literally tells you to roll TWO dice when exploring. And it makes this mistake like 3 more times through the tutorial. On one hand I appreciate that they are reiterating the instruction to really nail home what to do, BUT, on the other hand for pete's sake move that bolded instruction BEFORE the other paragraph. I sat there and rolled two dice for each of my 4 characters and then started going through the motions of the negative effects and then when I read on I realized I was only supposed to roll ONE die each. So, back to the terrible stress tokens and moving those back and forth constantly, which really "stresses" why those tokens need to be better than they are. You use them a TON.

Anyway, so far it's looking pretty good overall. I am keen on getting back to the game and starting up the campaign to see how it is. I'll pop back in here with updated thoughts as I make progress through it. No rating for now.
