Update after first dungeon run:

------------------------------------------------

Made my way through my first dungeon run and it was alot of fun! I think the provision dice are a bit better than when playing in the tutorial. They just felt more interesting since you are rolling those exploration dice multiple times depending on where/how you move around on the dungeon square. I like how you know what the rooms are BUT you don't know where they are placed so that gives the game a bit of push your luck if you want to go exploring down that hallway or not and waste valuable provision dice resources.

I really enjoyed the battles. It's not like a typical dungeon crawler where you either lay out all the dungeon tiles and slowly explore them or keep laying additional tiles as you explore. When you encounter a battle, you just draw a card from the room deck to determine WHICH single tile to lay down and you will stay on that, super large, tile the entire battle. The tiles are big enough and have enough spaces to move around to, to at least give some tactical depth to the battles though. Plus the battles only last 4 rounds of combat so if you don't have all the enemies cleared by the end of the 4th round, the battle ends anyway. So, taking that into account, they don't pull you totally out of the overarching game of dungeon exploration to an extreme level.

I guess my one complaint about the battles though would be that you don't really GAIN anything from them as far as I can tell. They are there merely to drain your health/sanity, kinda like the videogame. You gain XP purely from completing whatever quest objective you picked at the beginning of the dungeon run and that's it. I mean, there are usually treasure chests on the battle tiles that you can gain to give you resources or gold etc. so that's a bonus. But, I feel like if you are going to have a whole separate setup for battles AND they are actually fun, at least give us some xp for killing the monsters or SOMETHING, anything at all would be nice.

That said, this is still only my first dungeon run and I realize the entire point of the runs is to try and gain as much XP from your quest objective as possible. So, for this run my objective was that I gained 1 XP for every 2 rooms I cleared. Thinking on this a bit, I would have wanted to try and avoid any battles while clearing rooms as they don't REALLY have any benefit (other than the treasure chests which I don't think are worth it). I don't know, it just feels weird I guess to have this really fun and enjoyable experience (the battles) and yet they are meaningless. BUT AGAIN, perhaps there are objectives that really give the battles meaning, although I still think adding in some kinda benefit to defeating monsters would be better.

So, I finished the dungeon run which is also interesting as you can basically leave anytime you want before exploring. You just have to manage the risk/reward of how much further can you explore without dying.

I got to the Hamlet phase and started it (but haven't completed it yet). It looks pretty awesome, and it's basically like a little mini worker placement game. You will roll a d10 and place that aggravating caretaker mini on one of the spots, blocking access to that space for the day. Draw a Hamlet event card, which in my case was an "uneventful day" so, nothing happened. No idea if most of the cards are negative or positive. Then in position order, which I think is kinda weird here.....like, can you change position before the Hamlet phase or do you have to plan it out before you end your dungeon run? Anyway, in position order you take turns placing your mini on a space and taking that action. This is where I stopped for the day. I know that I have 3 total days to take actions (based on the event card) and the caretaker mini moves each day to a different space. Which is nice so he's not blocking out an entire spot after each run.

In summary, I am really enjoying it thus far! There have been a few little oddball things which I mentioned previously but unsure if they are oddball because I am just not understanding them yet or if they are TRULY oddball.

Update: Continuing these long, drawn out "thoughts" in a session report over on the forum for the game. However, I will say that based on my first full dungeon run I would be comfortable rating the game an "8".

This is a mixed bag. On the one hand, mechanically its fairly clean once you get going. Initial start up was a bit clunky as we deduced all the different types of cards needed to set up the initial Quest, Boss, etc then we got going.

Thematically vs other dungeon crawlers , DD is more of a slog/demoralizing adventure. I get that its supposed to be hard. While you gain gold, it doesn't buy you enhancements like other crawlers so much as just ( attempts ) to fix all the damage you emerged from the dungeon with. And you'll always come out beat up , sometimes a lot . Getting back to the Hamlet with a lot of damage and drawing a card that only grants one day to heal can really set you back. It seems weird that you can't do more in the Hamlet if you're really beat up . I guess we could have swapped out a beat up character for a new one, but the thematic disconnect still exists - why not heal more if you're beat up ? Most crawlers give you a clean slate once you get back to town.

About the only "good" object you can gain are trinkets - but even they have downsides . You use them for a good effect, then you rotate the card and have to endure a negative effect to flip it back. There are Positive Quirks, which are good.....but they are usually replaced by Negative Quirks, which will replace a Good one if you get more than 3 total Quirks, which can happen fairly easily .

The characters to choose from have good variety, and each one has several different ways to build them via Action cards.

We may go back and play again at a later point, but the grind makes it a bit less appealing. We got to the Level 2 Boss Quest , guessed incorrectly where his room was so had to explore every room to get to him. When our Crusader died 3 rooms from the Boss room we stopped as there was no way with two more monster rooms before the Boss we'd beat it.

In short its good if you wanna hack and bash, not so good if you want to collect items and outfit your characters with cool gear.

I will give the game credit that we were able to get it all back in the box with zero lid lift after we were done; unusual for a big KS these days.

This game is an innovative and tactical coop dungeon crawler.

It has legacy game elements with new items and classes to unlock, new treasures to find, etc. But the game can be fully reset and played with full enjoyment. Some legacy elements such as envelope X and Envelope A unlock journey are frusterating or disapointing, but this is not the core of the game.

What this game really masters is being a truely cooperative experience. Most cooperative games involve everyone working to win or loose together, so one alpha personality often takes over and starts dictating what to do. Even if others do not like having their turns dictated, they can't choose do what they want if it is not seen by the group as the optimal play. But in Gloomhaven you have reasons to not work together in perfect unison. Perhaps you have a battle goal or retirement goal that you want to achieve. Or perhaps you just want to generate XP or collect more loot (which is not shared). Often some of these side tasks/distractions have to be laid aside to make sure the scenario is won, and it hurts when you are the one sacrificing your battle goal for the team. But that is the point, when you can choose to cooperate or not, then cooperation feels more meaningful than when you have to cooperate. It is also fun because you can cooperate to win the mission but still compete to see who get more xp, retires faster, etc.

This game is great if you want a campaign game where you come back to the same game with new missions every session. Each mission is fun on its own if you have a friend who wants to play just one time. It is amazing how you can seemlessy add or remove a player without ruining the game (between 2 to 4 players). If you want to see the fullness this game has to offer it will take commitment. Level ups and prosperity increases come slowly.

The caveats: You have to read a 50 page rulebook and invest a great deal of time to really get the full Gloomhaven experience. Even after many hours of playtime, we still have to look rules up. It's also worth mentioning that our plays are limited to holidays, when we have enough time off work to set everything up and concentrate. And our concentration is mainly on playing the game, not on the world-building. Yes, the characters are cool and the artwork is cohesive, but the storytelling is disjointed; I couldn't even begin to retell the plot. Now that we've started the forgotten circles expansion, I feel like I've had enough of the campaign.

The positive is of course that the core gameplay is really excellent. The cooperative simultaneous action selection mechanics mean that you're constantly having to communicate and anticipate what the enemies might do. Furthermore, the attack modifier decks (instead of dice) are a fantastic way to resolve combat. Having to rest to retrieve cards also adds heaps of tension (why isn't action retrieval used in more games??)

The sequals: I'm interested to see whether Jaws of the Lion offers the same kind of gameplay without having the time-consuming campaign. Frosthaven, on the other hand, adds more between-scenario admin, which will be too much for us to spend time on.

The Fantasy Adventure game that sets the bar for all comparisons. A product of love and inspiration that dared to aim higher that any of its predecessors and broke a series of thresholds as it hit its marks to the surprise of most.

The Pros:
1)It's so epic that it will redifine the word for you.
2)Amazing monster and player class variability.
3)Amazing in-class replayability.
4)Solid mission design.
5)A fully fledged world that will seep into your adventure one mission/event at a time. It's high fantasy but believable.
6)Great gameplay with an amazing hand management system that is both simple to play and difficult to master.
7)Pure co-op with an amazing AI (the best I've seen so far) that allows you to predict it just as much you should... most of the time, and more as you get more experience with each particular enemy.

The Cons:
1)The futility of the level up design is more profound in such a long campaign. From a point on you simply realise your level doesn't matter (other than giving you more options), as the monsters level up with you.
2)The fatigue mechanism is generally solid after a few games, but it's still very anticlimactic and can feel like a real bummer for new players as they won't realize until too late that they need to conserve their strength/cards.
3)Losing a mission nets you benefits in the long term!, as you keep any gold/xp and get to replay it as many times as you need. There's a clear design hole here.
4)The retirement mechanism is interesting, and the upgrade (cards) mechanism absolutely fantastic, but one kind of kills the other.
5)The game is difficult to store it its box, and that has a side effect of increasing set up time until you get a storage solution.
6)I don't really like the loot system, and it's difficult to explain thematically why the heroes don't just loot the area clean after they win. This hurts more once you realize gold is what gives you an edge in battle.
7)The components are lacking in artwork. The boards are plain, the player cards have no artwork at all and the summons get a generic token that isn't even practical. The only exception are the monsters that have great artwork, and the items that are fine.
8)The gameplay is fairly prone to analysis-paralysis especially while you learn a class.

The game is a blast to play. None of its flaws is fatal, and each of its strong points is mindblowingly well achieved.

Before Gloomhaven, I had two groups of game friends: table top role playing gamers and board game enthusiasts. My board game friends were reluctant to try campaign based role playing games because of the knowledge that it required commitment. They also mentioned a lack of bits and pieces—that the games don’t automatically come, all in one box, with all the fun miniatures or physical elements. Conversely, my TTRPG friends would be way down to spend hours crafting minis and building terrain but be reluctant to set up a board game because most of them are self contained experiences. Why would I spend 8 hours playing twilight imperium and the hour of setup and take down when I could pull out a sheet of paper and pick up where I left off on a continuous epic adventure?

Gloomhaven brought all of this together for us. I bought it and it acted as a gateway between my two groups. It had enough of what everyone wanted that they were able to get into it long enough to see the value in the various experiences that each style of game offered. Soon the TTRPG folks were enjoying all the little bits and premade terrain tiles, and the board gamers were looking forward to having something more long form to develop as a character and a party.

Gloomhaven was the first co-op board game I ever played. I bought it in 2020 but only started playing three years later. I decided to buy it for two reasons: first, because I love fantasy role-playing games; and second, because of its high ranking on this very site.

My friends and I only finished our campaign this year, after playing for two years. The fact that we stuck with Gloomhaven for so long speaks for itself — we truly enjoyed the experience. More than that, the game helped strengthen our friendships, and I think Isaac Childres should be proud that his work has brought so many people together.

I know countless reviews have already been written about Gloomhaven. My apologies if I repeat what others have said or if my impressions add little, but I’ve arranged my thoughts in a simple list:

PROS:
-You’ll spend countless enjoyable hours with your friends — even outside of gameplay, while preparing the next session.
-Difficulty can be scaled easily.
-Huge variety of classes.
-More than 90 scenarios.
-Node-based campaign structure.
-The world reacts to your choices through a reputation system.
-Failing a scenario isn’t as punishing or frustrating as in Journeys in Middle-earth.
-Some scenarios are genuinely challenging and rewarding.

CONS:
-109 pages of rulebook and FAQ (!)…
-…largely because of confusing writing and a terrible layout…
-…where important information is poorly organized or even hidden (flowcharts, bullet points, or mind maps would have helped).
-No organizer included.
-Some components are of mediocre quality.
-Additional expenses are almost necessary: sleeves, organizer, and accessories.
-Increasing prosperity and reputation feels too slow.
-Players must track too much information…
-…and yet there’s no official app to help manage it.
-The sheer number of scenarios can discourage completionists.
-Some scenarios feel repetitive.
-The first few scenarios can be overly difficult.
-While many boss fights are fun, the final one is poorly designed and disappointingly easy.
-A few classes are noticeably overpowered.

You open a door, and the dim torchlight reveals six more enemies awaiting you in the shadows. You glance at the five cards in your hand, already feeling the weight of exhaustion creeping in. You’ll need to be careful and resourceful, measuring every move if you hope to survive this ordeal. Discussions with your companions spill into tense whispers—each of you focused not only on the mission but also on your own private battles and elusive personal goals. Gloomhaven isn’t just a dungeon crawler; it’s a marathon. It demands a careful balance of rest and risk, strategy and hope.

After Jaws of the Lion, Gloomhaven feels like a natural expansion of that universe. How could you not like it? Mechanically, it’s ingenious and incredibly engaging. This time, the light legacy elements add variability and a level of customization that keeps each player’s experience unique.

Of course, as with any lifestyle game, some fatigue sets in after a while. The story itself leans on familiar fantasy tropes—after playing narrative-rich games like Tainted Grail or Aeon Trespass: Odyssey, Gloomhaven’s storyline can feel less compelling. Still, it’s a standout experience and remains a masterwork in the genre.

Some flaws worth mentioning:

Despite these issues, the overall experience remains unforgettable.

The narrative aspect can be overlooked but should not be as it describes a rich fantasy world. The story in itself is generic but it is often told with a nice touch of humour.

An absolute must for campaign tactical combat lovers.

The current monarch of BGG combines a tactical dungeon crawler with an overarching campaign, like many did before and like no one did.

Gloomhaven is somewhat majestic, with its 9,9 kg box full of cardboard. It has something novel in the mechanic department, like the clever use of two cards per round combining upper and lower halves, but it’s peculiarity lies in its grandiosity: almost 100 scenarios, a campaign with new characters coming and going with a few legacy quirks.

I deeply admire this magnum opus by mr. Childress: it has the taste of something never tried before, like packing an entire video game world and hundred of playtime hours all in a box. It immediately feels like epic.

I don’t know, however if I can fall in love with it: the tactical puzzle players are faced with in each round seems enticing and fun to solve, but could also become stale and repetitive after a while. The story, on the other hand, seems quite standard fantasy fare (but going out of the known path with out of ordinary characters and classes is very welcome).

The initial tentative rating is 7.5. Could definitely go up or down.

Well this ended up being interesting and unexpected for several reasons, and genuinely great. TLDR: (1) I loved it, after a decidedly mixed experience with JOTL. (2) I think it’s a rare digital-is-better situation. And (3) Less than 4P is the way to go.

(1) JOTL was my introduction to the system and I have a lot of mixed feelings about it. One can see my full comments there but I played a full campaign with a group of 4. I loved playing with friends but it suffered from a tedious story, mediocre sloggy level design, overlong game sessions, and we were all glad to be done with it. Still, the system and card play was a real winner and I could grok the seed of what it *could* be. Swapping Full Gloomhaven for the underbaked JOTL, playing digitally on Steam, and with 2 or 3 mercenaries, did the trick. I've been straight up obsessed with this game. I've now played two full campaigns and just about every class thoroughly. The character retirement mechanism is brilliant to keep things moving and let you try out multiple experiences.

(2) This gets a rare endorsement of digital over physical. There’s still part of me that longs for that big box, for the tactile experience, to imagine rather than be shown the details. But why deny it: the digital implementation is fantastic. The dungeons come alive, the allies and monsters are great. Lightening the load of all the crushing, error-prone overhead on this one let me focus on gameplay and cruise through scenarios in half the time. I hesitated to award the full 10 since digital is mandatory for me. But the design still comes through. Consider it a caveat.

(3) 4-player JOTL was too much. Too many monsters and way too long. I get the extenuating circumstances with the particular needs of JOTL to get it on the shelf at Target, but it meant cramming scenarios into a printed binder and artificially creating complexity with irritating spawn points or monster powers, but either way, 2P is just so much faster and cleaner. Spent part of my weekend a few times playing with old friends, initially to see what all the fuss is about. Completed various scenarios. What I experienced in Gloomhaven was a few funky mechanics wrapped in an excessive amount of blandly decorated cardboard. I was uninspired by its generic setting.

If you combined together the best card mechanics from Gloomhaven and Mage Knight, supplied one hundred properly sculpted miniatures and presented the campaign set in an engaging non-generic universe then I’d be inclined to feel engaged in the game experience. The game is crunchy in terms of its weight. There is more complexity imbedded with its design than other dungeon based board games. The pace is a slow grinding configuration of unrewarding meaty decisions.

Gloomhaven is a generously sized package filled with surprises which included a lack of attention to detail in two fundamental areas; 1. Quality miniature sculpting 2. Forgetting to bring talented fantasy artists in to illustrate all its blank cards and other mundane components.

It’s lazy roleplaying, straight out of the box, hence the immediate popularity spawned by convenience. If I was feeling too lazy for a pen & paper campaign and wanted something easier to unbox with nicer art and a lovely selection of models to collect and paint then I’d be waiting for the relaunch of HeroQuest.

Gloomhaven is even more plain than its unimaginative title suggests, so it’s never going to be my fantasy campaign game of choice. I’d always prefer to be adventuring in somewhere drenched in tomes of arcane lore that matters. Somewhere like Mordheim.

Gloomhaven – The undisputed king of campaign-driven dungeon crawlers. You lead your mercenary through the grim streets and twisted wilderness of Gloomhaven, uncovering dark conspiracies, forging uneasy alliances, and sometimes embracing the shadows yourself. What sets this apart is the deep, card-based system — more Euro than Ameritrash — where every choice matters, and your deck is your lifeline. Tactical combat blends seamlessly with evolving personal stories and goals, and unlocking new characters feels like leveling up your own heroic saga. It’s long, it’s complex, and it demands your full attention — but the payoff is an epic adventure that sticks with you long after the last scenario ends. If you want your dungeon crawl with brains, heart, and a little bit of darkness, this is the gold standard.

Why it is a 9:

Asymmetry: Everyone plays their own character with their own capabilities.

Progress: Characters get more options and feel more powerful over time.

Decisions: Most decisions are pretty important. The ones which aren't are usually quick to make so you can get back to the meaty decisions.

Variety: Enemies, level setups, character builds, mission goals (to a lesser degree), lots of variety promise to keep things fresh for a while.

Why it is not a 10:

Logistics: This game is somewhat of a logistical nightmare. Keeping track of the enemies AI, shuffling all the enemy decks when appropriate, knowing how the AI should act in an ambiguous situation, remembering all your own abilities and effects, going in turn order. Lots of things demand the attention of the players and it is easy to miss things. That's to say nothing of table space requirement and storage requirements.

You like dungeon crawls? You like tactical combat with tough choices every turn? You like a massive world where your decisions actually shape the story? Here it is, Gloomhaven which is KIND OF A LOT OF BRAIN POWER THINKING XD! A 1–4 player cooperative campaign game where you and your party of adventurers dive into dangerous dungeons, forgotten ruins, and branching storylines that change every time you play.

How do you win? By working together to survive the scenario in front of you slaying monsters, grabbing loot, and making choices that ripple across an ever changing world. But don’t get too comfortable… every decision changes what comes next, and like a giant “Choose Your Own Adventure,” your story can twist in ways you never expect.

The core of the game is its brilliant card-based combat system. Each round, you’ll pick two cards from your hand, using the initiative number to see when you act. Each card has a top and bottom ability attack, move, heal, or something crazy powerful and you’ll play one top and one bottom every turn. Sounds simple, right? NOPE, until you realize cards are your lifeline. Use them too recklessly, and you’ll burn through your deck and exhaust yourself before the dungeon is done.As you play, your characters grow stronger, unlocking new abilities, gear, and even whole new adventurers to swap in. But the world of Gloomhaven changes too—scenarios unlock, cities evolve, and your party’s reputation can shape the fate of the land.

It’s tactical, it’s massive, and no two campaigns will ever be the same. Will your adventurers carve out their legend… or be swallowed by the darkness of Gloomhaven? XD

Probably the best board game I've played. Hadn't played a fully co-op game before this, so was pleasantly surprised at the dynamics. Works best at 3p, seems easy at 2p, and takes a lot longer at 4p.

Pros -

1) Keeps you invested for way longer than other board games - I'm expecting a good two years before I tire of this game
2)The concept of unlockables is brilliant and keeps the enthusiasm levels high.
3) Every scenario is different (we are just 10 scenarios in), and every monster type adds a new dimension to the game
4) No dice rolls. The random luck elements are restricted to certain card events and attack modifiers
5) Players get to customize their characters and develop them the way they want to. Further, each character is unique, so meshing different playstyles is an integral aspect to the game

Cons -

1) Takes too long to set up and pack up
2) Storage. Need a good organiser or a 3D printer if you want to store all the pieces carefully
3) Tracking damages and monster HP's can be tedious, but we've solved that problem using apps on the side to reduce downtime
4) Need a dedicated crew

All in all, I think that the pros totally make up for the cons and this is a game worth its price and weight.

- Rest system: Take a full turn of inaction to take a better version of a card refresh action? Or take the instantaneous one that adds penalty of luck of the draw?
- This decision is also important for tempo/longevity, as taking Short Rests leads to more quickly running out of cards and becoming Exhausted.
- (Not part of the cards) Traps combined with push/pull effects make for some clever turns and fun postioning

Things I dislike: (Everything else)
- There are just too many things to maintain and manage in a scenario. It isn't complicated, but does feel like a chore and takes me away from the fun of playing the cards.
- Combat resolution via the combat cards is clever, since they may be upgraded, but slows the game down (and again feels like a chore).
- The dungeon crawling aspect just feels lacking somehow. Maybe it is the slow chore (3rd mention) of collecting money and loot, or maybe it is that your character isn't able to upgrade (level ups or gear) mid-scenario, so working through the scenario just feels like a ...chore. I'd rather Diablo's approach of rewards *during* the combat, or Final Fantasy's shorter combats with rewards given inbetween.

It is a game I hope other games will draw insiration from, but not one I recommend.

I’m absolutely in love with Gloomhaven. I’ve completed the entire campaign twice, which easily adds up to over 200 hours of gameplay, and honestly, I could keep going. It’s hands-down the best game I’ve ever played. Everything about it – from the mechanics to the world-building – just clicks.

The core hand management system is pure genius. You start each scenario with a fixed hand of 8–12 cards (depending on your character), and each turn, you pick two cards to play. These go into your discard pile, and when you rest to recover them, you lose one to the “lost” pile until the end of the scenario. To spice things up, some powerful card abilities go straight to the lost pile, so every turn is a tough decision. To make things even more interesting, you can sacrifice a card to avoid damage, which makes your cards the ultimate resource – they’re your stamina, your abilities, and your lifeline all at once. It’s such a clever system, and it keeps every moment of the game engaging.

The variety of characters is mind-blowing, and they all feel unique, even though not perfectly balanced. Character progression is probably my favourite part of the game. Levelling up, gaining experience, unlocking new cards, and completing perks to improve your modifier deck is incredibly satisfying. I was sceptical about the character retirement system at first – the idea of giving up a character you’ve built felt strange – but it turned out to be one of the most exciting parts of the game. Retiring a character and unlocking a new one (with fresh abilities and challenges) is a blast, even on a second campaign.

The game is definitely challenging, but even when we failed scenarios, it never felt punishing. You still gain experience, so even a loss contributes to your character’s progression. The combat mechanics – from the enemy AI and ability decks to the initiative system – are incredibly well-designed. Every round feels tactical and rewarding, and the game always keeps you on your toes.

I know some people think Gloomhaven is too complex, but I found it more approachable than I expected. Sure, it has a lot of depth, but once you get the hang of selecting and playing your cards, it’s pretty straightforward. Some ability interactions can be a bit tricky to figure out, but the Gloomhaven community is amazing. If you ever get stuck, there’s plenty of help online, especially on BoardGameGeek.

The production value is off the charts. The components are fantastic, and the artwork (shout-out to Alexander Elichev) really brings the world to life. The setting is unique too – it’s fantasy, but not the generic kind. It’s immersive without being overly grim, which strikes a perfect balance. I also love how the campaign branches, making it impossible to play every scenario in a single run. The dungeon tiles are another highlight for me – they’re much more immersive than a flip book.

I’ve seen complaints about the setup and tear-down time, which can be a hurdle for some players. For me, this was never an issue because I invested in a third-party organiser from day one. It keeps everything secure and saves so much time during setup and gameplay. Honestly, it’s such a game-changer that I can’t imagine playing without it. I guess requiring an organiser could be seen as a downside, but for me, it’s just part of the experience.

One feature I absolutely adore is the random dungeon generation mode. It’s like a Diablo-style rift run, and it’s everything I’ve ever wanted in a tabletop game. It’s perfect for when you want a quick, one-off challenge.

I know a lot of people suggest starting with Jaws of the Lion as an intro to Gloomhaven, but I actually disagree. If I’d started with JOTL, I might not have been interested in the full game. JOTL is fine, but it’s much more limited – no retirement system, fewer unlocks, fewer tiles, and much simpler gameplay. If you’re new, I’d recommend jumping straight into the full Gloomhaven (or waiting for the second edition in 2025). After that, try Frosthaven, and treat JOTL as a fun mini-game later on.

For me, Gloomhaven is a perfect 10 out of 10. It’s an absolute masterpiece and a must-have for anyone who enjoys tactical combat puzzles, cooperative play, or RPG-style character progression. If you haven’t played it yet, trust me – you’re in for something special.

- story choices in road and city events are really obvious like 'help or steal' 'protect or kill', there is no moral ambiguity. Your evil or bad choices should be subjective and not universally bad. You shouldn't be forced to be either good or bad to everyone. That's a really traditional aspect of storytelling.

You either need to use some replacement parts (like dice instead of life chits) or get a really big table.
- Tracking choices is hard. And even if you write down what is this scenario should lead to, you can open the scenario book and find out that it is locked by some achievement you haven't heard yet. Map serves a purpose of tracking your campaign progress but after a while you will fail to remember what place is what.
- Rules are well written but still contain many quirks. You can be certain at least some rules. Instead of expanding the FAQ, Isaac could have add some reminder text on cards to help you understand how to use them - the cards are quite big, have no art and usually there is plenty space.

Despite all that the game is really, really good.
- The combat, it's core, is fun and challenging. Choosing what cards to loose for good, predicting how will the enemies move, optimizing your moves with other players - engrossing.
- the progress really feels deserved - going forward a single level easily takes 3 or more scenarios and when you do level up it unlocks so much that it makes a difference.
- the scenarios are well thought out. Many times we would win by a hair's breadth and it was so relieving to know we do not have to replay this scenario ( because it take so much time). I actually thought that the game was too hard out of the box - until I've found out I've placed too many monsters for the first scenario for the first two attempts.

Eventually we've completed the campaign and sold it. Realistically we will never spend 60 hours on a board game campaign.

Let me start with this: Gloomhaven has an outstanding combat system. It's fun to play, rewards good tactics and strategy, and continuously throws interesting decisions at you. If it only was for its core, Gloomhaven would be a 9/10 game, only despite a few issues that can be lived with.

However, every single other aspect of the game is an absolute disaster. I'd rate these aspects a 3/10, so the average is 6/10.

- The progression system is flawed by nature. You get XP for playing certain cards and as a reward for completing certain quests. If you get enough XP, you level up. You get a nice new card and a perk for your attack modifier deck. That's terrific. The problem is how the game system responds to the players leveling up. It just increases the monsters' stats. This, combined with the fact that items and sticker upgrades don't count towards your character level (and they can MASSIVELY improve your character, even more than leveling up) makes the game easier as you progress. You will reach a certain point where the characters are too powerful. Fanatics always answer this saying that you can change the difficulty level to compensate that. That's recognising that the game isn't properly balanced.

- Retiring characters feels wrong to me. You've spent weeks building your character to a point you really enjoy using it. And someday, even by accident, you will complete your personal quest and be stripped of your beloved character. That just feels wrong. I know that the game encourages trying new classes, but it shouldn't impose it to you. Fanatics defend this system saying that you can perfectly create a new class of the same character you had. But you have to start again at a lower level, depending on the city's prosperity. This means that you've just lost all your items, most of your perks, and several levels. This, combined with the above point, makes progress undesirable. The fact that game dynamics punish progression is bad.

- But wait, retiring characters unlock really cool new classes. The unlockable classes are one of the worst aspects of the game. They are terribly unbalanced, with most of them overpowering the starting six, or being so niche that low player counts can unlock classes with total anti-synergies between each other. The whole progression system is just wrong. Team composition should be more in the hands of the players. It's nice to unlock new classes to try out different things, but forcing the players to change characters feels wrong. It's more problematic in low player counts.

- The story is pretty generic, but I don't play games for the story.

- Scenario design is wildly inconsistent. You have a couple great scenarios, highlighting the most simples: just kill every enemy on the board. That's the best kind of scenario. You have variety in the map layout, the monsters it has and, of course, your team composition. However, sadly most of the scenarios are poorly designed. Bosses are way too swingy, and so are the summoning enemies. They turn the game into a coin toss: if you get lucky, you may win easily. If you get unlucky, the game may be unwinnable. This phenomena also appears in many scenarios that can be way too random. And others can be cheesed with easy strats.

- Everything outside combat is pretty flawed as well. City and Road events are one of my most despised game mechanic: making uninformed choices. If you already know the game, you can memorise the events and make the best choice. Also, the fact that some decisions require certain classes to have a good effect, and the fact that this information is hidden, is just wrong. Events add nothing in terms of game mechanics, but if you like role playing you may like them, but this is not a game for role players, as the combat system is a brain burner. Battle goals are nice in theory, but everybody ends up revealing what they have to do. "Let me open that door" or "Let me kill that enemy" are common phrases within this game. Finally, legacy elements, in particular the closed envelopes, add nothing relevant. It's just hiding content for the sake of hiding it.

This game has the foundations of what the community claims it to be: the best board game ever. However, everything that surrounds the great combat system, which I had lots of fun with it, takes away the overall enjoyment of the game.

Gloomhaven is a relatively engaging and gamey implementation of a dungeon crawl that treads new ground rather than relying on familiar mechanics like 20 sided dice. The story creates a side veneer of interest that propels character advancement and investment in the proceedings but the whole thing would be overwrought and uninteresting without the core card play mechanic.

Said card system is both the strength and weakness of this game as a whole. It creates a puzzly situation each turn where you have to think through optimum play for both now and the future while also trying to take into account what the monsters are going to do (semi-random) and what your team is going to do (contextual on good communication and teamwork). The system does make for more interesting decisions than most dungeon crawlers, but the reliance that the system creates on effective teamwork is both good and bad in that it requires a fully invested, pretty cooperative team all on the ball to really hum as it is challenging enough to require that level of engagement, even with lower level monsters the inherent nature of the card play requires several steps of look ahead and makes this a fairly challenging game to play competently.

I admire the design, as having this quantity of legacy material work, with the sheer number of player classes, all of the abilities, and so forth is quite an impressive feat. This base game is quite difficult to get into cold, as the game has no real introductory scenarios. For that, you need to check out the later Jaws of the Lion box which plays similarly but has a slimmed down campaign with less legacy but way better intro rules.

Aside: you want spin down monster token holders (for HP tracking). It speeds play a lot. Having initiative round tracking markers (which are included in Jaws of the Lion, but not here due to the number of monster classes) is also a big gameplay aid. Even with those, this thing is fiddly to set up and play in terms of the physical stuff you're dealing with and keeping track of.

Final assessment: I like the idea of this, but the implementation leaves me dissatisfied. All of the issues of slow combat in D&D are exacerbated here by the straight jacket that the card system puts on everything that you do in game. I find it odd that the most challenging thing in this game often ends up being just having the ability to move enough to effectively take your combat actions.

While this gamey puzzle element is undoubtedly what the fans love about it, I find it obnoxious in practice; as so much of it is reliant on the team working together and a single action taken by one player can have negative cascading effects on the other players because of how actions are selected at the start of the round. Hence, optimal play would be the living hell of alpha player dictating actions to the team. Not having some table talk would make this impossible to be successful in though, so it ends up trying to split the baby with the suggestions in the rules (which effective amount to: table talk, but in general terms only) that try to obscure this core issue. I think I would have ultimately enjoyed this game a lot more if initiative was a separate roll or mechanic from the actions and players were allowed to just choose their actions when their turn comes up. Having movement not being tied to the cards would also likely have improved my enjoyment of it as well. The existing system is moderately more elegant, but it makes the play pretty dissatisfying to me and some of the players we may have otherwise enjoyed this game with.

At the end of the day, this takes the thing I dislike most about post 3.0 D&D (endless array of special powers you have to keep track of and combo with each other like a video game) and ports it into a puzzley board game that makes that the whole shebang. It's not a bad design per se, but it's not for me and I don't care to play it again. My ratings ultimately reflect how much I want or would be willing to play it, not its "objective" quality, hence the 2.

More structured than D&D, less simplistic than Heroquest. Gloomhaven sits in the sweet spot between these two extremes in the genre of fantasy role-playing games.
It entertains in two ways: the individual scenarios provide you with sometimes really difficult tactical combat puzzles, and the overall campaign provides an intriguing story line, with many possibilities to explore and for individual players to choose their own path.
If you're a fan of the genre, you should definitely check out Gloomhaven.

Gloomhaven – A Heavyweight Classic That Shows Its Age
Rating: 7/10

There’s no denying that Gloomhaven is a landmark title in modern board gaming—ambitious, expansive, and offering hundreds of hours of content. Its tactical combat system and legacy campaign structure were groundbreaking at launch, and it’s easy to see how it captured the hearts of many.

That said, playing Gloomhaven in 2025 feels like wrestling with an outdated system. Setup and teardown are a chore, made worse by the complete absence of an insert or organizational logic. For a game that costs over €170, the user experience is surprisingly poor unless you're willing to invest in a third-party storage solution.

Component-wise, the disparity between expectations and reality is stark. A few unpainted miniatures, a sea of cardboard standees—even bosses feel underwhelming on the table. And despite the deep mechanics, the rules often feel more convoluted than clever. Even after multiple sessions, we kept stumbling over interpretations and edge cases.

When compared to something like Arydia, which offers painted minis, streamlined gameplay, and a beautifully engineered box—all at a similar price point—Gloomhaven starts to feel clunky and dated. Arydia simply delivers a smoother, more elegant experience straight out of the box.

In the end, Gloomhaven remains a notable and sometimes thrilling ride, but one that requires a lot of patience, housekeeping, and tolerance for rough edges. For some, it’s a masterpiece. For others, like me, it’s a good game trapped in a frustrating package.

Gloomhaven is a truly great and unique experience packaged in one enormous box. If you want a huge, well thought out, fleshed out dungeon crawl RPG in a board game format, this is the game for you. There are a couple of caveats, however...

The game is presented like a lot of RPGs, where you create a party of characters based on a set of pre-defined classes. Your party exists in the town of Gloomhaven and you complete various quests and tasks within the town itself as well as the surrounding area.

These quests are physically built from a very large collection of double sided tiles that provide a nice functional and aesthetic backdrop that defines each encounter. Typically speaking, your earlier and more simple encounters are smaller and as you progress through the game, the maps increase in size and complexity. Alongside the tiles themselves, you have a large stash of various environmental objects which serve as additional flavor to the environment but also serve as functional additions either in the form of impassable tiles or ones that break LOS, etc.

Quests are played in rounds, with each player character and each monster performing a set of actions based on initiative. Each player selects two cards, all of which have a top and bottom action, and chooses the bottom action of one card and the top of the other. All action cards have an initiative, and the player may choose which of their two cards will be their initiative for that turn. Monsters, likewise, have an initiative assigned to their action for any given round, and all participating parties from both sides take their turns in order. Once a player or monster resolves their actions for that turn, it goes to the next in order, and so on until the round is ended. Once used, a player's action cards are either discarded or lost for the remainder of the quest, depending on the card type. This serves as a sort of soft "enrage timer" for any given quest, so parties can't simply rest and heal between every encounter. There's always a sense of urgency in Gloomhaven. Any time a damaging action is resolved, the entity performing that action (Monster or player) will draw from a deck of random modifier cards that can change the impact of that damage by adding or subtracting damage, adding elements or other effects, doubling the damage, or even outright nullifying it.

As to the quests themselves - Including set up and tear down time, you can expect anywhere from 1-2 hours with some that fall outside of those bounds. There are 95 scenarios in the campaign and while you can't experience all of those in a single playthrough (Certain junctions force you to choose a path in a quest so you can't experience all of them while adhering to the rules), you can easily expect 150-200 hours of playtime out of this box in a single playthrough, not including messing with your characters, buying items, dealing with city and road events, etc. The quests are delightfully varied, and some of them impressively complex in design. The game has a natural difficulty modifier mechanic to make sure that players don't outpace the difficulty of the game, but it is left somewhat up to the player how challenging of an experience they want. You are rewarded for taking on higher difficulties, but enemy strength ramps up quickly. The game also modifies enemy spawns and strengths based on player count, so more is not necessarily easier.

In between missions you will have random encounters with the other denizens of Gloomhaven as well as encounters on the road to your quests. These serve to provide not only lore and flavor text, but meaningful ways for your party to gain a reputation - for good or ill - which has in-game impacts on various things. As usual, these things come with tradeoffs. Rob a defenseless merchant for quick gains, or be the good guy and slowly develop a good reputation that will pay dividends over time? The choice is yours.

Character development is one of the game's most robust features. Your party can contain anywhere from 1-4 characters, each required to be a different class, with one player controlling one character (My friend and I actually ignored this rule in order to experience more classes at once, and went through the game with 2 people controlling a total of four characters at once), and the rules are very intentional about keeping mid-mission communication vague and at a minimum, i.e. you don't reveal your actions for a round until everyone has already chosen theirs, and you can only speak in generalities as to your intentions.

As you gain experience through certain actions and complete missions and quests, you will find your character leveling up and gaining perks. Character progression includes your standard increase in health, but is also represented in two major ways: gaining perks and getting new action cards. Perks are mostly related to a character's action deck, either adding positive cards, removing bad ones, or adding effects like piercing shields or adding elements to attacks. There are other perks such as ignoring negative effects from scenarios and items as well. This is a sort of slow burn progression which serves to lessen the randomness of the modifier deck and make a character more predictably powerful over time. New cards are also ramped in their impact based on the level requirements but can also provide a more dramatic shift as certain key cards are drawn. This comes at a tradeoff, as the number of action cards for any given class does not change as they progress, so as new cards are acquired, old ones must be left out of the active deck.

In addition to character progression through perks and cards, you also have at your disposal the usual acquisition of helpful items and gear as well as the ability to modify your action cards after a certain point in the story line. This is an expensive but powerful means to permanently add a large number of different effects to your card such as extra damage, extra targets, extra area of effect, shield piercing, etc.

As you go along throughout the game and satisfy certain requirements you will also unlock the remaining classes in the game eventually adding 11 locked classes to the base 6. I cannot stress how different each of these are and while they're not all equal in their effectiveness, they are all certainly very interesting to play and very unique from one another.

As to those caveats I mentioned earlier...

Some of these things can be circumvented by a couple of house rules, and some with the purchase of the removable sticker pack. First off, the rulebook almost reads like you're really only allowed one playthrough of the game. It dictates that a lot of effects are permanent, not just for your party, but for your box. I don't like that. It's my game, I'll replay it if I want to. And apparently the good people at Cephalofair Games felt the same, and produced a very cheap set of reusable stickers to solve just that issue. I would highly recommend this for anyone playing Gloomhaven.

The second thing people might not care for is the stringent rules around character creation and retirement. When any character is created they draw two retirement goals and choose one of them. These vary wildly from "Kill X number of this type of monster" to "Complete this specific quest line". These all come with some form of reward, usually unlocking a new class, and generally speaking, take a long time to complete barring some freak occurrence. Here's the catch however, once you have met the requirements for a character's retirement, they retire and you have no choice in the matter. And for the most part you do not get to keep any of what they've acquired. The major exception to this is that the card augments you acquired are permanent, even for future iterations of that class, but since there are so many classes, the odds of you realizing the benefit of that are low. You can, of course, just recreate the same character again, but that's highly unadvisable given the number of classes the game has to offer.

On a more practical note, this game suffers from its own design quality in a few ways. First of all, there are a huge number of mechanics to keep track of. I'm not saying this is the most complex game I've ever played and for the most part the rulebook is a great resource (Though I have found myself googling for clarity on a fairly regular basis), but for the average board game player, this would be a daunting amount of rules to follow. It's simply too easy to accidentally forget to keep up with things and only remember later.

Secondly, even though the only miniatures in the box are the player classes and the monsters are all represented by cardboard icons, there is an intense amount of tokens in this box, with absolutely no thought given to how players are supposed to store things. This all but necessitates people to spend extra money on either a homebrew storage solution, or an expensive after market solution like broken token, etc. And I might add that regardless of which path you take to resolve this, none of them are ever going to allow you to fit everything back into the original box and have it close. While that is minor compared to a game with bad rules or bad gameplay design, that's pretty disappointing. Furthermore, there just isn't a good solution for how to store the map tiles, which I'm sure is why in the Jaws of the Lion side expansion, they changed their strategy to having the scenario book be the map. I personally like the map tiles but they are an absolute nightmare to manage from a storage perspective.

All of that being said, Gloomhaven is a truly amazing experience for any psuedo-hardcore board game enthusiast. It's a very well thought out design that produces an incredible number of unique play sessions with a great depth of player choice and freedom. The storage and rulebook challenges should be taken note of, but if you can get over those hurdles, you're in for one of the best board gaming experiences available.

First I don't care much about the legacy elements or the story parts, but it's a great way of slowly unlocking content. It means new players have a limited amount of characters that are easier to learn while more complex ones become available later. Also the starting level of new characters increases over time, meaning even the first character you played will have new options later on that increase or change the experience when playing the character again.
Where this design choice really shows is the personal mission each character has. If your character fulfills his secret mission he retires, unlocking new content. This gives you a very specific goal you are trying to fulfill beyond completing the scenario in front of you, and adds so much to the feeling of the game.

What makes Gloomhaven so great is how ridiculously well designed it is. The difficulty is well balanced so that each map is finished just about in time before you run out of actions - and balance is great for different player counts as well. The characters are fun to play with combos and cool abilities. They play very different to each other, much more than in other similar games.
The card based based combat is awesome. First you don't draw - your cards and available actions are fully controlled by you. All your options are available as the game starts and slowly you lose cards until you are exhausted - its very clever as it adds an aspect of resource management. Your character can burn very bright for few big moves, but you have to rein her/him in to last till the end of the scenario.
Next you don't play a card - you play two cards. Each card has 2 possible actions, top and bottom. For one card you have to do the top action, for the other card the bottom action, in any order. Meaning with only 5 cards left you still have more than 20 possible combinations not to mention that cards can be used as a default attack/move action ignoring their text. On top of that you know which of the cards you might get back after this or further turns and which not, meaning you want to plan ahead for future combos. It's a brilliant system that deserves way more credit than it gets.

In contrast to this there is a damage modifier deck adding up to +/-2 to your attack (we're playing variant without miss/crit). It's a good distribution with +0 being very common, +1 or -1 less common and finally +/-2 being rare. While I dislike this (bad luck on most luck based mechanics), you mitigate this over time - permanently. First you don't roll die, you draw from a deck enforcing a certain level of distribution, second as characters level up they change the distribution of the deck removing negative cards adding positive ones. With new characters starting at higher levels you very quickly skew the deck in your favour. To give you an idea - after 3 scenarios I was level 3 with 1 perk, removing 2x -1 cards and adding 4x +1 cards to the deck. I didn't actually count the cards, but I think you start with 20. You can even add powerful bless cards to it for 1 mission by spending some gold.

This level of randomness in a coop game is fun and I wouldn't change it (coming from someone who wouldn't play the game if it had dice rolling for to hit rolls). And if you like games of chance (first go to a casino and don't ruin boardgames, but second..) you can make the deck more "chancy" by removing most +0s and adding few stronger cards to it.

Note that I find the rulebook terrible to use. The rules individually are easy to read and comprehend, but there is many of them and the structure of the rulebook is painful, so finding specific information can grind games to a halt.

TLDR summary: Absolute must-play and #1 is very deserved for its brilliant design and perfect execution.

Gloomhaven has some great card strategy and deck building elements, but it is initially very slow and suffers from repetitiveness. I initially did not like my first few games due to overly simple plots, set up time, and limited variety in play. The story and strategy grew on me, but over time I would call this game samey in a way that many will hate. There's also very little story for a legacy game. You basically just fight over and over, which is really puzzle solving. There are a plethora of scenarios to play, but they are predictably samey. Get in quick, kill, and repeat.

Setup and teardown are extremely long. An organizer for setup and tear down is a good investment, else you'll have to dedicate the table for a while. You can only slightly deck-build compared to LCGs, but there's decent variety between the characters. There are enemy AIs, but again, many feel samey. The narrative is less hit than miss, which is unfortunate, but an imaginative group can add a lot with a little role-play.

The worst part of the game is the grind; unlocking cards, new characters, and equipment is very slow compared to many games. Slowly the prosperity allows new characters to start at higher levels, but even that is too slow. I don't see how people don't complain more about this! I house rule that you gain one level per game and double the income, and it still feels slow.

The brilliant part of this game is the ability to control the balance of the game no matter the number of or level of players; so you can easily get this to the table more than most campaign games. Similar to Mage Knight, there are times where players may have dozens of choices and slow the course of play, so best player count varies.

I don't really care for the art, the lack of art on the cards, or the programming that can waste cards just because someone else takes your action first. I'm also getting annoyed with rushing through every quest just to fit the way the card management works. It didn't bother me at first, but when you realize that you're going to repeat a dungeon, and you still have to finish out the play for the experience points, it becomes tedious to me. I'm glad this game exists, but surprised at the ratings, because this is a grind!

So as my rating would suggest, I am not on the Gloomhaven bandwagon. I cannot fault the ambitious scope of the game (if you love it, this game is fantastic value for money) but I find little in the gameplay that I enjoy. This is almost certainly connected to my own biases, as I can recognise there is certainly a good game inside Gloomhaven's giant box, but it's not the game for me.

Gloomhaven feels mechanically disconnected from its theme. I certainly wouldn't consider it the highly 'thematic' game (it's high 'thematic rank' on BGG annoys me more than anything else about the game). What is meant to be dynamic fantasy combat maybe a few minutes in length is simulated by slow, considered card play that takes place over hours. My decisions felt more strategic than the cut and thrust of skirmish combat. Tactical decisions on which card to play need to account for longer-term strategic goals, as powerful cards are often lost from the deck once played. This makes the game ponderous, as each player decides how to best solve the puzzle in front of them using the resources they have available. I enjoy both tactical and strategic thinking in games (see my highly rated games), but prefer that be married to themes that feel strategic (wargames representative of multi-year conflicts for example).

Where my biases are specifically relevant to my feelings on Gloomhaven are that I love tabletop roleplaying games. So much so that I was involved in running RPG conventions, have played over a hundred different systems across multiple genres and enjoy reading the rules and splat/world books in my spare time. But....there is one aspect of roleplaying I have never enjoyed. I dislike the classic Dungeons and Dragons dungeon crawl (DC). A DC, in my experience, is more about solving a puzzle and displaying rules knowledge than getting into character and generating a collective narrative. In fact, I've often said..'if you want to play a DC, why not just play a boardgame?' I guess I've now played that board game and realised I don't really like that either. The boxed text for Gloomhaven reminds me of all the parts I hate about DnD pre-written modules, with their 'on rails' plotlines and almost irrelevant backstory (who cares about the villain's goals...we're just going to kill them regardless).

The caveat to all of this is that I have only played a small number of missions. But I saw nothing in those missions that makes me want to ever play the game again. I'd much rather play a simpler dungeon-crawler, where the gameplay may have less depth, but where the game feels more dynamic and fast-paced. Clearing one room should not take 2-3 hours!

I play this primarily solo with 3 characters, and it's worth noting that it is, more so than any other game I play solo (including Aeon Trespass: Odyssey) a bit overwhelming to do so. The rules recommend that solo players up the difficulty because there's no hidden information, but in order to take advantage of this lack of hidden information you have to be very analytical in your moves. Finding the perfect turn from 3 decks of ~10 cards simultaneously can be laborious (not to mention ~5 items each), and often the first round of the game can take me upwards of 15 minutes because of this. Things proceed more rapidly as action cards and options deplete.

You can of course decrease the difficulty and play less analytically, but that's half the satisfaction of the game.

In the few scenarios I've played with others it's generally been a good experience, but it requires calibration of the difficulty to how good the players are at making good moves. I've played the starting 2 scenarios with 3 groups of players, with results ranging from losses to absolute stomps, based largely on how well the players do (rather than luck).

There are few games I feel as controversial about as this one. Regarding the amount of contents provided, the amount of contents that can be unlocked throughout the campaign, the huge amount of story paths and the puzzly aspects of the scenarios, I think this game is without a match and absolutely ranks at the top. However, the set up is an absolute pain, and so are the continuous shuffling of decks and book keeping (the book keeping is far from the worst I have experienced, but still a negative). The game play quickly becomes repetitive because you play the same small deck, usually in a similar pattern, over and over again, and it very much has a feel of an efficiency game in which you have to clear a room of enemies which only seem to exist to exterminate your heroes. On the other hand, the repetitiveness is very well offset by the fact that you regularly add new heroes to your team and that every hero plays very differently, but once you get familiar with a new hero, there is just not sufficient variation in the game play to keep the game exciting for long. There are several scenarios that feel different and unique, but the majority of the scenarios consist of disposing of all enemies, which ultimately only adds to the slog. The game is lacking in pacing to qualify as a great hack-and-slash game, yet that seems to be exactly what players will be doing throughout most of the scenarios. The efficiency aspect of the game play also prevents players to take their time to explore every corner of the dungeon and discover its secrets, which makes Gloomhaven loose its dungeon crawler feel. Despite all this I have been very much impressed by Gloomhaven and have great memories of playing through the campaign. Because of this the game will stay with me as one of my favorites, but the obvious negatives as well as the legacy aspect will be unfortunate barriers to bringing this game to the table in the future. This review is based on solo game play only.

Gloomhaven is still an excellent game, though I have to deduct a point to drop it to a 9 for three main reasions.
1. The repetitive nature of the far too numerous "kill all enemies" scenarios
2. The extremely negative sheen that the wholly hideous Forgotten Circles cast on the game
3. The janky and gimmicky nature of multiple boss fights and certain enemies that negate core tactics that your characters might use. This is difficult to cater for given the variety of characters, but some scenarios can be hideously difficult or laughably easy depending on your party.

There's a few other irritations - the semi-coop battle goals(while they attempt to coax non-optimal play for personal benefit, these quickly get tedious and you've seen them all), not being able to share gold/items (so you're telling me that I'll save a teammates life, but I *won't* give them a couple of gold pieces?) and the silly initiative/action communication rules(just say what you're doing and ramp up the difficulty). It's also not really designed well for 2 players. I'd recommend 4 to be honest, and 3 is probably the realistic minimum.

Yet despite all those flaws, Gloomhaven IS still an exceptional game, because those flaws are in part due to the breadth and depth of the game. That it works at all when given the dramatic differences in all the playable classes and the item loadouts players might have is a testament to the game's design.

So why a 7?

The biggest drawback for me is the combat system, which is the main reason I docked some points.
Sooner or later unlike DnD you will end up fighting in a dungeon of sorts, and while those encounters are well built, I hate the "impending doom" mechanic.
What I mean is, you get a set of cards (bit of a deck builder) with abilities you can use, some are one time use and they get "Lost" others are discarded upon use.
You run out of cards? Rest, short rest you put a random discarded card in the lost pile, long rest you chose.

B) impossible to complete without leaving the game consulting online resources to plug the developer's website/email list
This alone would not be rage inducing but there is never any feedback on whether the player is on the right track *and* the original solution contained a typo that was then reprinted in later editions. So players could have spent so much of their life on this one element of a game that they loved, only for it to wholly and utterly disrespect their time

Update 2, some 50-ish scenarios and one year later: We still haven't played all scenarios, so this attests to the longevity of Gloomhaven. So I will preface this by saying that because Gloomhaven is so hyped, I came in with very high expectations which may be a bit unfair. And was only able to play a couple scenarios. But at the end of the day I was really underwhelmed.
Obviously the positive of Gloomhaven is it is a big box full of a lot of components that can entertain an individual or group pretty much indefinitely. There is almost no limit to the amount you can milk this game for, so I understand the appeal. Also, from an economic and mechanical perspective I can appreciate the game. Your figurines are very nice, and from a financial perspective, making the rest of the components cardboard makes sense. And the monster cards that can easily scale difficulty for your needs are a brilliant idea.
However, I had a lot of gripes. First, set up was an absolute chore. It took us twice as long to set up as it did to play the actual scenario. This could be mitigated if you could leave it permanently set up somewhere, but is absolutely prohibitive for a normal game night. Second, some of the mechanics were interesting and sort of fun. But the fact that you have to spend your valuable action cards whether you want to or not is thematically and mechanically obnoxious and silly. For example, I had to waste two entire turns (and therefore burn 4 of my dwindling action cards) just walking across a large room. I'm not quite sure why that mechanic exists, but it bothered me to no end. Likewise, there was a pit trap blocking a door. There is no way to disarm it in the game (besides jumping or pushing enemies into it, which my character couldn't do), so my character just had to walk over it and take damage. So for both of these fairly basic tasks that could be solved by some light exercise and critical thinking skills, my character was severely and illogically punished.
Finally, and in summary, I guess my take away is that Gloomhaven is basically a mash up of a DnD game and a Zombicide game, and it is far, far worse than either of those. If you want role playing dungeon crawling, Dnd is far richer and more fun. If you want a simple monster bashing game with your friends, Zombicide Black Plague is far easier to set up, more tense, and narratively interesting than Gloomhaven.
I guess in the end, the best use of Gloomhaven I can think of is if a person who doesn't have a game group can just set it up permanently on a big table at their house and just play alone when he/she has time. It just doesn't feel worth it to bring it out for even semi regular use for a group.

Gloomhaven surprised me, not because it's a good game, but because it's actually pretty streamlined! Given the box is the size of my torso and punching the boards takes a full hour I was expecting some really complicated game that was a bear to play, but the play is super smooth and the phase order is so simple: play 2 cards, determine initiative, play turns in initiative order, rinse/repeat. The rulebook was admittedly intimidating, but things are relatively intuitive once you get going. I found it simpler to learn than both Descent and Mage Knight and it seems to do imitations of both very well

Don't get me wrong though; there are a lot of nuances in this game. If you haven't played games like Descent and Mage Knight then it might be a good idea to start there to properly appreciate how the core ideas of those games has been incorporated here. This at its heart is a cooperative game and as such it is missing some of the finer competitive elements of its predecessors. Then again Mage Knight and Descent hardly ever hit the table unless I'm playing solo, so we're not losing much

So the tactical dungeon crawling of Descent and the puzzly hand management of Mage Knight. What else is here? Robinson Crusoe's returning consequences is here too with the presence of travel events. There's an AI that is somehow even better than Gears of Wars's excellent AI system. I'm sure I'm missing a few others, but I'd say those together make up the core

The game is puzzly and thinky but not overbearing with process, and that makes it a slam dunk. Each class is complex and intricate with clear overarching strategies. Each kind of reminds me of a class in a MMORPG. Moreover, I've only played with two so far (both of which I'm thoroughly impressed with) and there are 15 more! What the heck?? I just got 4 hours of play from one session with these two and I haven't even scratched the surface with these characters. The amount of legitimately interesting content here is staggering

Gloomhaven just has to be a 10 for me. This is the perfect tactical dungeon crawl (unless you want something with a DM, then play Descent). There are a lot of effects but they are all relatively straightforward. There is a lot going on, but a good teacher could very easily abstract away the details from you. I love the classes and I love the puzzly nature of it all

I will criticize it for a few things though: first there's way too much stuff here. The game is starting to rival my Netrunner collection in terms of how I need to find ways to systematically manage it all efficiently. And I just opened the game. Moreover, sifting through cards during setup, digging through bags of tokens - it all really adds up. The game is not short by any means. My learning game took around 4 hours which included searching for clarifications on BGG. I don't see this ever taking less than two hours. Lastly, I should clarify: this game feels streamlined to me compared to other similar heavy games. There's still a lot of rules and a good amount going on - I just find it easier to remember than in other games which tend to have more branching conditions

Overall though, I'm extremely impressed with Gloomhaven. It far exceeded my expectations and I look forward to playing it again

EDIT: I've gotten to play about 10 games so far and wanted to update my thoughts. So far I'm still really enjoying the game although I think it's just shy of perfect for me. All of my plays have been solo playing two characters although I just introduced a third character on my most recent play.

The good: lots and lots of content, tactically very rich, streamlined phases, interesting characters, challenging, not a lot of rules referencing mid-play, progression is well-tuned and compelling, enemies require different strategies, clean and strong AI

The meh: bookkeeping is fiddly, attack modifier decks are cool but fiddly, long playtime, pacing seems a little slow considering how long fights take, a few of the scenario elements seem like they don't add enough value to justify their overhead (prosperity, reputation, events), you need to work if you don't want to legacy-ify your copy, rulebook is passable but not excellent, the randomness is tableflip-inducing at times

I tried out a few apps and am really happy with Esoteric Software's web app for managing combat. It let me toss all of the enemy cards/trackers and the character dials back in the box forever and has easily shaved 30m-1h off of the playtime for me. It's let me pick up a third character without much trouble and I don't think a fourth would even be too much

Overall I really love the game - my biggest complaints would be the bookkeeping and the pacing. It's a little frustrating to see two hours go by and realize you've only cleared two rooms but that's the cost of such a detailed and puzzly game. Still a winner, just knocked down a half point

It is great ... and a commitment! Gloomhaven is basically a RPG brought to board - you can develop your character, send him (or her) to rest after slaying through dozens of dungeons, equip your character with tools (as long as you have the coins for it) and you can spend hundreds or thousands of hours playing - it is absolutely amazing, once you made it through the rules and got the principle. The box is huge, a lot of content and of good quality. None of the hundreds of scenarios feels the same.

After 5 games played (doing a 2-player campaign):

A dungeon-crawl system like Descent, which I used to love way back when, but with:
- a more elegant campaign system built in right from the start. You pick one of 6 characters to start the game, play for a while developing it, then eventually retire it and choose another (with more options being unlocked as you play the game). You have just one scenario to start the game, but that opens up two, and from there game paths can diverge (a lot, it seems?).
- a simpler but more interesting system for character development: as you gain experience, you can customize your combat deck and action cards
- a great action card system: players have unique decks of cards each showing an initiative number, a top half, and a bottom half. Each round, everyone uses 2 (one on top); turn order set by the numbers on top. On your turn, use the top of one card, the bottom of the other. Tops are usually attacks (melee, ranged, variable additional effects or bonuses), bottoms are usually moves or special effects. You have to plan but can change your plans on the fly if necessary (in a limited way).
- a very cool AI for the monsters, once you can figure it out (I think we've almost got it!).

At this point, the only negatives I see are:
1. It's a co-op. Fortunately, gameplay is interesting enough to overcome this shortfall.
2. The rulebook is big! There's a lot to learn, a lot of nuances to grok. Fortunately it's mostly straightforward.
3. I guess it would be nice if we had the super-pretty minis like we did in Descent, but the box is already ginormous so I'm okay with standees!

—-
75+ plays later (all 2er): yeah, pretty fantastic design! The co-op thing is fine, I don’t mind it here since everyone has to manage their own deck without interference (with the exception that in a 2er game, you can end up with some VERY dissatisfying character combinations!). But the rulebook is annoyingly large and I still haven’t really internalized several things (especially monster focus/movement, and dealing with advantage/disadvantage)! I think I’d like this more in its app form which presumably deals with all that crap! And, after wasting a bunch of time trying to decipher one of the puzzles, you find out
