Ich wollte dieses Spiel sehr kritisch betrachten. Ich hasse Kampagnenspiele und kann auch mit Legacy-Elementen nicht wirklich viel anfangen (auch wenn eine gewisse Spannung mich immer wieder in ihren Bann zieht). Und wie gesagt: ich möchte wirklich nicht jedes Hype-Spiel automatisch auch selber klasse finden. Ich setzt mich also total kritisch an dieses Spiel ran- wünsche mir fast, dass es kacke wird- und habe 2 Stunden später ein neues Lieblingsspiel! Ja, der Aufbau dauert Ewigkeiten. Ja, man zerupft sich die Pappteile an den sehr festen Aufstellern. Ja, zu viert ist das Spiel nicht halb so gut wie mit weniger Spielern. Aber das sind alles Punkte, über die ich hinwegsehen kann, weil die Stimmung im Spiel einfach fantastisch ist. Die Flavourtexte sind kurz, aber erzeugen trotdem Atmosphäre (ein großer Kritikpunkt bei anderen Kampagnenspielen ist, dass man 5 Seiten Geschichte vorliest, aber alle schon mit den Hufen scharren und zocken wollen- das ist hier deutlich besser). Beim Spielen fühle ich mich, als würde ich mich wirklich durch eine Horde Gegner kämpfen; das liegt vorallem an den Charakterdecks, die meines Erachtens der Aspekt sind, der Gloomhaven einfach besonders macht. Man hat auf den Karten nicht nur thematische Effekte, die das Spiel einfach irgendwie spannend machen, es bietet auch spielerisch/taktisch interessante Entscheidungen- vorallem weil das Deck klein ist und man eigentlich alle Informationen darüber vorm Spielen hat (und nicht einfach zufällige Karten zieht). Und damit nicht genug: die Mechanik des Levelns und der Rollenspielcharakter machen das Spiel sogar noch besser. Nach 60 Spielrunden hatten wir die Kampagne ein erstes Mal durchgespielt- da war unsere ganze Spielgruppe auch erst einmal satt und ganz froh, erst einmal eine Pause zu bekommen. Denn: Gloomhaven war für mich in manchen Runden sehr anstrengend. In manchen Squads waren die Charaktere zu schwach, in manchen zu stark. Oft hat man das Gefühl, dass manche Krieger nicht für zwei Spieler ausgelegt sind. Und dann kommt es schnell mal vor, dass man seinen Charakter hasst und einfach nur loswerden möchte. Das war aber nur ganz selten der Fall; meistens überwiegt die Lust, den neuen Söldner zu spielen und wirklich kennenzulernen. Und deshalb haben wir mittlerweile auch Bock auf einen neuen Durchgang der Kampagne- mit neuen Entscheidungen und anderen Squads. Und das ist ein Zeichen dafür, dass Gloomhaven ein bahnbrechendes Gesellschaftsspiel ist.

This game is just too much in every aspect. To much setup time. To much trial and error. Too much space. I really wanted to like it since the mechanisms are solid but I would honestly recommend the digital version since it simplyfies evey aspect that feels excessive on the tabletop game.

I have played 100 hours+ of the digital game and here are my thoughts (warning that they are mostly negative as the positives of the game are pretty obvious and the game is in the top 5 on BGG so is quite safe).

The game is broken. The game at its best is when you use a completely overpowered and unfair ability to clear a room of enemies or stun multiple enemies to make their turns useless. However this is not good game design.

Furthermore, the brokenness becomes unfun. The personal quest design is horrible. I have had players not be able to retire because we don’t want to replay scenarios to kill specific enemies needed for the quest. We haven’t even be able to retire one character who needs a specific scenario appear whereas another player has retired twice in 20 scenarios.

The scenarios range from trivial to nearly impossible with 4 players without using specific stun heavy/insta kill builds. It is incredibly tedious to replay a scenario you have sunk 2 hours into. The second scenario in the game seems to be one of the hardest for no apparent reason, how did that get past playtesting? There are definitely fun scenarios though.

The story is not interesting. There are no chat after motivations or nuanced plot points. You lose track of what’s happening very quickly with the story.

Some cards are utterly useless and some are must-picks, forcing you into certain play patterns across scenarios.

We have been using the house rule within digital to remove the x2s and misses. A lot of the time when you get a x2 it is wasted. However each time you draw a miss and you waste a whole planned out turn involving other characters it feels so incredibly bad.

I'd rate the physical version lower than the digital as I cannot imagine how tiresome it would be to do the monster turns, especially with 4 players where sometimes there are 10+ enemies acting each round. Well I can actually because I’ve played Jaws of the Lion with 2 players and that was enough.

Still a 7 because the card play and systems are great and fun with friends but the game is just too big in every way, causing it to be quantity over quality.

Tl;dr It's 22 lbs of amazing. This is like having an epic DnD campaign where no one has to be the DM.

Mostly dungeon crawls, and mostly about killing all the enemies, but as you explore, you unlock new locations. Players can also travel back to the city to re-equip and get random encounters on the road. All players form a party that can gain and lose reputation, increase the prosperity of the town, unlock global achievements, etc. Individual characters have personal goals that once they achieve, will retire and unlock new character classes.

Characters who complete missions will gain gold and experience, and can level up, gaining access to new skills and abilities. Characters can also improve their odds in battle by completing mini-goals during scenarios. They also can buy equipment, loot dead monsters, or open treasure chests to reveal more stuff.

Combat is handled by cards, and selecting which hand of cards you take into battle can be it's own puzzle, because your hand size is limited. Each round, you use up two cards, but if you run out of cards in your hand, you can shuffle discards, permanently losing access to one of them. If they all run out, you're exhausted and out of the scenario. There are other ways you lose cards from your discard pile as well If everyone becomes exhausted, you lose.

Randomness is also a factor, because each character has a combat deck that could improve or hinder their attacks, with one critical hit and one critical miss card. Players can modify this deck through achievements that grant perks. Players can select which perk to gain, and when a character retires, they can pass some of those perks on to the next character that player will use.

Monsters are controlled by some pretty basic A.I. rules, but each type of monster has its own deck of cards telling the players what they will do that round, as well as a monster attack modifier deck. Difficulty of monsters can be scaled from level 0-7, and each monster type has stats for basic and elite units (with special abilities). There is a fair bit of bookkeeping that has to be done during the round, and lots of little cardboard bits to help keep tack of temporary modifiers.

What's great about the game is the narrative arc that takes place during the scenario. Each player starts out with a whole lot of potential, and facing some known enemies, but no one knows what lurks behind closed doors. As they go through combat, their ability deck acts like a countdown timer until they will be exhausted, so there is a rush to blitz through all the enemies, but you have to have a plan.

In our first mission, there were three rooms, and after clearing the first room, two of us were almost exhausted, and I didn't think we would make it. And when we opened the third door to a room full of monsters, I was certain we were going to fail. But we managed to eke out a victory, and it was very satisfying to do so. The icing on the cake was the flavor text in the scenario book, which has 95 different story-driven missions. Add to that a map that unlocks locations as you play by placing stickers, and you have a very cool game.

This is a dungeon crawl game with a sprawling ongoing campaign and certain legacy mechanisms where you alter the map, and your characters across multiple plays. The game is completely diceless, so it relies on a flip-luck card driven combat modifiers, which are a little more interesting as over time you can customize the contents of the various combat decks to a certain extent.

The writing is well enough for a game like this. Not terrible, but not very compelling. The components are rough, as rather than this being a game with tons of nice minis, everything outside of player characters are standees which can be hard to see or differentiate from each other. Health and monster stats are also tracked off on the side of the board, which means it can get confusing as to which monster does what and who has however much life left.

Mechanically players are fueled by ability cards, where you choose two cards from your array, then use the top half of one and the bottom half of the other. At times this can be an interesting puzzle, but over the course of the game you wind up losing cards from your array, and when the players lose a map, it's more often to players falling over due to not having enough cards left to finish than it is to actually getting trounced in an interesting tactical puzzle. I find this to be somewhat disappointing when it happens.

Downtime between turns is also quite long not only because of the awkward bookkeeping but also because as players chose their cards for the next round. They aren't allowed to talk about what they plan to do specifically, so turn order flies a little blindly with players stumbling over each other at times.

This game was number one for a reason. However, I will say from the get-go that this game is not for everyone. It will require a big time commitment and a consistent game group in order to take on this beast, but my oh my, is it worth it. For those who like grid-based fighting systems and are interested in added complexity with card-management and team-based tactics, I would highly, highly recommend looking into this game. In addition, the story elements are amazing; facing city and road events, unlocking of elements as you progress, and experiencing twists and surprises within the plot of the game really elevate this game to a unique and memorable experience. The variety in scenarios and environments also adds a breath of life into each gaming session, and where the game could have easily become tedious and repetitive, it adds just enough to feel both familiar and foreign.

A potential negative could have been the semi-random modifier deck, similar to rolling a d20 in DnD. But while there is some luck with the modifier deck system with each attack, the game offers plenty of ways to mitigate this, and even ways to swing the randomness in your favor. There is so much to unpack with this game, but if you have the time and opportunity, there is not a more rewarding gaming experience than this.

Verdict: Play (Why would I say play after giving such a glowing review? Well, with the high cost and such a large time commitment, I would recommend trying to play a session or two first before investing. I would also suggest finding a group of people who would agree to help you go off on this wonderful adventure. But if you find a group and are interested, I 100% recommend a buy)

Extremely fun and engaging combat and movement mechanics, secret unlockable characters, random events between scenarios, addictive character development and soooo much content. We spent many happy hours exhausting all the content in this game and still went back for more. The legacy aspects are certainly a draw too as there's a sense of permanently making progress every time you play.

The setup is time-consuming as there's so much going on.

The game takes way too long, the enemy AI is unintuitive, the overall look of the game is bad, the two-card system isn't a fun mechanic, the gameplay is too puzzly, the setup is tedious, and combat can be very swingy because of the random decks.

The terrain rules should be streamlined. There are difficult terrain, obstacles, and traps that all have slightly different rules. Similarly, there are too many conditions that overlap.

The element track is an annoying afterthought that rarely has any effect on the game.

The end result is that this game just isn't fun to play. Upgrading your character between missions is fun, but unfortunately you have to suffer through the rest of the game to get to that part.

With some heavy streamlining, a total graphic design overhaul, and getting the play time to about an hour you could have a really solid game here. Unfortunately the sequel, Jaws of the Lion, only improved the setup while leaving all of the game's other problems intact.

A solid game and I had a lot of fun for the first 2/3 of the campaign, but it dragged on long and the disjointed aspect of the narrative started to show its bloated nature. There was no excitement building to the final encounters, but rather a checklist that we had to look up to figure which scenarios were needed to unlock the final battle and then worked out way down that checklist mechanically doing some of the more boring and less engaging encounters.

The game also takes so long for a 4 person group for each scenario that failing a scenario would mean throwing away 3-4 hours. Because of this, it means that our group was not willing to fail a scenario and try again because we have limited time and the entire campaign was already a year+ endeavor. If the scenarios were shorter, then failing and trying again would have been a much more palatable option. A fail forward option would have also been a solid way of handling it with scenarios as long as they were.

The puzzles were a major disappointment and should not have been part of the character unlock system. There wasn't any excitement about encountering them, just puzzlement and then irritation.

The gameplay however, was a lot of fun for each character. Balance was very much all over the place, but with 4 players and a cooperative approach we were able to deal with the issues and keep it fun for everyone. The gameplay is why we kept playing it as long as we did and why we all enjoyed the sessions even when the game's narrative felt like it was dragging on long.

I am a bit flummoxed by Gloomhaven. I really enjoyed my time with it, but a third of the scenarios feel underbaked, and it is a strange case of there simply being too much for a tabletop format.

The cardplay is great fun, and I'm glad other games have similar systems that work a bit better (Pavlov's House), the characters are very interesting and do play differently, and I think the shoddy-but-fun writing hits on the 1980s Fighting Fantasy novels some of us grew up around.

But it's too much. It is full of fluff like varying-similar enemy types with not enough to differentiate them; you don't need multiple decks of cards for them, add optional "flavour" cards into the existing Skeleton deck or something instead?

It's heavy, bulky, and very impressive. But with distance and time to think on the positive and negatives, there is some truth to the video game version being a much better experience. The board game replicating some notable dungeon crawler video games is telling, but the writing isn't good enough so it doesn't stand up to actual high quality tabletop RPGs, and the scenarios can be actually pointless and mundane copies of other mundane scenarios.

A great achievement, but with all important distance, I'd rather play a more refined game. I'm not spending 30 hours on a character's personal life goal card ever again, certainly. That sums up the rough edges of Gloomhaven.

As a side note, I enjoy the pretty grand Founders of Gloomhaven. If you get a chance, give that a go! I would love to see Isaac do more away from dungeon crawler campaigns due to Founders of Gloomhaven.

I went through a phase where I was simply tired of dungeon crawlers and I started to completely ignore any new ones that came out. They were often pricey, long, fiddly, random, took up a lot of precious storage space and I just had no interest in playing them anymore. As much as I had fun with games like the original Descent, I had pretty much grown bored and moved on to what I considered better games. Over the years I'd get the itch to play a dungeon crawl again- I'd try games like Zombicide, Imperial Assault, etc... but afterwards I was just "meh" towards them. I thought maybe I'd just outgrown it.

So it took me a while to even glance at Gloomhaven. It popped up in a math trade and that dungeon crawl itch came back again. By this time Gloomhaven was very highly rated on the geek and I actually started to dig into it. It looked different and fresh and interesting! To my surprise I ended up with it in that math trade.

Wow. This is quite the game. This is what I'd been looking for all those years. Finally, a thinky, tactical game where you are in control, and randomness is not overpowering. The puzzle and tactical experience is brilliant, and there are so many clever ideas in this game.

There are a couple of things that bother me:

I dislike the idea of leaving loot on the ground after killing all the enemies. I understand it in some scenarios where you are just trying to get the objective and get out, but if all the enemies are dead- no reason to not casually loot everything on the way out.

I wish the levelling was faster, retirement was faster, and you could get to more content in the game quicker. It's a bit of a slog. And the fact that you don't fail forward is demoralizing to the point that I've just packed it away a couple times with no desire to retry.

I also wish it was a little... looser. This is a very tight efficiency puzzle, and a single misplay can doom you. I wish there was a little more room to let the game breath and allow for creative solutions, instead of just the optimum move. I feel like there are things I'd like to do in this game, but if I'm not solving the puzzle as efficiently as possible I'll likely lose. This makes for a tense experience, but brings the puzzle more to the front than I'd prefer.

It starts of as a great game, the more you play it, the more the game feels repetative. Sure the enemies might change and you can get different characters, but staying with the one you got isn't an option. If you unlock a new character you have to play it. And that makes the choice to invest in upgrading your playing cards hard. Sometimes unlocking a character isn't soly in your hands.

I think we have unlocked 50/70% of the main campaign.

There is just one downside to this game - Getting the same friends together and make time to enjoy this monstrosity of a game.

If you can do that however you have one of the greatest and richest games on the market.

EDIT: After about 20 scenarios into the game, it becomes greater with every hour! We started to upgrade our cards and start to develop proper strategies and the more we play, the more fun we have.

We do use 2 house rules though:
1: Adding both cards with level up into your pool or cards - we played this wrong before and I didn't want to take away cards already being used
2: full control over summons - it is way more fun this way for us even though it makes the game a little bit easier

EDIT 2: We now finished our campagne and started with Jaws of the Lion, to get our fix of Gloomhaven every week. There has been one major change since last time though. We only play the Steam version now, once a week. Even though I loved the game, we really feel like a hurdle is gone going digital here. Thats also the reason why we will wait for the (hopefully soon to be announced) Frosthaven digital version.

Gloomhave is to date my #1 ranked game.

This is the pinnacle of a tactical action dungeon crawler. It often gets the criticism that it is a euro puzzle game with a dungeon crawl skin, but my position is that this is a dungeon crawl with euro elements.

Pro's:
- Reduced randomness: there is still randomness of deck draws, but you know up front what your deck consists of so you have evolving probabilities which you can gamble on. I love this so much more than dice throws that have no or limited mitigation. Even though you can still have the bad luck of a full miss, I feel I have much more agency
- Good for solo play. I play 4 handed, which is only advisable if you have enough experience and are really fluent with the game
- Hero characters are, for once, completely different. I have played so many games where the difference between the heroes is in a couple of stats and a special ability or two, but this game shines when it comes to the heroes. Totally different play styles are encouraged naturally
- Fantastic card system, mainly in the abilities. The builds you can do with each character are not endless, but at least two different builds are possible, plus the tied initiative system and flexible top/bottom action system allows for in-turn changes of tactic, albeit limited, which for me is again thematic.
- Great and thematic rush timer. I normally hate most kinds of rush timers, whether it is a fixed turn system, increasing spawns or some other mechanic, this one beats them all in my opinion. Fatique grows during a mission resulting in your deck decreasing. The speed in which it does, is partially under your control which again increases player agency. It's thematic in a way that after x turns, your hero gets tired (more exchausted) and has less abilities to choose from.
- The game is huge. I have personnally played all 95 missions, played all playable character up to level 9, experienced all events etc. There is no way to do this 'legally' so after finishing the campaign I played 'one-shots' on the missions that were blocked. This is cheating of course, but I've never played a game where I wanted to complete all missions when experiencing a branching campaign
- The battles themselves are just great and while some call it repetitive, I did not get tired of it, and when it started creeping up, retiring characters and playing as different characters immediately brought back variety to last another dozen missions.

Con's:
- Mentioned many times: story is subpar. Because of the structure of the campaign it is also very fragmented, often resulting in confusion as to what happened previous to the mission or what event initiated the mission as that event might have occurred easily ten missions ago. The book assumes you are always up to speed on the story despite the fragmentation. My advice would have been to write short recaps of previous events for missions that are a chain in a story or initiated out of a specific event (they probably haven't implemented this in Frosthaven).
- Tiles are very generic. Some mission still generate quite a thematic setup (especially in the expansion) but better alternatives exist (Jaws of the Lion to stay in Gloomhaven territory).
- Can be fiddly, best played with an experienced Gloomhaven player for the bookkeeping. Campaign tracker app was also useful to mitigate bookkeeping
- Long setup time. Requires preperations or a well-thought out system of efficient setup. Once you get this down, it because less of a problem, but it will remain relatively time-consuming

My pro's carry much more weight than my con's, which are nitpicks really, but shows that there is still room to improve

Some general info:
For new players the hefty price tag can be hard to overcome.
But if you like story driven games, such as mansion of madess, with great combat elements this is a game for you!
I would say that the game is OK on 1-2 players but plays great on 3-4.
I myself have played it with my SO and have a 2 player experience and have tried 4 players a few scenarios.
Before buying this game you also must have a “dedicated player group”
This is meant to be played with the same people.
This doesn’t affect a solo player but the game is hard to play “multiple groups with” since much of it leans towards a single playthrough” experience with the stickers.
This game takes 100h+ to finish if played properly so depending on time and number of sittings this can take up to a year to finish. So when buying this game it can be a huge commitment for many.
However the game is quite forgiving if you change a member or one member drops (thinking of 3-4 player party)
*

**
The cons:
Shure I gave this a 10/10. But that doesn’t mean it doesn’t have issues.

-As I said I play 2 player playthrough and some scenarios and some characters lean very much to a bigger playgroup and is not greatly optimized for smaller parties. One of the starting characters, the tinkerer, is a healer and does very little to none damage. It is hard to choose that character in a 2 player game because the game does have a hardness curve that requires all characters to participate in the fight, not just heal. But in bigger parties, especially 4 players, Tinkerer is a great character.
-This game requires some sort of sorting. If it is with bags or if you buy some insert solution. You might also need to but a set of sleeves for all the cards and that can be quite expensive. So Aside from the hefty price tag you are going to need to put MORE money into it to make it playable.
I still think its worthwhile. I have played this on an off with my SO for 1.5 year. If I break down the amount of hours vs what I have paid I still think this has been cheaper than going to the cinema. And we have had fun. Even if I defend this it is quite the bunch of money.

With sleeves and sorters and removable stickers set you can get another playthrough out of the game, or even sell it if its in good shape.
-There is a lot of components and a lot of building scenarios and put away scenarios and it takes A LOT of space. We actually have it on two tables. You have place for cards. You have a map. You have your player sheets. You have your scenario that you paly on and you have all the pieces for the scenarios somewhere. And all the monsters and so on. It takes spaces!
I like the description that Gloomhaven almost becomes like a lifestyle when you play it.
-I fell that a tablet is essential. So I bought one just for the game. You are going to need help of scenario trackers, characters (companion tracker), and bet of all: monster tracker!
The game can be played fully on the board but the monster setups and control can be really heavy to deal with.
**

***
The pros:
There is so much to be said about the good of this game that it is hard to begin with. Your characters have A lot of customization to them that makes them interesting to play. And interesting to play several times. The character system makes you cycle through characters, adding story to why, and unlocking new characters.
On higher levels towards the end of the game if you feel like “there is nothing to customize” there is this huge enchantment shop for your battlecards that is super expensive because it is meant for the late game characters. The way this is built makes the game last long and feel interesting. Characters feel fresh and exciting to play and have several ways to be played (at least 2 ways). Shure one playstyle is in general a bit more effective than the other.

The way combat works and monsters fight makes it interesting and can create unique playthroughs if you end up having to play scenarios several times. I like the battle system. Is is a combination with a lot of tactics and decisions involved, and math, with a small luck modifier deck that you can modify to make better.
The story isn’t to heavy, more on the lighter side. You have some story about how your journey starts and then it sort of goes through there. Every scenario has a “why are we here” and a conclusion. I did try tainted grail and there everything is story. You go through a journal at every corner, and I like that, but here you get some text, fight for an hour or so, and then get a conclusion. It makes the game much more “accessible” even though I like story elements to a game.
***

****
Some sort of summarize:
Gloomhaven is a huge game with a hefty pricetag that needs some extra items (sorting solution &/or sleeves and scenario/battleapps) but it gives you a long story driven campaign where all stories connect. Interesting characters to play and many, oh so many hours of fun. In a way Gloomhaven takes “the best” of many different game mechanics and put them into one game and it works, most of the times. It also brings a game genre a face to the board game community. Before Gloomhaven (and tainted grail that came roughly at the same time) I have not seen games like this. And when searching around it seems that Gloomhaven was first with creating a game breaking formula. Managing story, combat and character creation almost in one go!
This game is for everyone loving boardgames and can be a great friend, family or solo player experience.

When I describe Feast for Odin to people, I may overemphasize how big it is, not because that game is small (it’s not, it’s massive by the standards of most other games), but because it leaves me with a limited ability to emphasize just how big Gloomhaven is, but I suppose I need to try: If FfO is a beast, than this game is a Balrog. Not sure if that works. Perhaps using less flowery language would be best: The game weighs 20 pounds. This is simultaneously the biggest box I have, as well as one of the most tightly-packed. The game has around 100 scenarios associated with interconnecting plot threads, has something like 20 different playable characters, and regularly unlocks new and exciting mechanisms. More importantly, however, the game is a masterclass in design. In many thematic “go fight through the dungeon” games, theme can take precedence over gameplay, but in Gloomhaven each turn feels brings interesting decisions (even choosing to do nothing can mean the difference between winning and losing). Further, I don’t recall any scenarios where winning felt easy or defeat felt inevitable. For a game this big with this many moving pieces to feel this tight is a rare combination, and for such a game to also have an interesting story with a unique and original world (this is one of the rare fantasy worlds that feels like it owes nothing to Tolkien) is something that I don’t think any other game matches. Being willing to commit to a campaign is important though. From a purely mechanical “let’s play one scenario” perspective, the game is probably around a 7.5 (good, but not a favorite). Having a steady group and playing it regularly, however? Easy 9.5 for me. This is not a game for everybody, but if this is a game for you then I cannot recommend it enough.

Comments: Gloomhaven is a cooperative game about hand management, scenarios, campaign, deck construction, variable players powers and simultaneous actions. The ideia is that players will use the characters in order to meet the demands given by each scenario (normally killing everyone), and will use their action cards to do so. Cards have two uses - bottom or top - and an iniciative number; players pick two cards to use (will have to use one top and one bottom, but doesn't have to commit to which will be which right now) and one of the two to be their initiative. After everyone have done the same, the initiative and actions for the creatures of the scenario are also revealed. After many rounds of this, players either win or lose; as time passes players will more and more lose cards that they can no longer use in the scenario.

Once a scenario is done, players return to Gloomhaven to buy items, have encounters, do their upkeep regarding leveling up, retiring, etc.

Varied comments:

- Earning experience by the use of cards is great, as it makes players think in the best way possible to milk the value, while also having to deal with the threats of the scenario;
- Perks that make your deck better and more unique are very nice;
- Campaign and class advancement. Nothing truly new here, but I like these two.

Scenarios & Events
Scenarios are actually well written and are more than just bash monsters and collect loot. You will do these two things regardless, sure, but isn't the goal sometimes. Yet, there are, maybe, too many scenarios in which the goal is to kill everything - still is hard to complain about variety when the game gives that amount settings.

The inclusing of battle goals (drawn at the start of each scenario), does add a lot, making scenarios with similar resolutions be dealt in different manners, while at the same time making players go out of their comfort zones.

The manual is very helpful in preparing the scenarios - giving right away everything that will be required - tokens, monsters, tiles. And since the scenarios are opened in parts, the set up is very reasonable.

The city and road events are well written, often witty and gives a lot of mood to the setting.

Balance of characters:
This is a truly hard task, yet, for the most part, the job was done. The classes aren't the usual - there is no "tank", "healer", "spellcaster". Though there are classes that fit better with these archetypes, they arent't boxed in this. Main ranged PCs like Cragheart can heal, attack melee and can soak damage very well; for instance. The PCs not only play highly different, but are also pretty even out in power level.

There are a couple that did showed more range and stronger actions, such as the Tinkerer, and the bag of XP that is the Sooth Singer. Others appeared to be more limited - both in available actions, as well as in XP: the Sunkeeper, for instance, has a rather dull character; the Bladeswarm is very weak with its summons.

Still, it speaks to the design of them that, when I asked my friends to make a list going from favorite to least of the PCs they used, all of them (and I) have or favorite in one of the starting classes. Maybe it is because we used them from level 1 (most of the others started in 3 or 4), but I don't think so, as the overall time using the PCs is roughly the same.

Difficulty of the scenarios:
Gloomhaven is quite easy. We knew this from the get go, and always played on Hard mode. Yet, our win rate is over 80%. While in many scenarios we don't feel it was easy - as many wins were by the skin of our teeth, in the last action of the last PC still standing, when just counting win/loss, the percentage doesn't lie.

This is even more so in 4 players than in 3. With four, in spite adding more enemies, the addition of a full character actions - damage, healing, element generation, and more, with 4 players we needed to increase the level of the enemies further.

I read and heard comments that, if wasn't this way, the game would fall flat: the scenarios are long (usually from 2 to 3 hours), and playing one over and over in order to get a win could be frustrating. Add this to the fact of the campaing last from dozens of scenarios, you could truly have a Campaing for North Africa in our hand - a game admired by its bold approach, but one that no one have the time to play it to its completion.

Yet, since I enjoy challenge (easy co-ops I tend to sell/trade right away), I got more and more to the side of going to the scenarios to challenge myself: thus I took unlikely battle goals and tried to fulfill them even at the cost of the whole mission. Furthermore, in this less co-op approach, the fight for coins was bigger, as well as going for XP rather than efficiency. It was like some solo games, in which the goal is to get the best result possible, and, in Gloomhaven, meant making your battle goal and having the highest amount of coins and XP you could in the end.

I guess this was, maybe, always the correct way to play, as the PCs are jerks in regarding to loans and trading (see Money and Items, bellow).

Cards (dual options, exhausting, damage):
Each PCs has an unique deck of cards and a size for the hand of cards, which has a lot of tempo and conducts the players to different approachs to their characters. All the cards are of dual use, which is the heart of the game - on each turn, two cards must be played. These will give the player his Initiative, and once is his turn, the player will have to activate the top half of a card and the bottom of the other. This creates a great amount of possible interactions, not only between the two cards, but with the scenario (you can change your deck before going to a scenario - for instance, adding more cards with Pierce when you know there are enemies with high armor) and with the other characters (with the Initiative, and by creating elemental energies that other players can use). Also, the top can always be used to make a melee 2 attack, and the bottom to move 2 spaces; giving more malleability to the decision process.

The exhausting mechanism is a superb mechanism. Once the player has gone through her deck (or sooner, but this isn't, usually, very good), she can rest. If she does a short rest, she loses one random card from the discard and get all the others, ready for the next turn. If she does a long rest, she loses one card she picks from the discard, activate the exhausted items, heal for 2, but this is all she will do for the next turn. Therefore, the more a player burn through the cards, more are the chances that she will fall of exhaustion and won't be able to continue in the mission.

Also, the cards that can be used for powerful effects, but once used, they are "Lost", going out of the deck. This adds pressure to the character and player, since the cycle of cards will become even shorter, increasing the chances of the hero to fall.

When damaged, cards can be lost to prevent it. Nice and effective both to avoid a luck hit to the PC, and also to bring more tough choices.

Money and Items:
By the rules, is impossible to give or loan gold to the others. This is, at the same time, dumb as a mechanic and anti-climactic as theme. There is no real explanation that truly explains it, thematically, why it works this way. Mechanically? Yes, yes, balance and such. I don't care. Almost all the other campaing driven, thematic dungeon crawlers were able to make money be of the group, or at least be allowed to give to others, if the person chooses. In Gloomhaven, no. Everyone is, apparently, pathologically attached to their money. You can go to adventures with these people, trust your life and limb to them; but hell to them if they even ask for some coin!;

This brings to the next, and closely related issue: you can't pass/give items to the others. If the above is dumb, this is ridiculous and doesn't even make sense, let alone be anti-climactic. How is impossible to pass a potion to someone? In Gloomhaven, it is. If you find an item, that you think you can use, but later found that truly isn't for you, you can give it to someone. No, no. Get this: you need to sell it to the market, for half its price, then your companion can buy it from the market for the full price! Gloomhavenians do love their money (see above), but they hate their fellows even more, to the point that you can't even sell the item, for say, 75% of its price to your companion, with you gaining 25% more and she saving 25%. Apparently the merchant guild did something really awful to the mind of the people.

Furthermore, the use of items. There are sense in some of them: potions can only be used once - sure. Some special effects, also - the poison dagger can be used again after a long rest, as you have time to add more poison on its blade. But for what weird reason my Axe was just one swing per scenario on it? If the game explained that isn't the items you can use, but a one burst of some magic they carry, that would be better - but, no, is just a mechanical cog that keeps players away from the theme.

Overall:
Gloomhaven is a very nice game. Strong in decisions and in mood. Lots of things to do, to upgrade. Scenarios are well put together and the book of them is huge; there is also a load of side quests to be done (or not). Highly unique characters - each having their own way to face the problems and to earn experience. After over 100 plays, I still think Gloomhaven (and also Frosthaven) would be better served by having multiple (3, 4, 5) campaigns of around 15-20 scenarios, than one huge; as new paths could be explore more freely and players wouldn't be so tied up on a game for so long, as the end points would allow for a breather; but is a personal preference, for sure, as who can deny the success of the formula when Gloomhaven sprung up a whole family of games and became number 1 in rankings for a good while, right?

A tremendous work from Isaac Childres - one that should take near a lifetime to make, but he made it seem easy. There are a number of features I have seen in other cooperative and thematic games, but the whole of Gloomhaven feels fresh, smart and fine-tuned. It is truly an amazing achievement.

Outstanding game in terms of depth, character evolution and replayability (about to finish all the scenarios in approximatively 400h). It is full in moments of pure happiness: discovering new characters and character combinaisons, a huge amount of road and town events, new gear you unlock even after hundreds of hours of play time, etc. The whole game is supported by smart and innovative design choices: choose-2-card system, the fact you start a scenario with all your abilities and feel your character getting more and more tired by loosing cards, an easily adaptable difficulty that allows you never to worry about the order you should play the available scenarios, and a rather clear rulebook along with a rich player community to help with edge-cases questions.
It is however not perfect: a long set up and tear down time and an annoying lack of storage solution (you shouldn't expect players to buy their own boxes and plastic bags just to avoid having hundreds of tokens and standees getting all over the box). Also, the 95 scenarios offer a diverse spectrum of quality: some have not been correctly playtested and are too easy or insanely difficult depending on how many characters your party holds.
Still one of the best games I have ever played, and loved every single hour spent on it!

Where to begin for this one? Perhaps chronologically is the simplest way. After several years hearing about how great Gloomhaven was, my friend finally received the French version he had kickstarted. We dove straight into it and haven't looked back since. (Edit : Well, this enthusiasm has since been stopped by the COVID crisis, but at least this gave me some time to reflect on the game and finish this review).

Gloomhaven is a phenomenal game in many aspects. The sheer amount of content is one thing, but what's really impressive is the way everything seems to work together. There is no part of this game that feels disjointed or unneccessary. It is huge but feels really easy to play.

I love the variety of the road and city events, and most importantly how logical the consequences of your actions are. We spend a good time discussing every one of them because we understood early on that there was no reward for dumb behavior, which means now we trust the game (a very important part of being engaged in a story).

I love the sense of discovery in this amazing world that reminds me of my small character wandering around the huge Final Fantasy maps. By the way, it's not the only way Gloomhaven feels like a videogame, I have the same flashbacks when we're kiting enemies, learning the patterns of enemies, or understanding the weak point of a boss. And of course, all the upgrading aspects that we only started unlocking, with the prosperity levels, the items that come with it, the enchantments and so on... they also feel like a great RPG taking place before our eyes.

I love how precise the rules are for such a complicated game. There is very little room for interpretation, and most of the rules make perfect thematic sense, which helps the immersion. The one flaw to me are the angles you can draw line of sight. I think they are too generous, but the rule is clear and easy to follow.

I love the sense of improvement I felt as I started to master the gameplay of my character, something I didn't think could happen in a dungeon crawler. I started out truly awful and cost my team an entire scenario with a string of bad decisions. I felt really bad afterwards, especially since we couldn't replay it right away and I had to spend the week thinking about what I could have done better. But this failure made me much stronger, and in the next game, when my friends complimented the way I juggled with elemental infusions, I couldn't be happier. And although I'm sure I'll be sad when my character retires (another great mechanism to feel the scale of our adventure and the sense of time moving on, by the way), I can't wait to discover more characters with specific tricks and combos.

I love the excitement when we open a treasure, and even I loved the betrayal I felt when it turned out to be a trap that exploded in my face !

You can see I'm very enthusiastic about this game, but there is only one aspect of Gloomhaven that I deeply regret, and that keeps Pandemic Legacy on top of my personal rankings when it comes to narrative campaigns: you don't suffer from defeat hard enough. I said earlier that this game evoked great memories of past videogame experiences, well this is the one aspect I wish it had not copied. By allowing players to fail a mission without penalties, keeping all the gold and experience they accumulated without dying, Gloomhaven lowers both the immersion in the world (how are we keeping the gold from this monster when his friend killed us all 2 turns later ?) and the emotional investment in the outcome of a scenario. I understand that the designer thought the time lost during the defeat would be enough of a penalty, but I can't help but think of the great moments of our Pandemic Legacy campaigns. And these were especially great because a loss would have been hurtful to our cities (through population decreasing), our characters (through scars) and even our entire world (in the final missions).

In the same vein, I wish the game was more assertive about the difficulty level. I understand some people want to experience the story more than nail-biting battles and painful restarts, but with the way the scenarios are adapted to the experience level of your characters, they all feel the same difficulty-wise, no matter the order you choose to go through them. As the old French saying goes, victory without risk brings triumph without glory. And in a world as immersive as this one, the triumph deserved to be as epic as possible.

Really wanted to love this game, but over time the cracks started to appear. After about the 10th play session, I created a document for things I didn't like as a way to brainstorm house-rules to fix them. They might be crap but figured I would post it as it highlights the issues I have with the game.
Major Issues:
1) Upkeep and admin during play – Keeping track of events during play is a necessary, but should be reduced to its simplest form and should be combined to incorporate the major mechanics of your game. You can have many changes during gameplay as rounds/turns are completed. But it is necessary to create a system that changes the same things every time a round is complete. If you have a combat system that could include magic, special abilities, or experience points, then 1 mechanic should be included that does all of these things. For example: Magic the gathering is one of the most varied and complex games there are, but the foundations are the same for most games.
- Roll for who goes first and then turn order is determined clock wise. This is established at the beginning and continues until the end. You Upkeep your board (turning everything active again, draw a card, and usually playing a land. Follow the same steps everytime to complete your turn. The mechanics are the same across the board but a simple combination of letting the player play specific cards in a specific order at a specific time, greatly adds variety without changing the core order of how things go. Once you have the basics, you build on that.
2) Repeatability should emphasized in the rules as well as the content. Combat should be the same across the board on who goes first, enemy movement, and attack patterns. However, fighting the same creatures that do the same thing every time or adding more of the same enemy or elite versions does not add more fun. Do not have the same enemies for consecutive missions or quests. For example, if you only have 10 different enemy types, you can easily make them stronger as the game progresses. But do not make the players fight 4 consecutive scenarios with different variations of the same enemy. For example, after completing 4 scenarios in Gloomhaven, we fought skeletons (move 1-2 spaces, attack range or melee) Bandits (move 1-2 spaces, attack range or melee) Marauders (move 1-3 spaces, attack range or melee). This is the same enemy with a different name.
3) Make events thematically correct. Don’t include stupid missions like helping a kid find is cat, becoming exhausted from doing so and then removing experience points the player has gained from previous missions. That makes no sense. Have a negative consequence relate to the situation (while looking for the cat in the abandon warehouse, you stepped on nail and take damage, or have to go last in initiative, or have no movement on your turn.
4) Give all players the ability to revive or safe their teammates. For fucks sakes Gloomhaven’s system could have 1 party member get attacked by 2 enemies and go down and be out of the scenario completely. Then the player has to sit there and watch. At least give each player the ability to save their friends and bring them back once a scenario.
5) Give the players basics they can fall back on that actually matter. Don’t let them just move 2 and attack for 2 if they can’t use their abilities. Let them double their movement, or double their attack, or Heal themselves or their teammates for a small amount. Some times moving 2 and attacking for 2 does nothing when enemies are 4 spaces away and your party is being slaughtered.
6) Encourage tactics and cooperation. Do not state in the rules that they have to be vague on what they are going to do. This is confusing and discourages players from working together to maximize their efforts and leaves each player fending for themselves and only encourages the maximum play for the individual. When its obviously more satisfying to play weaker cards that could boost the effect of a member of your party.
7) Make rewards simple. If your system rewards gold for killing an enemy, then do not make them sacrifice their turn or action just to collect that loot. (In Gloomhaven, you can also be robbed on the road and loose everything you worked for). Incorporate picking up the loot in their actions. Do make them use an action to “Loot” or end their turn on that square to pick it up. Let them easily collect the reward by having to at least touch that square during their movement.
8) Don’t gatekeep powerful items. In Gloomhaven, you only have access to a pool of items that is based on party’s reputation. Fuck that, not only does that not make sense thematically (Why would a vendor care who buys an item if they have the coin) but it also railroads the players. Make the really powerful items really expensive so if the party wants to pool their gold and buy that one item to do something cool, let them. Make one time use items cheap to purchase but focus on permanent items they can keep and build over time. These items can complement the exact build they are looking for.
9) Use dice, not cards for variety. Instead of making 50 different decks for modifiers, create a system that uses dice to add bonuses for combat. Dice, like a standard D&D starter, can be customized for each character type and can even be used outside of playing your game. There are too many cards that need to be in order and numbered at the bottom for each character and enemy and is completely unnecessary. You can scale level progression by the type of dice used. Oh, your level 5 now, so your attack bonus is a d6 instead of a d4. Gloomhaven will want separate piles of cards for each modifier. Also, the board gamer type will always appreciate and see the value of more dice. Not paper cards that are ruined with one drink spill.
10) Make level progression meaningful. Gloomhaven, I received 1 more extra point for HP, got to pick 1 card that had to replace 1 card from my hand but still only had 10 cards to choose from. No new items in the shop.
11) Let players swap items or loot unconscious party member items during gameplay. How dumb is it that a player could have a potion of healing they didn’t get to take before going down or unable to give that to another party member that may need it to finish the scenario.
12) Cardboard is inferior to laminated paper maps. For fucks sakes Gloomhaven has cardboard cutouts to link together with different sides and digging for some symbol on the underside of another. Then provides punch out cardboard for traps or other things to add to those pieces that get moved around during gameplay anyway. I know this is for adjusting the level of difficulty based on the number of players but why not create a scalability difficulty not based on the terrain. For example, have the same traps in a given dungeon, just have them do less damage or reduce the effects they have. Its dumb to build a difficulty system based the number of environmental factors as it is to adjust their impact. You could laminate 25 paper maps, with different dungeons on the underside and have 50 unique locations that already have everything set up besides the enemy locations. You can even design them so that they connect on either end as the story progresses. This would protect the maps from mildew or liquid damage and make it easier to set up each scenario. You can also control the quality of the art, so door ways look like doors, instead of an off centered punchout of cardboard art that looks like a rock.
13) Status effects should go on the mini and combat board, not the life tracker of each enemy. I only have 4 plays under my belt so far, but I think it's been sufficient to get an idea of the general slant of the campaign experience. The parts I enjoy are mainly legacy-level and the use of delayed consequences, the slow reveal of scenario chains, sidequests, simple Crossroads cards events, and world state changes. The legacy conceit works very well with this genre.

However, I'm still not quite sure where I stand with the core of the scenario play. It seems to take the concept of a D&D 4th edition session, deconstructs it down to micro-events spread across dual purpose cards, then re-assembles it into something where you spend every initiative round frowning at cards, deciding which to chain together, which will be ok to discard for the next X rounds, which will be good to burn for the rest of the scenario at certain points, table-talk about who moves where, who can infuse the battlefield with an element that someone else can use with their card, etc, etc... all for a single round in a skirmish with a handful of bandit fodder.

It sounds interesting on paper but it can be taxing, especially if taken as an experience of playing a board game emulating an RPG-in-a-box. Looking at it from that angle, I feel like the freedom and playfulness, and straight up velocity of the genre is pared down to cardplay that feels oddly restrictive, fussy, and slow despite the agency that it provides in the game (and those cards do allow you to do some really cool stuff). It's like you have to squeeze through this gauntlet of boardgamey analysis, just to pull something off that would have taken quick clearance from a DM and the roll of a d20.

But I think I have to resist looking at it from that angle because I suspect that the smaller narratives being churned through game mechanics is exactly what a board gamer coming at this genre from their own angle may expect. Case in point, there are tons of Mage Knight fans. I'm not one of those fans, for somewhat similar reasons as I'm conflicted about this game. This takes Mage Knight's crunchiness of systems propelling simple diegetic events and extends it, almost obscenely, across potentially years worth of play.

It's kind of a baffling game for me, at this point. It's something to be marveled at, but it's also a commitment that I'm not sure I'm going to find anywhere outside of solo play. My game group is most definitely not ready for this, and my son, who normally eats up this style of card play, is turned off by endlessly shuffled, swingy modifier cards (effectively a mutable d20, disguised to assuage die aversion) that can easily tank an hours-long scenario. So yeah, there it is on my table: a sea of solo campaign play, but also a brain burn. I'm not sure how often I want those two aspects joined together.

Edit: I don't need those aspects joined together, like ever. When I'm in the mood to play Brass Birmingham, I play that. When I want a satisfying dungeon crawl or adventure system, I play anything *other* than this. Donated to a curious friend, with zero regrets. This game simply isn't for me.

After all those years I need to revisit this rating.

Gloomhaven is now an established classic. I have a better opinion of it that what I had before and I think it deserves praises as a modern day classic. I still have reservations and at this point, they won't go away:

- The game game is unavoidably fiddly. Too many chits, too many details to take care of, too much preparation before a game and too much time to put back in the box. This affects the player's capacity to immerse himself in the game universe.

- This is a very SLOW game. It's even more apparent now that I decided to play it on Steam instead of using my physical version, being too bothered by the first aspect to go on with the physical version. A mission with just 3-4 rooms and two players playing a total of 4 characters, even online with the Steam digital version that handles everything, can take about 2 hours. 2 hours is fine in itself, but it's the slow progression that is fascinating. It's incredible to think how slowly you crawled through a very small area in 2 hours...

- The Encounters are a major miss. You get a vague context and then have to decide between two options without any reason to pick one answer instead of the other. It's always a coin toss. Too bad the effects are also quite dramatic. Get a curse and lose 4 life is a dispiriting way to start a mission. Then you play 1h30 only to find yourself out of cards and you blame the initial coin toss for it.

Otherwise, this is an achievement in boardgaming, just not one that I enjoy playing in the physical version. I find Jaws of the Lion much better from that standpoint.

Played, some models painted. Includes 3d printed organizer and 2 wooden player storage containers

------ What We Liked -----
- Character and story progression. Level up characters and cards. Unlock characters and scenarios.

- Detailed story elements and theme. Feels a lot richer of an experience than some other boardgame RPGs I've played.

- Lots of strategy, choices, and planning (which we find fun)

- Immersive components (which we also like)

- Other than some of the punch-outs having slightly unaligned art, the components are good quality. Boards and tokens are sturdy. (I cannot speak to the cards because I sleeved them all.)

- The game is graphically interesting to look at and the art is beautiful. I'm glad that the monsters are standees because it makes the board look really nice and is easy to identify what is where.

------ What We Didn't Like ------
- Takes FOREVER to set up and put away. All components are by picture and many are double-sided so it takes quite some time to sift through enemies and tiles to find what you are looking for. All characters have to be crammed back into their boxes which (especially with sleeves) requires some tetris. An insert is a MUST HAVE but only helps cut the setup time in half to like an hour instead of 2.

- Repetitive gameplay. Seems like every scenario has the same objective (kill all things or kill a specific thing) just different monsters/bosses. After playing a few times I get fatigue because the sessions are just SO LONG for what we're doing the whole time.

- The materials included in the game did not include a clear, easy way of how to get started. I had to download a bunch of fan-made documents off the files section in BGG and watch a bunch of tutorials before I could figure out how to get started.

- Very long games when playing with people who like to think things through and plan. We typically see about 4-6 hours per scenario (for a total of 8 hour session).

- Scenario booklet really needs a hard or thicker cover. The cover is the same material as the pages and since the book is so large and heavy, I'm constantly needing to be very careful not to tear the front and back pages off by accident.

- Some of the finer points to rules are hard to locate in the rulebook. When we first got started we spent a lot of time on BGG trying to look stuff up. We ended up making a cheat sheet for ourselves.

I hadn't heard of this game, and neither had my friends. It was only chance that we were able to pick up a copy and begin our campaign, but I'm glad we did. It turns out to be a great dungeon crawler and a fascinating legacy design.
The game starts out introducing you to the world and the combat system, and from there, you pretty much have free reign over how your campaign develops. There's always a choice of missions, event outcomes, and plot forks, so every session you have to decide where to steer your adventure. (This may suck up some time in discussions between players.)

The legacy aspects work on a number of levels, shaping the events, character classes, scenarios, items, etc. that you have access to. There's a lot of stuff to unlock, and you'll be looking forward to it like a kid with an advent calendar, checking each box of the town's rising prosperity and each step of your character's personal quest with anticipation.
I will make a slight complaint about those quests. Some of them are much easier to do than others, and many rely on circumstances that might not be fully within your control. Without more than the slightest of spoilers, one of our group got a pair of quests to get/spend a bunch of cash. It just happened that the characters he was playing were really good at hoarding money, and he had them done in no time. Meanwhile, another player had a quest to kill a bunch of monsters, while playing a support character with minimal combat ability. (He also had poor looting capability, so the expensive quests would have been just as bad.) I’ve been stuck like this a couple of times, and ran 2 chars at a time, so that I could at least advance on one of their quests. Nothing stops you from doing this, just be aware that your quests may not finish in a timely manner. You may have to bend/ignore the rules as written to play the characters you want to.
The main content of the game is quite good. The character classes available all feel distinct and offer good variety in play styles. The card selection system likewise gives you a lot of freedom to choose how you act (and some tough choices about when to use which moves, what cards to replace with new ones, etc).

My complaint about the game balance extends to the classes and items as well. Our group quickly identified which pieces of gear were powerful, and which useless. There are an awful lot of cards that have a once-per-mission ability that really doesn’t do that much.
The character classes are even more skewed, with several that have decent-to-strong damage potential, a couple that are hard to use and finicky, and a couple that are seriously OP. All (nearly) have the potential to be good, but dealing massive damage to a room full of enemies or repeatedly refreshing allies’ cards/items is just a cut above what other classes can do. With the exception of those couple, they’re all fun to play, but the personality of the players starts to become important. It can get old in a hurry when you get in position to unleash your big attack, only to see all the nearby enemies mowed down by the glass cannon guy well before the earliest you can act. Conversely, it can get real irritating playing as a support character if you’re always trying to get next to your teammates in order to refresh cards/hand out medpacks/etc and they’re forever running away from you to get close to the front lines. The rules preventing players from sharing specific info hamper your efforts to coordinate and avoid such mishaps. Consequently, they tend to get undermined pretty quickly.
The scenarios can also be kind of uneven. Some are seriously tough, while others are trivial with the right characters.

The events and story stuff are fairly interesting. Each session, you get a couple choices that may impact your reputation, money, condition going into the next mission, and so on. You have to choose based on incomplete information, and the writers like to try and obfuscate things. Without saying more, I was somewhat satisfied with the way they developed things, but not entirely. They went with a different style than most fantasy works, eschewing the tired elves/dwarves/orcs thing and inventing new races & such. The story’s big reveal and conclusion was kind of lame, but the rest was decent.

Components are good quality in this one, and you get a ginormous pile of them. It’s a pricey game, but as a value proposition, very good. The monsters are only cardboard standees, but there are dozens of types, with different behavior. Between the main campaign, the solo quests, the randomized missions, and the bonus online campaign, you’re got over a year’s worth of content to work through.

This game is a brilliant mix of traditionally "Ameritrash" concepts--a dungeon crawl, randomized combat outcomes--and deeply "Eurogame" systems--action selection, hard choices from limited subsets. It's also a very lengthy campaign game, of which I've only seen the first parts; as of this writing, none of our characters have retired yet, although some are close.

I love, love, love the puzzle-y aspects of figuring out your turn, the best actions to play and the order in which to play them. And then the enemies do something that wreck your plans and it all goes to hell. Or you keep drawing that whiff card in your deck; Gloomhaven doesn't care. I like those parts a little less, I have to admit.

Physically the game is a monster, a genuinely massive pain in the ass to set up and tear down and track information with. The vast majority of my play has been with the digital version, which has its own issues (it's rife with bugs), but the amount of bookkeeping that it eliminates is worth the pain.

The game's not perfect; the balance is all over the place, enough that they're making a second edition of the game. The randomness of the combat results can often feel entirely too random, which is harsh for a game that often takes hours per mission. And AP-prone players can drag the whole thing to a halt constantly. I suspect 3 is the perfect player count, although I've been having fun with a 2-mercenary game in the alternate game mode in the app; the two of us are considerably more strategic than the friends I play the main campaign with, and so it's been interesting to watch the difference between well-dovetailed plans and ones that are... less so.

Still, a great game, and one I look forward to continuing to play. Digitally, though; ain't nobody got time for the physical board game.

Pros:
1) D&D without a DM. This really makes it easier to play and organize a session without needing one person to brunt the responsibility of DM.
2) Better combat mechanics than D&D. The rules are clearer, the objectives are simple, things are unpredictable and therefore also very exciting. It is well-balanced over the course of the scenario - loose too many cards early on, and you are likely to run out of steam at the end. Each PC has their own secret objective during the scenario and cannot share loot, which encourages tactical selfishness and makes it again very unpredictable. Every other player action heavily influences your battle ideas and may force you to re-evaluate and adapt. Better initiative system than boring, unbalanced D&D "Roll once and add your modifier".
3) XP bonuses for using certain abilities promotes the use of those abilities. These are normally powerful or very beneficial to your team. So not only do you feel satisfaction from gaining the XP points, but they are normally very impactful and help newer players learn the best moves.

Cons:
1) D&D without a DM. Yes I repeated the same point above, because the DM has a critical function that the game fails to replace. The DM is responsible for ensuring the game is immersive, the story is interactive, your characters are integrated well. When I played Gloomhaven, I felt like some generic character with no background. Why was I adventuring? Why were my compatriots adventuring? Why did we form a party and adventure together? I have zero emotional ties to anyone and even my own character.
2) Without RP, game can be rather flat.

Popular BGG number 1 rank Euro dungeon crawl legacy game by Isaac Childres. Very puzzly hand management: choose two cards and use the upper part of one card and the lower part of the other card. One of these cards also determines your initative for a round.
Gloomhaven has two layers of gameplay: tactical combat and questing on a world map with trading for equipment and dealing with random (binary choice) events.

I like:
+ Great app on Steam that takes care of the annoying set-up, tear-down, rules, and bookkeeping
+ Massive amount of content (to unlock) and play time for hundreds of hours
+ Great tactical combat hand management system (card driven, a lot of decision making: discard the card for the rest of the combat, pick one of the different action on the card, modifier cards add uncertainty). Your remaining cards also act as an additional life meter for your hero (no more cards, hero gets exhauted)
+ There are also strategic aspects which cards to burn (unavailable for the rest of the encounter)
+ Monster combat AI is quick but sometimes stupid and unthematically. However, monster movement is complex and error-prone (not deal breaking)
+ A lot of different characters and monsters to unlock who play very differently (some may be better or more fun than others)
+ Unusual retire mechanic where your hero disappears and you choose a new, different character (variety). This also mitigates problems that normally occur when playing with (overpowered) maximally leveled heroes
+ Equipment and perks provide additional boosts
+ Difficulty adjusts well with different players and levels
+ Artwork

Neutrals:
# Mostly deterministic, however, some luck of the draw (resolving combat modifiers)
# Life goals are neat and fun in the beginning
# Mixed components, overall good production
# Player count: 3-4 players complement each other better than 2 players. 3-4 player will unlock more envelopes but takes longer to complete a mission. 2 player is more difficult
# Solo: play two heroes
# Simple multiple choice quests that may change the story of the game
# Drawn battle goals may be hard to achieve with certain characters
# Players' summons are controlled by AI who act quite stupid and inefficient
# Elements add another layer but also more bookkeeping
# Big game box (which is necessary for its content)
# Table hog
# Kill all monsters as usual win condition
# Story is okay at best. Focus is on the puzzly combat
# Combat system is good but can also be frustrating when you have to waste actions
# Restricted communication: initiative values.

I do not like:
- Some scenarios are hard to win (requires very optimized play or certain abilities) and may stop you from progressing the campaign.
- Repetitive, slow grinding is a big aspect of the game's progression
- Very stupid monster scripts.
- Long setup / teardown (longer than an actual game)
- Big rules book and the rulebook has several ambiguities. Hard to learn
- A custom storage solution improves usability a lot
- Random events between encounters where you choose one of two options which provide negative effects
- There are some semi-coop elements (personal combat objectives, life objectives, looting, no equipment sharing). Thematically, all players are selfish rogues. This feels a bit odd at times, because overall the game appears more like a fully cooperative dungeon crawler.
- As you lose cards over the course of the battle, your options diminish over time.

Similar games:
* Sword & Sorcery
* Dungeon Alliance (very deterministic dungeon crawler and deck building, scenario-based, story expansions available)
* Middara (fully cooperative JRPG inspired miniatures adventure, dungeon crawl, campaign game, simple dice-based combat, weak story)
* Too Many Bones (dice-based skirmish game, more randomness, less deterministic, no big campaign, less time consuming)

Dungeon crawl game with a bit of a legacy game feel. The core mechanisms are relatively simple to play there are some rules that require referring back to the book at times. Card play feels a lot like Mage Knight but far less irritating as you can play any card for a basic move/attack action. At the end of the day though, it's just a hack-and-slash game where you move and attack over and over again until everything is dead or you've run out of cards; it just feels like an absolute slog. While I'm used to random combat from D&D/Pathfinder and having a personal combat modifier deck is a neat idea, the randomness of combat in this irritates me as the best laid plans can be blown away by 1 bad card draw. With RPGs you can react to a fluid situation whereas Gloomhaven requires you to plan your part ahead of time without knowing how things will be situated when it becomes your turn to act, and you can have a turn completely go to shit because another player or NPC acted before you and changed the state of the board. I hate the losing a card from your hand when you rest mechanic which serves as a rather heavy-handed game timer; run out of cards and you're forced to retire from the scenario. Did you lose your one remaining good card for this scenario? Too bad unless you want to give up the few HP you have left because everything has been attacking you. Hahaha, hope you like trying the same scenario setup the same way again! In something so combat focused, this seems rather harsh. Personal goal cards are randomly dealt out at the start of each scenario and you can get stuck with a card that is almost impossible to complete for your particular character which makes advancement tedious. Not being able to share gold is also incredibly irritating; the rules basically say you're a group of mercenaries who are in it just for themselves and refuse to share with one another - you're just together as a group as a matter of convenience. If a character satisfies their overall personal objective, they just leave the group and get replaced by another character. Killed all the baddies? Sure hope you looted all of that treasure because while the scenario had ZERO urgency, you can't take the few minutes necessary to round up that loot and you're forced to leave everything you didn't collect behind because reasons. There are some good idea in here but the majority of the game just irritates the hell out of me. Childres' first game, Forge War, was an infinitely more enjoyable experience in my books.

I haven't put more time into a game than I have for Gloomhaven. Ever since I was a kid I wanted to play a dungeon-crawl board game with my friends, and this game gave me that experience in spades. We played for well over 4 years, and completed about 60% of the content in the game. I don't know how to feel about that.

The battles are very nicely balanced and extremely tactical. Playing off of your teammates actions is required for victory. The story provided is OK, serviceable and interesting, but not compelling. Finding out what happens next in the story is not what keeps driving you forward. Finding out what the next class is, or what powers your current class is going to get next, or if this combo of cards will be better than your current strategy is what keeps you coming back to the game.

A couple negatives. The game takes a very long time to set up and tear down. The dungeons are also very long. Our 5-player sessions (supported through online rule changes recommended by the developer) were constantly 2-3 hours long and only one dungeon each time. I did everything I could to speed this process up, and it's not something that was achievable for my group. If you are playing Gloomhaven on your Game Night, you are having a Gloomhaven Night.

Overall, I was very happy with the time I put into Gloomhaven, but asking for 4 years for any one game before you've completed it is a big ask. If you had a dedicated group that was playing more than once or twice a month, this would probably not be an issue.

I could go on at *great* length about the things I don't like about Gloomhaven, but there's already mountains of opinion so I'll keep this reasonably short. I find the game to be thematically nonsensical, the story to be tedious and forgettable, and the combat to be a dull, static puzzle that rewards planning complete, optimal solutions over active turn-by-turn play.

I find it obnoxious that the basic combat mechanic is "taking actions takes away your actions." Failure usually has nothing to do with whether your characters are defeated in combat, or whether you faced overwhelming odds and made actual poor choices, but whether you successfully optimized.

Then there are the actions themselves. Imagine D&D where your wizard's spell either "does 4 radiant damage and you fall prone OR turns lead to chocolate and you move 5 feet". There's nothing to relate these things except that you have to choose between them. This is how every Gloomhaven card works. The effect is to make the game purely puzzle solving, and all theme and story is dispensable. They do nothing for each other. You're not "fulfilling your quest". You're prioritizing your resources in advance and then taking an hour to see if you optimized properly.
