[Digital version review] One word comes to my mind when I think about Gloomhaven: meh. Everything about this game feels just meh. Although the core mechanism sounds interesting on paper, it can get repetitive quite early due of combos.

Furthermore, some actions are very situational (destroying obstables, disarming traps) but very often they're discarded by the time you would actually need them and it's not really possible to plan this ahead because many things are hidden when you enter a map. While it is possible to repeat a map after defeat - where is the fun in repeating every single map before finishing it? Considering how crucial action management is in this game it probably would have been better to use open maps with very little to no hidden information.

Writing of action management, I'm also not a fan of the "automatic miss" - attack modifier (you pull one out of a bag on each attack and they can be positive, neutral or negative) because misses can be tremendously punishing on big hits, if not scenario deciding.

Your bag of modifiers is one of three things that you upgrade during level up. The leveling system in this game is meh, too, imhb. It takes a while to level up and then you get +1 hp, one new action card with which you can replace an old one, a "perk" that let's you change your bag of modifers a bit (but none let's you remove the miss!! *groan*). None of these are particulary interesting or make you feel stronger. There are also ways to buff you by spending gold (items, blessings) but none of them are intriguing or necessarily game deciding.

Storytelling: also meh. It's your generic "adventurers meet in a tavern and go fighting evil guys, looting stuff and repeat the process ad infinitum." The story has no real depth to it, it just sets up hundreds of skirmishes that feel pretty much the same.

Overall, the mechanics had potential but the implementation is mediocre.

Full disclosure: I've never played the physical version of Gloomhaven. This rating is a combination of playing through the entirety of the digital version and knowing how it translates to the tabletop.

Gloomhaven as a video game is a pretty solid 8/10. The interface could be better and it could better clarify some of the poor rules text it inherits from the board game, but it's polished and made with love for the original product. For the fraction of the price it costs it's a great time if you're looking for a dungeon crawl.

Where this goes sideways for the tabletop version of the game is the sheer volume of setup/teardown/enemy automation/rules enforcement that you lose, and knowing that a 2-3 character party still takes 40-60 minutes to play out average scenarios in the digital version. Tabletop Gloomhaven has to be the easiest game to repeatedly cheat at by accident simply because there's just too many things to keep straight for the duration of time you're going to be playing it. The puzzle/scenarios are not interesting enough to warrant 2-3 hours grinding away on each, and the rewards of unlocking new equipment or characters don't keep the experience as fresh as one might hope. Sure there's new complexity to discover, but I actually found starting new characters to be deeply unrewarding because of the power hit your party takes by losing so much equipment. Truthfully, the one advantage I can give the tabletop game over the digital version is that when the randomizer deck throws out complete garbage that would lead to extending a scenario several more rounds, you could choose to just ignore this overall bad feature (mechanically the randomness is good, but in practice the lows stand out far more than the highs) and save yourself a bunch of time cleaning up a scenario you know you've already won.

You could not pay me to play Gloomhaven the tabletop game. I understand how it can be appealing to a certain gamer or group, but this is not a game for your average person. If you have even a passing interest in Gloomhaven, buy the PC game instead.

My verdict: I love this as a solo game. I am using 3 characters for my party. It takes me like 4 hours to setup, slog through a scenario, cleanup, etc. But I have enjoyed doing this on boring days when others couldn't come. My first mission played with other players and a couple times I have had people play as part of my party during my main solo campaign. Those experiences have been alright and everyone sort of liked it but were not sold on it. It took long enough to teach them and there was too much confusion to play combat with hidden card selection so I just am not seeing the ideal situation for multiplayer in it. But for solo, this satisfies a short term game solution for me. I will probably burn through enough of it that things start to get repetitive soon. But so far unlocking new characters (retired 4 of them in my first week of play after about 20 scenarios completed) has kept me interested for now. I am trying to keep the copy in good shape and will likely trade it when I am finished milking what there is for me to enjoy from it.

I can understand why people like this game, and the accolades it has received over the years for its ingenuity and replayability. The hand management and "advantage/disadvantage" mitigate a lot of the randomness of monster card draws, which is a pretty inventive concept that I haven't seen in other dungeon crawlers. There are a seemingly endless amount of missions to undertake, and the leveling up / retiring characters is another great way to add longevity to the game.

With all that said, there are a ton of moving pieces in the physical board game version of this, and I've never played it without some sort of digital helper, to manage the monster moves/stats, etc. Personally, I think the fully digital version of the game is the best.

Additionally, over the course of the times I've played (probably ~15 games), it's a bit tedious for me. This criticism isn't necessarily specific to Gloomhaven, but dungeon crawlers are generally pretty repetitive. Go in dungeon > kill monsters > grab treasure/complete mission > level up/buy armor > rinse, repeat. Theme is not particularly important to me in games, and I don't care too much about the story elements; I'm more interested in the mechanics and puzzle solving of board games, and dungeon crawlers are less focused on those things.

Overall, it's a great game for what it is — though possibly better suited for a digital environment — and just not the style of game I enjoy.

While I enjoyed it as an easy 10 for my first 10-25 missions, someone proposing a new campaign nowadays for me would be a pretty tough sell without a novel twist. I should try jaws of the lion sometime though...

Additionally, I find it doesn't respect your time on a loss, you get an insulting amount of rewards with the only cost generally being your time, and you're expected to simply try again. Ideally a campaign moves forward and adapts to your outcome (Pandemic's funding and scoring mechanics are stellar here). Early Pandemic Legacies fell a bit short on replaying a lost month, but even then your actions in the first attempt -mattered-, permanently affecting the board state and your resources both positively and negatively, so it was less than a tenth the frustration as losing in Gloomhaven.

Having only play digitally via Steam, I can't make a rating based on the full game including setup/tear-down and managing rules. The digital version works fantastically and I imagine I'd struggle to enjoy the physical game to its fullest, though I understand why it's rated so high. The game has some big flaws that make it hard for me to rate it much higher, including the complete and utter lack of balance between characters and items, the disconnect between character design and game play, and the pigeonholing design that forces you into specific play styles.

Starting with character balance, there are some characters that are so far and above better than others, that if you have them on your team and you play a lower tier character, you'll feel like you aren't helpful to the team at all. For example, Sawbones is supposed to be a great healer, but he can only heal in range 1 which means your team better be focused on being in position to get healed, or you just can't heal them at all, forcing you to play as a (weak) DPS.

In addition, some classes don't fit their archetype at all. The scoundrel excels at stabbing people that are adjacent to your allies and/or not adjacent to their allies, which is great if your teammates can help you with that, but there are characters that can do more damage and without any setup, so it feels painful to play when you know their are better options. I play the ranged scoundrel which is fun, but it's the only option imo. Scoundrel also sucks at looting compared to other characters that get to loot for free without burning a card, and you'd think they'd be the best.

Finally, the game just doesn't work well in terms of shields/retaliate/healing unless your team is specifically designed to work around that, and DPS is just more fun (due to the game's design) so your team will always just play DPS. The game forces you down a specific path with your class and a specific path with your team comp that you can't really play the way you want, and some characters are just unplayable. We've played maybe half of the scenarios and it's fun enough, but it's becoming rote since things don't really seem to change as we move forward. Unlocking characters was fun, but didn't change the game because most classes are useless. Unlocking new items is fun, but doesn't change the game much because of the same reason, some are useless. And enchantments are so absurdly expensive AND limited (to 9 I think?) that when you can finally afford ONE, it's hard to choose which one to buy since you have so few choices.

Overall, the systems are really interesting, but there are a few design choices that leave me disappointed and wondering how much I'd have to houserule to really enjoy it to the fullest. I see why people like it, but I can't give it a higher score due to these flaws.

I love creating a backstory for my character in Gloomhaven. I love integrating that story into the constructed snippets of story the quest book and cards dole out.

Gloomhaven is a game of Euro-inspired tactical combat in a persistent world of shifting motives. Players will take on the role of a wandering adventurer with their own special set of skills and their own reasons for traveling to this dark corner of the world. Players must work together out of necessity to clear out menacing dungeons and forgotten ruins. In the process, they will enhance their abilities with experience and loot, discover new locations to explore and plunder, and expand an ever-branching story fueled by the decisions they make.

Playing through a scenario is a cooperative affair where players will fight against automated monsters using an innovative card system to determine the order of play and what a player does on their turn.

If it seems intimidating, start with Gloomhaven: Jaws of the Lion. That version is for the more casual gamer.

This game I bought initially after hearing a lot about it. For someone who grew up playing the simplest of board games, I’ll admit it seemed very ambitious to try something like this but I did have a bit of a leadup after playing some dungeon crawlers like Hellboy or Dark Souls, yes they are completely different games but the idea is that I was delving into games with hefty rulebooks so this wasn’t too hard to consider trying. First there is a ton in the box and it is intimidating at first. If you are considering buying this game and are reading this review you WILL NEED a storage solution for some of the contents. For me all the standees for the enemies go into plastic bags usually a couple different types per bag, all bosses in one bag; etc. Apart from that I developed a routine over time for boxing so the box closes nicely and everything is somewhat organized. The game comes with 95 scenarios and in a playthrough you most likely won’t play them all. But after completion of campaign you can always continue and play as I have and when the game has cards that it says to tear etc I have not done that. You can make this game replayable if you really desire to. I also am a bit of a obsessive so I like to keep my games complete and everything as I bought it. The STORY itself is honesty kinda meh. It’s definitely not the reason to buy the game. The theme is great, the world is great, but the story very much is one thing leads to a next and so on. The GAMEPLAY is where this game absolutely shoots into the stratosphere. No dice, but in case you’re reading this and don’t know, each class has its own deck of cards you’ll start with base level cards and over time as you level and upgrade you can modify the hand you bring into scenarios. And also whenever you do damage you have a modifiable attack deck which will apply to your attack number. For example -1, +1, or a “miss” are possible ones you can draw. All enemies also use a deck like this too making the combat always intense and intriguing.
Overall I’d say if you are looking for a really really in depth game and want to spend hours upon hours delving into a world full of adventure and mysteries and unlockables, you really should get this game. Seriously. Also heads up, the game box does have some weight to it.

I finally got to start a campaign recently with my family after years of hearing the box beckon me. The hype is justified - Gloomhaven is captivating.

I'm sure I have nothing novel to add at this point. The core hand management gameplay is tense and interesting. The drop in/out flexibility makes GH much easier to get to the table compared to similar big campaign games. And while GH is very much a board game at heart, the narrative decision points and individual goals provide enough sense of role-playing for players to feel some personal identification with their characters. GH isn't exactly "D&D in a box", but it's close enough to scratch that itch for groups that don't want a real tabletop RPG with all the overhead that entails.

I'd also add that the rules are remarkably tight for a relatively complex game, particularly for a debut game with a novel system. In our first few scenarios, I've only hit a few rules questions I couldn't resolve immediately and they weren't critical anyway. The rules - like the rest of the experience here - are incredibly polished by any standard.

Withholding a final rating until I get further into the campaign.

But I will say where most of these games fall short is in the dungeon crawl itself, it is usually a fairly lame ability spam fest where you just run around doing your best DPS action over and over and then go back to town to gear up for another boring round of monotonous monster mashing. Why even bother leveling up and improving the characters if playing with them in the game is boring?

Gloomhaven flips this on it's head because it has come up with a card based action selection system that I can best describe as "streamlined Mage Knight". You have a small (8-12?) hand of cards to work with that give you 2 possible actions (a top and a bottom) with an initiative value. You have to chose which to use and then they are gone from your hand and possibly permanently. So you need to really think about what you're doing and maximize your card play. Brilliantly the cards in your hand also serve as a timer since your hand will shrink and once you have too few cards left you are out of the round.

I've really enjoyed playing the actual game here, and getting the occasional item or new ability card actually opens up new combinations and possibilities for more interesting card play.

The juice seems to be worth the squeeze here so far.

The story elements to this point have been typical expected surface level board game stuff, but I'm only about 1/10th of the way through the campaign so maybe that will change, but even if it doesn't the game play itself is fun enough to keep me coming back....and we haven't even gotten to experiment with a ton of different classes yet.

In short the system itself seems to warrant the amount of content the designer has created within it and that is a HUGE departure from previous titles of this type.

Engaging and intuitive - that's how I'd describe this game. It has good (but not outstanding) story, with some branching paths that unfortunately all lead to the same conclusion (although they affect other aspects of the game so it's not like decision making doesn't matter).

An interesting game, but too ambitious and trips over itself painfully.

Being able to scale between 2-4 players is a great feature to have, but having more enemies with higher stats just means that at 4 player every player needs to set up their character to be tanky enough to take a beating (since no tank can take that much abuse).

Having 100 missions in the box is great, but after you play 20 or so, they all feel the same. Also, since the game is non-linear and full of side quests, I lost track of any semblance of story long ago. Also, characters level at an anemic pace to try to dangle some amount of carrot in front of players.

To not force players to play the same character for so long, players can retire characters as they complete personal quests, except personal quests are horribly balanced. Some are trivial to complete, others take a long time or are literally impossible, depending on how far you are in the story. Also, since parties are composed of characters of different levels and still need to feel fun for everyone, characters don't get super powerful over the course of the game. Level ups tend to give you cards that are either basic cards with a number increased by 1 or are cool effects but single use, meaning you are giving up survivability for power. Similarly, items are very limited use and, as you level up, you just get items that are slightly better.

For me, after getting through about 1/3 of the campaign, half of the group was so miserable, that we were on the verge of not wanting to play together anymore.

This game deserves its success. The choices are tactical and strategic. The scenarios are tense, sometimes difficult. Even playing the same character from one game to another, it will not be the same because you have to adapt to the configuration of the dungeon. The choice of cards used for the scenario by our character will also have an impact on the style of play. The drawing of the modifier cards makes it possible to simulate the vagaries of combat and generates an appreciable element of surprise, generating tension and epic moments! We are only at the beginning of the campaign but it is interesting to see the world evolve, the city of Gloomhaven and our characters. The number of scenarios available is impressive and it takes a moment to go around the characters. Replayability is important. I don't think I will ever need the expansion or so head to the new Frosthaven iteration.

In the negatives:
- I have the first rulebook fix. It was very difficult for me to understand the setting up of a scenario and yet I am used to reading rules. Fortunately, I was able to speak to acquaintances to help me and watch a tutorial on the internet. After a few games, it's easy to remember the set-up and the rules (I recommend having a player aid nearby for the different effects that can occur during a fight).
- It is possible that a certain weariness sets in by playing too often in a row. I had this feeling when my character did not evolve in his personal goal or when we lost a scenario. Sometimes you have to wait a few scenarios before you have enough money to buy new items or upgrades in Gloomhaven.
- The story give life to the whole. However, this is not the element that made me want to continue the adventure. I play it more for the fun and tactical side than for its story.

The video game is also very interesting and enjoyable. Solo, it requires mental gymnastics to combine the powers of the characters. You must first familiarize yourself with the powers of the cards, the style of play of the character, to feel more comfortable. And one can get a bit schizo if one has to consider one's personal purpose and battle objectives.

Generally speaking, I enjoy starting a game of Gloomhaven. I highly recommend it.

Some odd features (i.e certain battle goals and having to retire characters at certain points although this encourages exploration of the many character classes available) are present but make action decisions more challenging. Our group can't get together to play often (sometimes 2-3 months between sessions) and this makes keeping track of the story and what we were planning to do somewhat difficult. There is an app to assist with many of those bookkeeping issues that is very helpful (but not required for the game).

Only 7 plays logged but we have completed over 50 of the scenarios. I have a love-hate relationship with this game. The combat is fun and crunchy, but also feels too restrictive. The character progression is addictive and satisfying, but limited by the amount of gold you have available. The gear and items on offer are interesting and varied, but you have a limited amount of use from them in any given scenario. And some of those scenarios themselves are absurdly unbalanced (looking at you green goo scenario...I have PTSD from that).

As such, I recommend Gloomhaven if you are willing to house-rule it to meet your needs. We like collecting gear and items and actually using them more than once a turn; as such, we have house-ruled that short rests refresh our re-usable items rather than long rests. We also hate the "loot" mechanic; we have adjusted so that if you end your turn on a coin, you pick it up. Looting is still required to get a mass amount of coins or treasure. We found this helped improve our gear gain just enough to actually earn more of the items we've earned in the market.

To mitigate the strength of these house-rules, we also typically play at a difficulty higher than base to keep the tension up. It's the perfect sweet spot for us.

I really wanted this to work, but after pushing myself through a full, honest 15 scenarios looking for anything to keep me on the hook, I just had to accept that the whole experience was pretty miserable.

As has been said by so many others, the setup and teardown is prohibitively time consuming, and even a short session requires so much bookkeeping on the part of the game owner that the widespread description of Gloomhaven being a DM-less experience feels disingenuous at best.

Enemy AI manages to be both error-prone and dumb. You would think that a system opaque enough to spawn a challenging fan-made online quiz would produce less robotic and less exploitable enemy behavior during combat. It's almost like the role of Dungeon Master or a robust digital AI system is necessary for meaningful enemy tactics in games like this...

The combat modifier deck feels like a downgrade to custom dice or a bag of tiles (ala Arkham Horror LCG) for seemingly no other reason than to give players the illusion of less randomness, but with the added headache of constant reshuffling.

The exhaustion/recovery system is needlessly frustrating and weirdly unthematic, and it is the only real source of difficulty in the whole game. Hoarding cards during the early portions of a scenario is crucial to ensure your character doesn’t become prematurely exhausted, but this means that most scenarios consist of hours and hours of piddling around with Move 2 / Attack 2 effects until you get to the last room and can actually start have fun playing the cards that make your class compelling. Gloomhaven makes no effort to emphasize the importance of this scenario cadence in the rules, and learning it yourself through several three hour delayed player eliminations early on is a vicious, depressing waste of time.

The plot is paper thin and the writing is shockingly cliché for how original the world seemed from the outside. The campaign is also pretty unresponsive to scenarios being done out of the "intended" order; random characters that the party hasn't met yet will pop in and out of story segments, only to later be "introduced" to the party after circling back to their branching scenario path. I get that this stuff is harder to get right in a physical medium (a recurring theme for Gloomhaven), but it shouldn't be this blatant.

The treasure looting system also breeds an unhealthy amount of tacit hostility with your "teammates"; treasure is individually gained and cannot be shared, and for some reason that has never made any thematic sense the mercenaries cannot pick up any coins or open any chests on their way out of a now-empty dungeon at the end of a scenario. The system incentivizes tactical greed, but all it takes is one overly-greedy move by a player to cost the whole group a scenario that may have already eaten up hours of playtime, and the only solution offered by the game would be to restart and try again from the beginning. Gross. For this reason I am convinced that Gloomhaven, like so many other coops, only really works as a solo game.

Considering that, why am I paying over a hundred dollars for a solo dungeon crawler that pales in comparison to even the most middling video games in this genre?

It is a bit intimidating to share a nuanced opinion about Gloomhaven among all the rave reviews, but I think there are some people who share my tastes and would benefit from my experience. Therefore, I will focus on the three major issues I encountered during my play time. If these points seem harmless to you, you can go ahead, I think Gloomhaven will be a blast. If these points sound worrying to you, I would advise caution before investing in this massive game.

1. Combat mechanics are great, but plagued by exhausting enemy management

The card-based combat and deckbuilding are absolutely outstanding. Everyone in my group loved selecting their cards and fighting with their class. Classes are all well-designed, unique and interesting. Combat is both the central mechanic and the main highlight of the game, making Gloomhaven very strong at its core.

However, combat is plagued by the constant slog of managing the enemy AI, health trackers, and decks. Fortunately, the Gloomhaven Helper app alleviates a lot of that busywork and makes the game more enjoyable. I would never consider playing Gloomhaven without the app.

Enemy AI, though, remains a pain to handle. Sometimes the situation is perfectly clear, and sometimes you have a hard time figuring out the intended enemy behavior. This won’t be a problem for people willing to bend some rules and move on, but I hate doing that, and I end up constantly triple-checking the rule book. I think there are ways to make AI management more palatable without sacrificing challenge and depth. A lot of Gloomhaven is excellent but would be more relevant in a video game.

2. The story is disappointing

Gloomhaven attempts some kind of ambitious branching narrative, with multiple interconnected storylines that flow differently depending on the choices you make. This sounds good on paper, but the implementation is a mess.

First, the storylines are drawn out way too much across multiple scenarios, which often makes you feel like you sat for hours accomplishing nothing (WARNING: Very minor spoiler in the two paragraphs below).

For example, there is a storyline that takes you to a mountain to hunt a dragon. You spend TWO whole 4-hour scenarios just CLIMBING the mountain fighting random enemies, with basically no story content and no payoff, before facing the dragon in the third scenario. That quest was such a slog that I started considering dropping the game. Such a basic mission should have taken two scenarios at most. A lot of “side quest” scenarios are also completely devoid of narrative ambition, consisting only in killing a few bad guys and looting a treasure.

Secondly, storylines are interconnected in a messy way that makes it hard to keep track of the overall narrative. You constantly unlock new storylines or standalone scenarios distracting you from your current objective. For example, when climbing the mountain to fight the dragon, you unlock one more branching storyline, and an optional scenario. Either you decide to do them right away, interrupting you in your dragon chase for something completely different, or do them later, completely forgetting why and how you unlocked them. The scenario books make no effort to summarize previous events when starting a scenario, so you end up lost and not caring at all about the story.

Finally, beyond the delivery format, the story itself feels quite average and bland, with a lack of memorable characters. You’re nothing more than a bunch of faceless henchmen who kill monsters in a pretty standard fantasy setting. There are a few interesting moral dilemmas, but they arrive too late in the story. The random town and road events are quite fun, but ultimately a minor part of the game.

3. Character progression is good, but way too slow

This is the main issue I have, and I will keep it short. Me and my group would have loved a “fast mode” for Gloomhaven, completely removing the superfluous optional scenarios, boosting gold and XP gains, and making personal quests easier to complete. Unlocking and upgrading cards is incredibly fun, so make it happen more often! I ended up selling the game before unlocking a single new class, though I would have loved to experience that feature.

Ultimately, the game is good but stretched out across too many hours of grind. The long-term commitment is too much for my friends, and the payoffs are too few and far between. If I had known, I would have skipped to Jaws of the Lion and its more condensed experience.

Congratulations! You have found the most overrated tabletop game of all time. I have a theory as to why it has such a high rating: given its huge price point and time requirement, I assume that most of the people rating are people who bought it after researching it thoroughly in order to ensure that they would enjoy it. This certainly is not an impulse buy game.

Positives:
* The action system is fairly clean; I like that all actions are card-driven, each card has default modes, and your deck acts as a timer of sorts.
* Lots of variety between classes.

Neutral
* Retiring heroes is thematically a bit strange, but I can see how it does guarantee you'll get to experience a variety of heroes.

Negatives:
* Tedium to the max. Repetitive quests. Yet for those who want a crunchy, heavy dungeon crawler that takes literally months to complete... this is it. In that sense, it is quite an impressive accomplishment.

If you want the gameplay stripped of all of the tedium, check out the digital version. I still find it too tedious even in this medium. So many better digital dungeon crawlers out there (Darkest Dungeon being the best, hands down), but I can see this being fun if you have friends you want to play with.

Many other negative reviews have already pointed out the ways in which this game is broken. Choices are limited, many of the game mechanics are anti-thematic, it definitely does feel like a cryptic puzzle rather than an epic quest with choices. Nothing quite breaks immersion like standing face to face with an armed enemy then taking a short rest to recover cards. Or how about having to choose between using a "Shield Bash" action to shield yourself but not bash OR bash but not shield.

Many have likened this game to XCom. I love PC games like XCom and Frozen Synapse and Card Hunter but none of those feel as much like a puzzle as this does. None of those make me feel boxed into making specific choices. While tactical at heart, those feel more chess like, in that I must asses what my opponent is likely to do and think ahead or do something unexpected to bait out my opponent. I'm not doing precise calculations for every single action.

I think most people are aware of the long setup, the high price, and the level of complexity that this game comes with. These are not deal breakers for this game. It seems to be the core gameplay design that dooms this game from the start, no matter how great the story, and no matter how varied the content.

Does it deserve to be at #1? I don't see how something that seems more like an activity than a game could be so high up the list. Do yourself a favor and try out the inexpensive digital version first before you decide to buy the big box based on BGG ratings alone.

So hard to score this game.

Mechanically and thematically the game is fantastic. Hell, I even loved the flavour text, leveling mechanics, branching story paths and how events can lead to good or bad consequences later in the game!

But here's the problem: The mechanics don't suit the length of the campaign.

I love long, thinky, heavy, puzzly games like Mage Knight, the Mistfall series and even Unicornus Knights.
But you sit down for a few hours and play them ONCE! Then you're free to pack them up or reset, change characters/scenarios and play again.

Mage Knight is my favourite game but I wouldn't want to have to play it 75+ times to complete a campaign and Gloomhaven, after about a dozen plays, starts to feel more like an obligation-or even another job rather than some fun for a few hours.

But I LOVE CAMPAIGNS!! It's just that I think I prefer campaigns for games that are lighter. Games like WarhammerQuest ACG, Descent 2nd Ed, Pathfinder ACG, Sword & Sorcery etc where combat can be streamlined with a quick dice-chuck and some clever card play to mitigate the risk of poor luck

I think I'd prefer this game to either be a dice chucker and keep the campaign
OR
Keep it the way it is but have the Set up, tear down, leveling and axe the campaign, instead making it scenario-based.


POSITIVES
+Brilliant tactical combat
+I'm really enjoying the story so far
+Character boxes/envelopes are great for storing active/locked/retired heroes
+Satisfying leveling system
+Shop/prosperity system
+Variety in Characters
+Battle and life goals really impact how you play and decisions you make not only in the scenario but during road and city events or even how you spend your money
+Removing/adding heroes to the party is pretty easy
+Gameplay is pretty intuitive once you've got the hang of it
+Lots of 'Kill Everything' scenarios which I love


NEGATIVES
-Game is too heavy for a campaign so long/Campaign is too long for a game so heavy
-Scenarios take too long to have a group of adults be able to commmit to the campaign. And if they do, they're likely going to want to play an RPG instead.
-Solo experience is great but takes away from playing other games
-Box insert is great for shipping but absolutely useless for keeping a campaign organised (except for character boxes-they're great!)
-Had to spend a small fortune on various folders organisers to be able top keep track of my campaign

WORTH NOTING:
I have a games room with a table and storage dedicated to Gloomhaven including folders, boxes and even a craft table that fits underneath so it keeps everything organised.
I even have a magnetic whiteboard with magnetised map stickers. map and an A3 sized party sheet to record where I'm at.
Now I understand that not many people have this luxury but let me put it this way: If I didn't, I WOULD NOT KEEP IT. Seriously, you're not going to get you money's worth if, over the course of a campaign, you don't want to spend DOZENS of hours setting up and re-organising.
This game needs its OWN TABLE and storage system.

I normally find setting up a board game oddly relaxing. Not Gloomhaven. I dread the set up-even with all the organisational luxuries that I have and have mentioned.

When I do play I have a GREAT time!!!
But when it's over and I realise how much work is now ahead of me. It's worth it at the moment in my opinion however I can completely understand anyone who abandons this game after a few sessions.

For being the #1 game on BGG by quite a large margin, Gloomhaven has more common criticisms than you'd expect. The setup and teardown time are arguably the worst in the hobby. The fiddliness both in rules and components is also very high. I'm still googling rules after 20 plays. Many people feel the gameplay gets too repetitive as most scenarios are just about killing all the enemies. Some people may be disappointed in the legacy elements, whether it be not being given interesting choices with how the story progresses or the quality of the story itself.

None of these things are major issues for me, however. I keep Gloomhaven on its own table which greatly reduces setup and teardown time (I realize not everyone can do this). There are also many apps that help reduce fiddle. I suppose I get what people mean by repetitive scenario design, but this hasn't bothered me. I'm still impressed that there are this many enemy types with their own decks. And as for the legacy elements, I don't really play board games for storytelling so I had no expectations for this aspect anyway. I wouldn't say I'm moved or grabbed by the story, but the scenario text is very descriptive and playful. It does its job setting the mood and doesn't intrude on the gameplay too much.

The core gameplay is just as brilliant as everyone says. It feels like they nailed every aspect of the gameplay: the amount of randomness (I absolutely love the attack modifier decks), short-term vs. long-term goals, scenario balance, and not being sure you've won or lost until near the end. The legacy elements really help make decisions more difficult because my god, you want to get that personal quest done and achieve that battle goal and oh I guess we also want to win the scenario. Pretty much every character has a very interesting set of action cards as well. You're not doing much with these besides attack, move and heal so the diversity is very impressive.

There are 17 characters to try, but 11 of them are locked at the beginning. You must retire characters to unlock the others which can be time-consuming. While I still love the core gameplay, I feel this is the real reason I'm playing the game so much. I really want to see these other characters and how they work. I can't decide if this makes me want to criticize the legacy format for wasting my time or praise it for making me so excited to see what's in sealed envelopes. I would have no qualms about this setup if the personal quest cards weren't so darn random. This is my one legitimate complaint. The card you get makes a big difference and you may have little control completing that personal quest. You aren't allowed to mention your quest to other players either so prepare to have an aneurysm trying to make progress. I may have just gotten very unlucky but I'm convinced my personal quest is not possible anymore unless I replay some scenarios in casual mode. I just want to play with the other toys please, ugh.

The fact that this overwrought monstrosity is #1 on BGG now seems like it should say a lot about where the hobby is now. Gloomhaven is pretty mediocre. It’s a total by-the-numbers design, with limited interest either narratively or tactically. It doesn’t have much of a sense of pacing or narrative direction. It doesn’t have an answer to the question of why it exists. As I say below, it’s total consumerism run amok; way too much physical product for the limited range of the game itself.

But it seems to have taken off; I assume on the strength of peoples’ affection for D&D back in the day (if they’re older) or MMORPGs (if they’re less old).

I think the reason I despair to some degree is that Gloomhaven is just such an uninteresting and unambituous piece of design and world building work. While certainly there is a lot of dreck in the boardgame space, there are also just so many people doing really interesting, thoughtful, and even meaningful games: Reiner Knizia’s Beowulf or Lord of the Rings, Spirit Island, Quartermaster General in all its incarnations, Catan in all its range and variety, Pandemic, Mystic Vale, Oath, the list goes on … that this relative mediocrity with little interesting to do or say is the #1 game on this site I think speaks to the problems in the hobby and, possibly, American society writ large.
—-
So, I finally played this - 5 years late, well past when anyone cares about my opinion I’m sure. Still, I’ll put a few words down here.

Firstly, in this age of impending environmental catastrophe, the amount of stuff in this box is just absolutely criminal. It’s not a bad game, but it’s a game of repetitive stabbing with very limited range. How many times is clearing similar dungeons really fun? The designer has focussed on quantity over quality here, which might have been fine in the 80s but in the 2010s and 2020s we all know what is going to happen here if developed countries don’t moderate their consumption, or at the very least get smarter about it. It’s going to be quite bad. This is a pretty grotesque example of Western consumerism.

So for me personally, I just find the dungeon crawler genre of accumulating body count kind of dumb. Neither D&D nor its many copycat computer games are things I’ve ever been deeply involved in, and the raw amount of personally killing sentient beings for extremely unclear reasons does not sit particularly well. So a game in this category really has to bring it to win me over. Gloomhaven can probably work for people who have a pre-existing sympathy for the format. If you require it to do more than scratch a nostalgic itch, though? Probably not. It has the same failings as all the games in this genre: super-repitive, grind-y, minimally thematic, and of limited narrative interest. It’s a lot more interesting than the previous entry in this genre that I got significant exposure to, the Pathfinder Adventure Card Game. But that’s a low bar; that game was quite bad.

I tried Gloomhaven out only once at SPIEL Essen 2017 and only skimmed the rules. My rating could well change considerably with further games, but a 5.5 is my best estimate for now, although the theme is right up my alley and I could like a game "like this" considerably better.
However, I already feel confident in saying that I think this game is overhyped and overrated. Apparently, the publisher contributed to that by prompting people "Don't forget to rate this a 10 when you pre-order!". Which I view as at least dubious behavior (on the publisher's part).
- As for how the game plays, I dislike the way the game tries to solve a possible alpha gamer problem by having vague and circumventable rules which information you are allowed to discuss during the game and by having secret battle goal cards. I don't think there should be any restrictions on which information players are allowed to divulge in a game like this. I searched the rulebook for this issue, thumbs up that the rules at least include a remark about playing without information/communication restrictions as a variant and how to compensate difficulty level if you do (on p. 16).
- The potentially problematic player elimination mechanism that the game has when a character gets "exhausted" gets worse if played without open information so that the dropped out players have a harder time to still somewhat participate in the game. How bad this is depends a lot on how frequently exhaustion happens, not sure about that.
- I don't dislike legacy aspects in general, but I think the game should be completely resettable - particularly when it is as expensive as Gloomhaven. I hate it when the rules require you to permanently modify your game. Gloomhaven includes numerous irremovable stickers. At least a third party company already offers a set of removable stickers to replace them. I would expect the original publisher to include such stickers in the game or at least sell them as an optional add-on themselves.

Well, my son really wanted to stick with this game, so I did (aren't I a good dad?  ). After the first several plays where we spent about 3 minutes looking for rules in the rulebook for each minute spent actually playing, things have evened out *a bit*. We still spend far too much time for my taste looking for things in the badly-organized rulebook, and setting up scenarios with functionally-equivalent but slightly-different-artwork pieces, but we have at least hit on a way to make the scenarios themselves enjoyable: we try each scenario for the first time on the "correct" difficulty for our level, and if we lose (and it wasn't close) we bump down a level and almost always beat it on that next try. This keeps things moving.

I still think this is the worst-organized rulebook I've ever seen. It's really, really bad. Almost like they tried on purpose. When you can find something, it is typically fairly clear; it's the organization that's just mind-bogglingly bad. Which makes it really, REALLY hard to start playing.

As the person who had read the rules and was teaching the game to three other people, it was a never-ending constant repetition of vague ideosyncratic minutae for literally over an hour.

The choices during the scenarios are basically how to best chain your actions together to force the dumb enemies to impale themselves on you and carefully plot your and their movements to minimize the massive amounts of damage they can do to your characters.

It was awful and I'm never playing it again.

Very great game. Interesting mechanics and a relatively simple yet complex gameplay make this game one of my favorite cooperative game. The legacy element is fun and makes this game even better.

This feels more like a series of puzzles than an actual dungeon crawler. I'm a big fan of Descent, Imperial Assault, D&D, and video game RPGs (Baldur's Gate, Skyrim, etc). But this just felt so constricted, like I am trying to find a solution with limited moves.

Although I love innovation in this genre, I disliked the core mechanic and found it a bit dull and unforgiving. You spend an hour finding the exact combo of moves only to die one or two turns away from the goal because of exhausted cards. But you often don't know how to play a scenario until you try it once. And you can't explore much because movement is limited.

At the very least, a house rule is needed for 1 free movement and/or a 1 attack once cards are exhausted. Dying with a complete fail seems like bad design.

After 25 hours of play, I find the story just typical. Even the Core mechanic is just passable and nothing worth playing for that alone. I just scratch my head at the high ratings for just an OK game. There's much better tabletop crawlers out there.

Edit 45 hours in: The lack of a compelling story and the same objectives (kill all monsters on the map) just confirms my initial feel. The leveling up, lack of a DM, and crunchy tactical combat is wonderful however. The characters/monsters are varied, even if the objectives/plot is unpespeakbly bland for an RPG. So it's really just a fun tactical skirmish.

In the end, I hope FFG takes Descent/IA and makes it solo-able like this. Not just playable via an app, but taking the best Gloomhaven parts and let you play against the game completely. Then I'd have the good parts of this (no DM, crunchy combat, leveling up, flipbook for easy setup) with the branching narrative, more forgiving deaths, and story flair that FFG provides.

As a computer game, I think this is outstanding. While the initial limitations on what you can do via the cards can be frustrating, after a few plays you start to realize that basic tuning of a character's deck, combined with managing the powerful cards for the right moment really makes for an interesting tactical challenge. No, it isn't really an RPG, and no, the story/lore isn't that deep; for this there are many deep RPGs that aren't centered on board game mechanics. The range of interesting characters, scenarios, monsters, and items is really huge and a source of hours of gameplay without repeating.

As a board game, I probably wouldn't play it again. I think it takes too much setup time, it's too fiddly with how the rules work, and there would be too much downtime waiting for other players. I would much rather play Mage Knight in this context; MK has the whole arc of leveling-up in a few hours of game play, while I can't even imagine how long a campaign would take with F2F Gloomhaven. Another problem with F2F is that I think it would be very challenging to play more than one character at a time, while in the computer game this is very easy.

'9' for the computer game version, '5' for the board game version.

(For context, I played through the campaign to completion once with my tabletop copy with 3 friends, and I’m now playing in 2 simultaneous campaigns via the Steam app. So my comments will be coming from both angles.)

This game, simply, is brilliant. It’s not perfect, and I have my criticisms, but the sum of the design is an outstanding experience. The game excels thanks to some very specific innovations that make this my #1 dungeon crawler of all time.

1) You won't play the same character for the whole game. You’ll choose a career goal (from a random choice of two), and when your character achieves their goal, they will retire and you’ll choose a new character. This means you can play as, for example, a melee character then switch to a spellcaster or ranger type or one of the other unique character types.

Changing characters throughout the game means you’ll never get bored because you change your tactics and get a new deck of unique action cards to explore. I also like that instead of going with traditional dwarf, elf, orc, etc. races, he invented all new races with unique professions.

Some goals are easier to achieve than others, and you have some control over how quickly you retire that character. I played my beloved Berserker all the way to L9 (the max) and kept playing her as I didn’t want to retire her. When I finally did, I moved on to a totally different, assassin-type character who played completely differently. Contrast that with any other game whereby your character stays the same and it’s the equipment around you that changes.

2) You get meaningful character progression. You get to choose a new, more powerful card at each level when you progress. Of course, you have to drop a card to add this new one to your hand, and those decisions are deliciously difficult. There are usually two different directions to focus your character depending on which upgrade cards you select.

3. Instead of chucking dice, you have a modifier deck for attacks. Instead of the usual “upgrade your white die to red and then red to black, etc.” dice improvement mechanism, here you add or remove cards from your modifier deck. A die can only have so many sides (and you can’t remove any!), but your deck can have many different cards, some with +X modifiers and some with conditions such as wound, poison, stun, or even heal yourself. Deciding whether to thin your deck first or add cards makes for very satisfying decisions and more interesting ways to tailor your hero.

4. The basic action mechanism is thoroughly engaging. It sounds simple, but choosing the top of one card and the bottom of another plus the dimension of some cards being reusable while some are one-and-done makes for very chunky decisions as how to pair your cards each turn. Furthermore, each time you rest, you have to burn (lose) a card. Having no more cards gets you knocked out of a scenario, so managing your hand of cards while trying to stay effective in battle is critical.

On top of those decisions, your cards have an initiative number. Of the two cards you play, you’ll choose one as your initiative number for the round which is compared to your teammates and the enemies to determine when your turn is. Factoring in how quickly or not you wish to act in a round on top of the other card decisions is Mage Knight-level satisfying and creates an effective fog of war.

5. Enemies each have their own unique AI deck. You never know what they're going to do, and they all act differently. Some are ranged, some are melee, some summon other enemies. They only move or attack if their card says so, so sometimes you get a break and they don't move or don't attack.

6. Each game you get a secret battle goal that you wish to achieve. While still, ya know, helping the team win the scenario. If you achieve it, you get a checkmark. After three checkmarks, you get to add a new card to your modifier deck as per #3.

7. There is a real element of team cooperation. You can play cards to assist your allies in various ways, from the obvious healing your partners to having them move on your turn, get cards back, make elements they need to power cards, or other bonus effects and actions.

Now on the downside, there’s a significant cognitive load put on the players to manage the enemy AI’s. Consequently, I will say that playing the game on Steam is my preferred way to play it. The downside to #5 above is that you have to parse the all the different enemy instructions.

When there are three to five enemy decks on the table, each with their own instructions, and you have to figure out if and how each enemy will target and activate, well, it can get to be a bit much when you’re poor brain is trying to parse all the considerations of #4. There’s an app that helps manage things, and I wouldn’t want to play the tabletop game without it. Playing on Steam relieves you of all that, and the app is very well made. Plus, it's a beast to set up and tear down.

Also, a minor complaint, but I find it odd that with so many brilliant aspects to the game, both the story and the events are, well, the events are poor; there’s no way around it. They offer you ostensibly thematic events, but the results are frequently completely random. Helped that stranger out? Well, you start the next scenario wounded. Avoid a rockfall? You take damage. Like… how could the same person who made such an intelligent game have made such a dumb event system. I mean, it's just dumb and a missed opportunity to add some good flavor to the game.

Also, the overall story is fractured into many mini-story arcs with the effect being that you don’t have a consistent through-line to make it feel like you’re in the middle of a single narrative. A coherent narrative story would also elevate the flavor. I expect both of these areas to be improved in future versions.

The scenario scaling is the game's weakest point IMO. There are some scenarios where playing on Normal vs Easy is considerably more difficult, and to move forward, you have to replay it on Easy because Normal for this particular scenario is more like Insane level.

Overall all though, I adore the game as evidenced by my having finished it once and yet going through it again twice more. Even though I know some of the major plot points, it's still replayable. In each of my three plays, I've encountered some of the 95 scenarios that I didn't encounter in a previous play.

I've played a couple hundred hours of this game via both platforms, so yeah, it gets a 10 from me.

In short, this is the best skirmish system I have played, DM-less or otherwise, supported by a functional campaign system and an excellent character progress and reward system.

The variety of monster traits and behaviours, dungeon topologies, and scenario goals and quirks provide for an astounding variety of encounter; to this the players bring their respective toolboxes of unique character actions and enhancements. There's always some way to step up, help out, be caught flat-footed, gamble, fall on your face, pull out the stops, save the day. There are years of gaming in here if you want it.

I can see this game working pretty much as well as anything solo, but you'd miss out on the whole "look what the heck I can do" aspect along with the "you blocked me so I'm going to sulk in this corner for the rest of the scenario" aspect.

Such a sprawling game isn't going to be flawless, and there are potential issues with card and item balance, difficulty consistency and scaling, side content unlocking, and a poorly implemented side of meta-puzzles. None of them is a dealbreaker for me. The game would be fiddly as heck played with all the monster decks, health tokens and so on, but Gloomhaven Helper works really well for all that. A hierarchy of ziplock bags and a few plastic cups work well for storage, no third-party accessories needed. You can ignore or circumvent the legacy aspects, some more easily than others.

Pros- Gloomhaven shows that it learned from its predecessors in the genre and has great rules that govern combat and the deckbuilding elements give an appreciative amount of control to the player.

Cons- Battle goals generally diminish the experience a bit if playing strictly as they should be done in the rules. They take away from the otherwise fantastic group discussion of how to work as a team to clear a map. Very few loss cards are worth running, and it feels like the developer underestimated the needed drawback/reward balance on them. Some items are clearly overpowered, and players that are quick to learn the governance of combat and movement will be able to abuse them to great effect. So we did it. We beat Gloomhaven.

So I can say with some confidence now: this is a mediocre game that makes up for quality with quantity. There's moments of brilliance, but they're surrounded by oceans of mediocrity.

The writing is abysmal. Just god-awful. There's a noticable dearth of unique ideas. By your 20th-30th scenario you'll have seen almost all of the scenario patterns and enemies that you'll encounter. By your 3rd or 4th character you'll realize how similar they all are. Even with the fan expansion, battle goals will become tediously rote. Personal Quests are just a complete disaster from a design perspective, with no concern given to making sure all quest goals are completable at any point in the game. The Legacy element is pointless and tacked on, it should simply be a campaign. The rules are a mess, with strange design choices that are unintuitive or unnecessarily fiddly. The monster AI is simultaneously too dumb and too complicated to operate (mostly when you get into weird situations) Almost every aspect and element of the game is poor, but obfuscated by the sheer magnitude of stuff the game throws at you.

Gloomhaven is a great prototype of a much superior game. It is not that game. I'd very much like to play that game, but I have no desire to play more Gloomhaven. I have Jaws of the Lion and a preorder for Frosthaven. Hopefully one or both of those games will build on the promise of Gloomhaven and achieve new heights.

The GF and I finished Gloomhaven Digital after 187 hours online. Previously we spent roughly 20 hours on Jaws of the Lion before starting the digital campaign. General thoughts on Gloomhaven:

- Digital is the most streamlined way to play. Not only do you get erratas, you get extra campaign content as well as Frosthaven rules integration. This all goes without saying that not having to set up the board game for each scenario is a massive plus.
- Digital adds an extra layer by letting you think about party composition and teams. No more "I really want to retire my character quickly because I dislike my class" - in Digital you can have one character of each unlocked class active at any time. This means when you retire a class, you can immediately make a new character of the same class (with own personal quest) that you put on 'standby' while at the same time making a new character of the class you just unlocked. Then when going into a scenario, you can figure out what team comp you're going to bring in, which is a level of depth and planning the base board game just doesn't have.

General game design thoughts on Gloomhaven:

- Isaac Childres did an amazing job on the core game systems and classes. Each class feels unique... well almost. Elementalist and Spellweaver felt like variations of the same thing, but otherwise each class feels like its own unique (and sometimes awkward) identity.
- The story structure is well thought out. We played the scenarios haphazardly and I was impressed by how the various questlines interweave with one another depending on what major characters you killed, no matter what order you do the scenarios. Massive kudos on the scenario and scenario unlocks design.
- Amazing boss fights (most of them anyway). Interesting mechanics that really make some of the scenarios fascinating.
- At the same time, some of the scenarios are extremely unfun. 10+ Forest Imps (with shields!) in the starting room all with ranged attacks that put curses in your deck - who thought a scenario like this was a good idea?
- Thematic dissonance of some monsters. Forest Imps can shields? Oozes can gain shield? Also, some monsters in the game can do everything - gain shield, heal, go invisible, attack at both melee and range - which to me is a major loss of monster identity and doesn't make thematic sense at all.
- Road encounters are random even if you have the right characters in your party, so sometimes the choice feels like a non-choice. There is an encounter where we get stopped by a bunch of Inox, but we can 'negotiate' with them and get through if we have an Inox in our party. There is another encounter when a group of Inox stop you, and even if you have an Inox in your party, the negotiation option and the non-negotiate option both result in a negative effect. Did the road encounters not get tested thoroughly in QA, or are some of them supposed to be 'random bad luck regardless'?
- Some choices in the campaign lock out other scenarios, but there aren't that many scenarios you get locked out of. You can be bad then good then bad then good again, which is... odd from a narrative standpoint.

Jaws of the Lion:

- Great side quests. Lackluster main story. Extremely disappointing final boss fight. Overstays its welcome.
- Difficulty felt like it went from just right to insanely easy once your party is level 7+.

Favorite classes by symbol (to be spoiler free):
GF: Sun, Music Note, Ellipses, Big Face
Me: Three Spears, Eclipse, Spellweaver, Cragheart

Both of us recommend Gloomhaven in digital form 100%. A memorable experience for sure.

I have a few issues with Gloomhaven which have made me lose my initial love and excitement for it. First is what i mentioned regarding time. My friends and I played Gloomhaven for 7 hours a day every Saturday for about 4 months and are still only halfway through the campaign and we haven't even lost once and only one of us is close enough to completing our characters story so that we can choose a new hero. Each Saturday we'd complete about 1.5 dungeons roughly.

This irks me because both the box and this website say 60-120min play time which is one of the biggest lies i have ever been told in my life. Even playing the computer game version is BARELY faster. The dungeons are slow even if everyone has HYPER fixation the entire time and campaign/story is impossible to complete in less than 20 sessions.

Now I don't actually have an issue with long playability especially if its good or entertaining but I can't help but feel that after you've completed about 10+ dungeons you've pretty much played them all. It gets very same-y just with different monsters and stats. The main story is extremely linear with the only real choices being 'good' or 'evil' campaign story. The story is not exciting at all and major plot points come up every 3 or 4 dungeons most of the time which is like 3 weeks time difference for us. Just not that captivating. There's no sense of doom or worry. Fail a dungeon? Oh well you guys just got exhausted and (i imagine) the monsters kindly drop you off outside the dungeons front door for you to try again. Gloomhaven will always be fine.

The gaining gold part is so slow that we had to create houserules to even begin to afford anything from the shops and gloomhaven city perks take forever to obtain that after 4 months of winning our shops items have a discount of 2 gold (most items are like 30-50gold). So basically diddly squat discount. After a while our characters have levelled up and gained things and were starting to destroy, and being able to up the monster difficulty is a great balancing idea. But yeah its just the same thing with tougher monsters so dungeons take longer. Like i highly doubt playing a new hero is going to make things more exciting.

Honestly i'd just recommend buying the computer game. It's way cheaper, EXACTLY the same as the board game but with better graphics and emersion and its faster than playing and setting up the billions of pieces as the game works out mechanics for you. Only downside is you can't do house rules so it will probably end up taking the same amount of time. Otherwise if you want to invest 7 hours every Saturday with friends for a good story with RPG and monsters, just play DnD.

The more I play this game, the more I love it. Each scenario is this wonderful tactical puzzle that keeps you on your toes and requires a nice mixture of long-term planning and reactive adaptation. I love how unique the player classes are and how differently each of them play. There's a satisfying sense of progression and player customization as you level up your character and add more and more powerful cards to your card pool. The use of cards instead of dice allows you to customize your modifier deck and minimize the risk of drawing poorly over time. The fact that your deck works as your life is so, so brilliant and adds a lot of tension to the choice of cards each turn. I can't tell you how many games have ended with us broken and bruised with only a few cards left in our hand and with us just barely able to kill the last enemy.

That said, the game is not without its flaws. The admin is very fiddly as there's a lot to keep track of and the monster movement rules could definitely be streamlined. Though I love the legacy elements of the game, I was a bit disappointed by the bare bones nature of the narrative, which doesn't quite deliver on the promise of an immersive, epic fantasy campaign. At it's heart, Gloomhaven is a satisfying, tactical dungeon crawler with great character variety and a satisfying core game-play loop. We'll be playing this series for a long time to come.

First of all, this is singlehandedly and without hyperbole the most impressive and ambitious game design I've ever seen. It's almost a miracle that Childres was able to pull this off: a deep, engrossing, extremely thematic and highly replayable, legacy "board game-RPG" with solid, intuitive mechanics and a reasonable number of rules.

The mechanic of having your hand serve as the "timer" is absolutely brilliant: it's a very elegant way of both simulating exhaustion and creating tough and tense decisions for the players (do I throw away this card now for its effect or keep it to extend my life?). I also like the added "loot" mechanic, which adds an almost push-your-luck element to each scenario (how much time do you think you'll need?).

The only problems I've found with the game are 1) scenarios can be really, really hard to win, and (partially because of the high difficulty), 2) it takes FOREVER to retire and get to play another character. I like my Brute enough, but I'm already jonesing to try a different character type, and at the rate I'm going, that will realistically happen in 30-45 more games (which might take years). I simply don't have the time, or the desire, to play this game as much as it demands, which means my rating will rise or fall depending principally on how often I get it to the table.

Even still, it's a masterpiece. Game of the Year at minimum, and (currently ranked 192 at the time I'm writing) I'm going to go ahead and predict: by 2018, this will have ousted Pandemic: Legacy as the No. 1 rated game on BGG.

While this is a great game, it has some drawbacks. The well known ones are that it requires a recurring group an immense amount of time to get through the campaign. Even granted that, there’s quite a bit of setup to get it on the table.

I think it’s less commonly noted that there’s an awful lot of luck involved for a diceless game. Both players and enemies have modifier decks, and enemies also select their move randomly although they carry it out with “AI”. Part of leveling up is improving your modifier deck to make luck less painful, but it’s always there.

After a carefully planning out your turn, you draw cards to determine how the enemies act and in what order, and when either a player or monster acts you draw more cards to determine whether each attack does 0 (miss), -2, -1, +0, +1, +2, or x2 (critical) damage. It's this process here that takes the game down a peg or three for me, as it's frequently rage inducing. Maybe it's just my bad luck. In a lighter game where I can freely pick moves, though, this isn't nearly as frustrating.

Playing is often called a “puzzle” despite the luck factor, because card selection is often a strange experience of figuring out just how you can take a few steps and swing a sword. While in most dungeon crawls these are simple actions with little or no cost, in GH this requires using up a dwindling stack of action cards, and figuring out how not to burn out too soon.

Despite this, the experience is neat. There’s a ton of variety in the scenarios and classes and equipment, and each monster has its own move deck which makes them distinctive and interesting. There is not much in the way of narrative at all but the setting is just a bit off the beaten high fantasy path which makes it distinct and sometimes intriguing.

It’s a fairly stiff challenge as well, which makes sure everyone is paying attention. However, the challenge tends to feel like you are fighting against the game’s artificially short clock and tightly restricted move set, rather than struggling against powerful enemies in dangerous lands. At least, most of the time.

All in all I can’t wholeheartedly recommend it or explain why it’s ranked #1. But it’s a really unique and interesting piece of work that does keep calling me back to give it one more try.

Gloomhaven's continued presence at the top of the charts is baffling. Sure, the game is -good- and definitely value-for-money, considering how much stuff is crammed into the gargantuan box. But it's not a -great- game, and a dozen scenarios and some hours with the digital version reveals the game's flaws. It's long and tedious to setup; very fiddly; is hindered by a poor rulebook and unclear AI system; and a lack of creative variety in its scenario design which, in the missions I've experienced, largely consists of 'kill everything that moves'. Perhaps worst of all, I found it thematically unconvincing: from the painful forced-repeat of lost missions, to the thin narrative wrapped around the scenarios which, at its worst, can have you unwittingly burning children to death with no foreknowledge of the consequences.

For all this, Gloomhaven does have many truly compelling elements. Most of the different classes are fun to explore and play differently. The levelling system is refreshingly different, with the biggest growth to a character's power being in the subtle tweaks to their combat decks. XPs being linked to actions rather than killings is clever, and there's just enough link between the action cards' titles and the way they play to generate some sense of theme - though this sits somewhat jarringly with the item system. There is definitely something addictive in playing a class like the Mindthief or Cragheart and growing it in power and getting to know the nuances of the class.

Ultimately, however, I didn't find it good enough to keep. It takes up too much room on the shelf for a game that, at its best, is still a slow slog of shuffling decks, tracking combat modifiers and puzzling through a somewhat opaque AI system. It may simply be that I'm at a point in life where I don't have the time and space for a game like Gloomhaven.

We really, really enjoyed this game from start to finish, with only a few minor issues throughout. The worldbuilding was solid, the scenarios were-for the most part—doable on our first try (though often by the skin of our teeth, which we really enjoyed). More, as a four-player co-op game, it gave us over two years of enjoyment with regular social time with friends. Truly, value for the time it gave us was incredible.

The only minor caveats were often based on the "retirement" mechanic, which seemed to just really work out unluckily for us; multiple times, we were forced to replay scenarios to make it possible to retire once we were past the mid-way point of the game, because new scenarios didn't have the right kind of enemy, for example, for a character to retire (we eventually just looked at all the scenarios to confirm, for example, that there were no new crypt adventures lying in wait, or no new adventures with Forest Imps, which meant two of our characters had no choice but to replay adventures to get to their retirement conditions). This could have been fixed by putting new personal quest cards inside the locked character classes to be added to the deck, and making the early-game quest cards the only options for the original six characters so someone didn't end up drawing the "Crypt" or "Forest Imp" personal quest cards long after those quests were done.

Still, that's a fairly minor quibble (though it did impact the fun of the game a few times) and overall the whole experience was great.

You know that game many seem to like...
.. but you can't figure out why?

So then you keep trying because the game is "the best out there" and you still can't find what the heck does this game does better than the others to be "the best out there"? Well, that is Gloomhaven for me.

I own this game on Steam - and nowadays I keep trying to convince myself I was drunk when I bought it.

The digital version plays pretty much like the boardgame, so it IS a good way to experience the game without investing a ton of money on the tabletop version; however, it is just a mediocre dungeon crawler at its core. The art is likeable, but not amazing; gameplay is okayish (in both versions, with pros and cons when comparing both); the campaign is nothing new... nothing in it is really, really bad, but absolutely nothing is mind blowing. Regarding the digital version, soundtrack and narrations are good, but again, nothing that spectacular.

Why is this the best board game ever according to BGG? My best shot is that it appeals to people that would like to play tabletop RPG Dungeon Crawlers but don't have the time or impetus to actually do it. Is it better than those mentioned Old School Dungeon Crawlers? Absolutely not. Now, when it comes to the digital version, besides testing to know the game, I can't really understand why you would invest hundreds of hours into this game instead of playing any one of the better Dungeon Crawlers RPGs on PC out there (not to mention you won't have much of a deep story here by comparison to even the Dungeon Crawlers for PC of the 90s).

I know you will find a ton of positive reviews in this section, that's the nature of this beast, but here I am leaving you with a counterpoint and a message of support so you don't have to feel bad to pass on this title.

So there you have it, I confess, I don't like the "best ranked board game on Board Game Geek".

After 60+ plays of this game, I can confidently say Gloomhaven is deserving of the hype. The world is so immersive, but the gameplay isn't reliant on that fact alone. The combat, while maybe a little difficult to learn at first, is so simple and rich with puzzling goodness as you try to succeed in each dungeon crawl.

There's nothing that bores me more than an easy cooperative game, and let me tell you, this game kicked our butt several times. The cheers as we make it through a scenario by the skin of our teeth were explosive each time. If the game isn't giving you that experience, it scales in difficulty quite well; don't be afraid to push your group.

Warnings: If you don't have a place to store this on a table for a while, or don't care for a 20 minute setup each session, this game may not be fore you. If you are a mega D&D player looking for that sort of role playing experience at the table... This game may also not be for you.

At its core, Gloomhaven is an excellent fantasy story game that immerses the players into a world brilliantly crafted by Issac Childres. Having said this, it is enjoyable for the niche group of people, the ones who thrive off of the legacy-style gameplay, combined with the freedom to create the character your way. Having played both on my own, and within a group, I ultimately realized that this is not a game without its flaws, and is frankly not enjoyable for the non-legacy playing group.
The biggest flaw of this game, is the mass amount of components, and the lacking way to store them, as well as limited replay-ability of missions. That certain encounters I or others enjoyed, would have to be destroyed, and how there was no way to reset the game, if you wished too.
All of this is to say, I believe Gloomhaven is a forth-right story-based game that gives the legacy lover all that he wants. For those who don't like legacy games, or have never experienced one, I would simply recommend a different game. Mostly because of the story complexity and puzzles of Gloomhaven, but also to save your pocket book because of the heavy price tag.

Gloomhaven is not a campaign game. Do not expect too much character development between games unless you take significant liberties with treasure and xp rules. It's not a particularly thematic game either. The main 'story' is threadbare and linear and doesn't qualify for me as 'passable' narrative experience. The legacy aspects are mostly superficial and are more akin to a video game trophy collection than anything truly impactful to your journey through the extraordinarily long scenario book.

Does this sound strange given how people talk about Gloomhaven? Well, people have a habit of locking in their first impressions and don't allow the passage of time and other games opportunity to claim the throne (probably because they've invested 300hours+ into this slog). At the time of release, Gloomhaven broke campaign/narrative ground. Now, it feels shallow in its progress and obtuse in its rule application.

AS A PUZZLE GAME, I'd say Gloomhaven is still "good", middle of the road, passible, and I would enjoy a few plays every month for a long time, but there is nominal difference between the 100+ scenarios - read; puzzles - and what little difference there is comes mostly comes from character progression (which, as previously noted, is slow and not nearly as strong as in other games). Honestly, I think you'd be just as well served and have a similar itch scratched by a sudoku book - which wouldn't cost $150 or take 30mins set up and 30mins tear down (I bought an insert which was absolutely essential; this games' box and insert gets a 0/10; the set up and tear down is that unacceptable in the face of recent Gametrayz production meta developments).

In 2017 Gloomhaven blew people's minds. I say that if it was released now that it wouldn't break the top 300. In the end, I binned the game but kept the character decks, models I painted, and good item cards, which I may put into Jaws of the Lion to spice it up into the game this always should have been.
