I've cooled on Gloomhaven over the years. I think the central card mechanism is pretty strong, but overall the game is a great deal of work. That work is too much once the magic fades a bit. It's also very samey in terms mission objectives.

I'm still enamored with the character retirement system and as stated above, find the depth of the action/card system excellent. This is the most mechanically rich dungeon crawler to ever exist and it has earned its popularity.

---------------------------------------------------------------------

The legacy aspects (reincorporating player decisions, branching narratives, and world permanence) are all breathtaking and excellent. As a campaign game, the narrative hangs together somewhat well and it feels like an enormous accomplishment. The scope is unbelievable and the world feels alive.

The majority of play is in the tempo-based card system that you will grapple with to clear out dungeons. This is a very Euro mechanism, albeit one infused with drama thanks to attack decks with wild outcomes. The card system can be difficult to strategically grasp in your early plays, especially when engaging with one of the more difficult classes like the Spellweaver. Losing cards for the scenario can feel punishing and it seems as though the game is fighting you, wanting you to hold back.

After gaining some experience and comfort with the mechanisms, the system will turn on its head and you will feel empowered. Even at that point, the game still is a bit of a slow burn with thoughtful contemplation and heady decisions making a bulk of play. This isn't a high-speed rip roaring adventure where you cut through foes like butter. It's very atypical for this genre as it's slow-going with a multitude of high impact decisions.

What's really amazing is how well everything hangs together. The system is pretty streamlined and feeds right into the larger campaign. This doesn't feel like an underdeveloped Kickstarter game at all. That is an outright miracle given the magnitude of scope presented.

Of course, it's the top-rated board game on the site (at this time), and has been for years. So, eventually curiosity got the better of me and I picked it up for my regular group.

My first real dive in to heavier board games and was instantly hooked. I recently completed all 95 scenarios, and enjoyed every minute. It's not perfect, with both some minor and major annoyances, but it's close.
To not just gush about the game, some of the minor issues I had were with how some events and scenarios play out. Usually it would be the way things were worded or said that didn't connect with the ending result. There is also a lot, and I do mean a lot, of shuffling tiny cards that can become tedious. Finally, there were a couple scenarios where they seemed to forget how many of certain game parts they gave you, and would require more than you had right out of the gate. Not sure how that even made it to the retail game.
Major issues would be the how fiddly it can be, and the setup and tear down. This didn't bother me for a while due to being overcome with everything, but eventually it did weigh down on the experience. If you have a dedicated space to leave it out, it isn't much of an issue. But, even then, you still need to find the tiles for each scenario, each monsters, their ability cards, then set everything up. There's also some secrets you'll run across that, eventually, you'll find out isn't even solvable in the game, and has nothing to do with the game. Lastly, the story is pretty forgettable, with only a few interesting bits scattered throughout.
All of that said, I'd still rate the game 9 out of 10 for the overall experience. The gameplay alone carries the game for me, with progression coming in at a close second. Many things to unlock and discover, and many different playstyles to be had. If this would be your first as well, Jaws of the Lion may be better if you aren't interested in figuring everything out on your own, as it does throw you in the deep end. Otherwise, if you want to dive in head first, this should provide many, many hours of enjoyment and be a great first game.

Many times you will be forced to choose from two stupid alternatives, and you get the feeling that the outcome from the choices is random. Some rules are strange. For instance, you have to loot all treasures in a scenario before you kill all monsters because the scenario ends when the last monster is killed. Just like that. You do not have time to open the chest beside you, but you can walk all the way back from the dungeon. The characters are not allowed to exchange items or gold. It just feels strange. You can make house rules to fix some of this, but that would mess up the balance in the game. This is a computer-game made into a board game. Sure, there are some fun parts and you can do some cool combinations with the different characters' powers, but the play-time is veeery long relative to the fun you get from it. If you have 12-year-old kids with lots of imagination, maybe it could be worth a try. I would rather play sudoku.

I played the game once and got a bad taste. A lot of work obviously went into developing the game, but I did not find it a fun multiplayer game. I found it to be a multiplayer puzzle and accounting game.

I like technical/accounting games, but it isn't what I look for in a dungeon crawl. In a dungeon crawl, I like playing a character and will keep track of odds to make sure I don't do something really, really, really stupid. The game mechanics forced me to play extremely out of character. I was a spell caster (Spellweaver) who was forced to leap (game mechanics "jump") through the entire crowd of final monsters in the first scenario to make the rest of the party attack, instead of taking it slow and picking opportunities.

You are forced to play cards or permanently loose cards every turn, sometimes both. There is a maximum limit to how many rounds a character can play before they are simply removed from the board. How you play and luck can reduce the theoretical maximum limit of rounds. The limit is not the same for every character and mine appeared to be the shortest. So I leaped in while half the party took a long rest (game mechanic), because I only had two rounds before I would have one card left and removed from the game. This is even though I was at full health.

I say I don't like it and I payed well enough to come out at the end with no damage, grabbing the main treasure, tied for second place for who picked up the most gold and I had the most XP (16 not counting the amount you get for completing scenario successfully). We did win on the first try with everyone still standing.

For a dungeon crawl, I would choose Mice and Mystic over Gloomhaven, because Gloomhaven can be more about card management/accounting than playing a character through a story.

That said, have fun and make sure everyone else does also.

I love the theme of this game. But, that's about it.
Gloomhaven is not for the feint of heart. This isn't a casual dungeon crawl by any means. This is a game requiring in depth knowledge of the mechanics, cards, and the ability to min-max to the extreme. You WILL get your butt kicked. A lot.

What turned my group, and ultimately myself as well, off to this game was the card management mechanic (which is the core mechanic to Gloomhaven). You're at a race against time, always. If you don't know and understand the symmetry of every one of your cards, and your allies the same, then you've lost before you've began.
Every single one of our/my play throughs left us feeling frustrated and unaccomplished. Regardless of if we won the scenario or not.

TL;DR:
Gloomhaven doesn't scratch that dungeon crawl experience itch for myself, or anyone I know. Lots of great potential in this big box, but the main mechanic spoils this 'could be' masterpiece.

My personal biggest board game disappointment, that fails for me both as a dungeon crawler, AND and a tactics game:
Heres why:

- You are in a constant pressure to rush forward, as your deck constantly decreases. Which disables any feeling of exploration, AND adds a lot of stress!
- When enemies are revealed, all of them get an instant action. Which will lead to a lot of instant-deaths.
Be prepared to replay missions, until you have learned what to expect, and can adapt.
- Combat is very random: You have to play your cards, before you even know the turn-order, and you then draw combat-modifiers for each attack on top. Which leads to very unpredictable tactics.

I’ve played through what I think is the main story and...wow! Gloomhaven has changed boardgaming for me. The game system is unapologetically complex. At its core is a dungeon crawler that pays some tribute to games like Descent and Heroquest but refines the premise to a highly strategic and finely balanced fantasy brawler that relies on careful hand management and careful map planning instead of dice rolling. While there is a randomizer deck and uncertainty about who gets the first lick in, I felt like my decisions had the greatest impact on the outcome.

Beyond the core combat, Gloomhaven continues to impress. Emergent map locations and effects, choose your own adventure style events between missions, evolving strategies from upgrading cards (by stickering them!), and writing that’s... actually pretty good.

Outside of the game is the thrill factor of opening little packets of skill and character cards, story things (I’m assuming that’s what those sealed envelopes are), and minis that are in individually sealed boxes reminiscent of heroclix or lego mini fig singles. It’s a joyful process of discovery digging into that box of stuff.

And what a box it is. The sheer amount of cards, location tiles, creatures, and tokens gave ample opportunity for some components to have issues. But no, they are immaculate. Each money token, every tiny sticker, every card is at the top of its... game. I didn’t find any frayed edges or ugly art. The WHOLE thing is beautiful. All of it.

Sure, I can find a complaint if I really tried. I don’t like the permanently stickering my pretty components. Maybe some of the rules are a bit fiddly. But realistically, both of those are things many players will find add to the experience.

So yeah, my expectation for board games has just leveled up. A new generation has been defined. There’s what came before Gloomhaven and there’s Gloomhaven.

When I bought this game, I was no stranger to fantasy gaming. I've spent a large part of my youth playing Dungeons and Dragons, and as an adult, I'm an experienced raider in World of Warcraft. When this pandemic hit, I wanted a game to play with my kids and my girlfriend and her daughter. Soooo, I found BGG and saw how huge this site is and decided to buy the #1 game on the list. Can't go wrong there, right? Wrong...

At the time it was too much and nobody wanted to play, so I sold it. The combat system was too much at the time. In hindsight though, I would have kept it for sure. A few months into board gaming now, I chose what I thought would be a lighter dungeon-crawler, just so I could say we have a dungeon-crawler, so I bought Descent 2nd Edition.

Now that I'm used to how dungeon-crawlers work with knowledge of both Gloomhaven and Descent, I can honestly appreciate how great Gloomhaven is. In addition to this, although I didn't love it at first, the original races, abilities etc... of the characters in Gloomhaven is fantastic and synergizes well with other characters. Original concepts are refreshing to me (age 50) at this point. Regurgitating concepts from Lord of the Rings although familiar, is getting a bit boring and Gloomhaven is different.

The combat system is a tiny bit more tedious than Descent, but I think it is better. The legacy aspect of the game is also great. We've been playing the app-assisted Journey to Legend with Descent, and it helps with my girlfriend's daughter (she loves dungeon crawlers, which is why we play it), I personally like it better without an app. Playing the game without an app, but also without needing a dungeon master is really important in my opinion.

The number of game pieces is both daunting and amazing. I had to buy 5 tackle boxes just to accomodate all of the pieces in this game (crazy, but in hindsight, pretty awesome). I think the game has an opportunity here to sell minis, so that gamers can upgrade all those cardboard monsters!

I may eventually re-buy this game, depending on whether or not Descent 3 is any good.

Based on these criterias: Mechanism, Dynamism, Complexity, Thematic, Art, Replayability; below is what I think.

Mechanism - probably the best and smartest mechanism ever imagine for a game. Alterning between city and dungeon phases, most part of the game will involve fightings, which is ruled by deck building combining combat and movement actions.

Dynamism - in this area, I though the game could have been better imagined as the setup time is extensive and the city phase, apart of the upgrade, is there for nothing really.

Complexity - the game has a great balance of complexity: really interesting mechanisms, multiple character upgrade startegies and extensive diversity in gameplay. This is one of the strongest aspect of the game.

Thematic - this game really brings you a new world where you feel being "the hero", however, while the theme is nice, I thought a story book would have really help connecting the different dungeons - only there to help leveling up your characteres, it feels - and replace a rather poor compilation of flavor text.

Art - another great game that does not only rely on warriors and sorcerers vs trolls and goblins. This game truly immerse you in an inovovative world to discover.

Replayability - the very diverse mechanism of the different characters makes this game highly replayable. Discovering the different characters makes the replayability extremly extensive.

All in all, one of the best game in the world indeed but truly in need of a storyline to make it more thematic, and an easier setup.

Gloomhaven is smartly balanced and crafted to provide interesting mechanics to the players as they plunge into each new scenario. Each of the six starting characters feel different due to their action cards that are exclusive only to them, and every turn each player plays two cards that can combo in different ways, allowing the players situational choices with satisfyingly different outcomes if used with discretion.

To balance this out, Gloomhaven has a thoughtfully crafted “artificial intelligence” to control the baddies. Thankfully they move in a step-by step manner that doesn't feel over convoluted or messy, yet also gives nuance to how each opponent type fights. Overall the enemy system makes each new creature a challenge and a new threat to try to handle!

I won't do much more than mention the hundreds of bits and bobs, eleven additional unlockable characters (complete with their action cards, unlockable upgrade cards and nicely crafted miniatures) that are tucked away in mysteriously secretive little packages, Event cards that add a bit of random flavor to the player's story and knit each play session together, “hidden agenda” cards that give each player a different goal to shoot for (some of which may encourage the player to act a little bit less helpful in the scenario). and an unfolding story that brings you back session after session.

Just remember to give yourself plenty of time and space for Gloomhaven sessions. You will appreciate the real estate while setting up and later to keep all those bits on standby as you will often need several of them at a moment's notice. And do a bit of homework before you invite your friends over so you can have a handle on the rules before the session starts.

While I understand the charm among people who like their "RPG-lite" adventure games the modern way (classic Ameritrash adventure made out of Euro mechanics), this is exactly the turnoff for me. The hand management gameplay, while mechanically kind of clever, makes every scenario a race, kill the monsters or reach a certain spot before you've had to discard down to one action card per character. As for optimization exercises disguised as adventures, I enjoyed Mage Knight a lot more at least for a solitaire game.
The scenarios are repetitive as well, kill all enemies, kill the boss, or move your characters to target hexes and that's it. Nothing really original in the story or the cliched fantasy world. Subpar punchboard quality for a game this expensive.
For lovers of the legacy mechanic Gloomhaven delivers, and I guess this is the main selling point. Clearly a lot of thought has gone to the characters' leveling up mechanics, and there are LOADS of ways to improve your skills. So at least that part of the hype is deserved.

It feels weird to comment on the top rated game, here at BGG. As though any take other than Best Game Ever is bound to be obnoxiously "hot." I'm not here to be edgy, just to report what I find (for whom? for what? who knows?), and... I like Gloomhaven alright. I mean, it's fine. It's good.

It's a good time, if you can commit and find others to commit -- because it takes a hell of a lot of commitment to play this game. The cost, the storage space, the time it takes to set up and take down and store, the time it takes to play. Gloomhaven asks a lot from you.

And as to what it gives in return, what can I say? It's fun. I mean, I don't have markedly more fun playing Gloomhaven than other games. But it's not as though it's bad. It's a bit of work, perhaps, a bit "fiddly." And it can be frustrating when other players play... suboptimally (and worse when one player tries to tell others what to do). But at its best, it's fun to play.

In terms of story, I don't know. I respect the effort, but it's not as though it can compare with a genuine roleplaying game (given a competent Game Master).

On the whole, as good as Gloomhaven is (and it is good, truly), I don't know if the whole experience is worth all of the investment required. An 8 score is excellent. It shouldn't be a disappointment, when a game isn't a 10... But I kind of feel like it is, here. For everything that goes into it, Gloomhaven ought to be a stone cold 10 experience, transcendent -- and I'm certain it is for some -- but for me, it just isn't.

This is a truly excellent game with tons of replay value. It's gotten me through the pandemic with a group of friends, playing it on Tabletop Simulator. Whether playing in person or virtually, it's a great deal of fun. It's a typical coop RPG where each of you have a character with different strengths and you work together to complete missions, gather loot, and improve your abilities. Not a game for role playing your characters though - strictly fighting. Where it really excels is the mechanics, where you have a handful of cards all different. Each turn you play two of them and you use only the top of one and the bottom of the other (resulting in many agonizing decisions). The cards then go into the discard pile. Once you use up your cards you need to rest to regain them, in the process losing one of them to the trash pile. Some of them can produce dramatic effects but then are immediately trashed. If you run out of cards, you're out of the run, so you have to pace them carefully. The characters are well designed and balanced (except maybe for Three Spears) and play very differently. The story arc is also engaging. Nice added twists are also every character has a secret battle goal every mission that may cause extra interesting decisions and events card decks that can present interesting choices in the City and on the road. The monster AI is fiendishly complex which is either a feature or a bug depending on whether you like brain twisters. The monsters follow a complex set of rules, which is fun because that means they are non-random so you can strategize while they have a random ability card draw each round that provides variety. There are tutorials and quizzes online to help learn the AI and at least one player should make sure to master it first. Also be sure to bring up the FAQ as there are many many nuances to how everything interacts. Not a great game if you are prone to arguing. Great if you are into cooperating. Set up and clean up can be time consuming, but not if you are playing virtually on Tabletop Simulator. Once you've unlocked all the characters and maxed out to level 9, it can get a bit repetitive and overly easy. I would recommend focusing more on the central storyline and less on side quests. There are many many custom classes made by fans that you can use to keep up the interest. All in all, great game!

This is (as of now) my favourite board game ever!!

The gameplay is so well thought out, and there requires alot of strategy for each player to think out each movement. There is alot of variety in each scenario, with the board pieces, enemies, and the obstacles in your way.

It is definitely the little touches that make this game a real game-changer.
- The restriction of communication - so you are all working together but seperate at the same time!
- Different difficulty levels - So you can adjust it accordingly so you are not finding it too easy or far too hard and give up
- Enemy variety - Alot of different enemies, and they all do different things, so you are not facing the same thing everytime you play
- Enemy attack cards - add a little variety so they dont do the same thing in every scenario
Envelopes - An extra bit of reward as a treat
I could go on, but i wont.

Everything is such high quality, and every component has a place, and ties in with the story. The campaign is also one of the main reasons i love this game so much. Instead of JUST killing enemies and collecting treasure, there is also a background to it, the unlocking of locations, the city/road cards, upgrading your character, items etc.

I really wish that for the price of £105, that it had come with an organizer in it, because i had to fork out almost the same just for an organizer, when they could have easily made a decent one themselves. I have had to bad everything and it takes a long time to set up, which is not too ideal as i only tend to have 2-3 hours here and there, which is only enough for 1-2 scenarios. That isnt really appealing to have to spend 30-45 minutes packing and unpacking it for such a short time.

I do reccomend getting the folded space organizer with the game. It is of a very good quality, made of strong material and it organizes everything easily. Decks of cards are seperated, and can be seperated from the ones the players are using, and the "inactive ones". It also displays the enemies and battle tiles in an accessible way so i can just scan the box and take the required amount as needed. This organizer has cut my setup time in over half, and you can also change it around to fit how you want it to be organized!!

I have ordered the forgotten circle expansion, so i will be playing that once i have finished the campaign. Im only about 8 scenarios in so that will probably be a while yet.

The third iteration of the Descent series brings an integrated GM app and 3d terrain - I had originally semi-dismissed both as gimmicky (the app less so), but having played the first two quests, I have to say that both *really* work and elevate the gaming experience!

The design gets a lot of things right: The balance between what's in the app and what's on the board seems just right - there is lots of player agency and die rolling, while the app handles damage to the baddies.

The 3D elements and the modular boards adds not only immersion, but the 'emerging'-board or 'rolling quest' style of revealing parts of the board at a time is a really neat feature, keeping you on your toes and boosting the feeling of exploration.

The character acting in campaign is somewhat hammy and overdone, but surprisingly it kinda works.

Overall this it a lot like the initial release of WoW: the elements by themselves may not be perfect or all that innovative, but the whole of the parts is very well done

There were many wonderful things that surprised me in Descent: LotD: how easy the app was to use and how it's used, how easy the 3D terrain was to set up and store, how flexible and still intricate the fatigue and card flipping is and, perhaps most wonderfully, how wildly different the missions are. Playing 2p with 3 characters, we finished the campaign (excluding only the second side quest) in around 40 hours.

And I do want to emphasize, that these surprises proved their worth time and time again. We were constantly impressed how different feeling the missions had, whether that was a rush to finish the mission, defend until a certain point, exploration or something else entirely. Of course it has the same mechanics, but it felt second to Frosthaven on flexible the game systems can be. I enjoyed the different versions of the same enemies so while they use the same figure, they might have quite different stats and weaknessess and resistances. The exhaust, flip and dice all came together in a wonderful combo where it felt light and easy to get in to, but still had depth to it.

Still, there are things that I found somewhat subpar: the "travel popup texts" seemed like an afterthought, there was at times too much story in the middle of a game, especially when playing with others, not to mention that Events are nothing but story, and at times the missions got quite frustrating, especially with the constant spawns, etc.

All in all, its a fun campaign dungeon crawler that surprised us in some wonderful ways. It's not perfect, but it'll offer some great fun.

I enjoyed this game at the beginning, but the more I played it, the worse it got.

After a few plays, the first thing that comes to mind is that this is just a glorified app. Don't get me wrong, all of the 3D terrain with many miniatures on the board looks impressive and enhances the overall experience. However, most of the mechanics happen in the app, and it could easily be just that. There is a lot of upkeep, maintenance, and setup with the physical components, which feels unnecessary when you come to that conclusion.

The gameplay itself was initially enjoyable, and I liked several aspects of it. The game is quite simple and intuitive to learn. Turns are usually quick. Difficulty level is adjustable. The exhaustion tokens and flipping cards between two sides are quite clever and tactical. I also like that despite you rolling the dice very often, the attacks pretty much never whiff entirely - you either do more or less damage, but at least you don't feel like you've done nothing and wasted your turn, at least in the beginning. However, later on, it loses that feeling, as dealing 4 damage to bullet sponges with 50 health and lots of armor starts to feel like you've done nothing anyway.

As already mentioned above, the upkeep of the game can sometimes be tedious as you constantly reveal new rooms, spaces, etc, and so there are frequent interruptions to the flow of the game. The scenarios feel too long, with 3-4 hours being the norm, and sometimes even longer. In addition, the game is often victim to bad scenario design - e.g., new enemies infinitely spawning from nowhere just to prolong the game and annoy you.

I am also not a fan of the graphical style of this new implementation.

And the worst part yet - story and writing. They are simply bad, on a level comparable to D&D fan fiction written by a teenager. Forcing the elements of modern progressive ideologies into the mix also doesn't help.

All in all, it's a light adventure game that can be fun sometimes, but after a while it becomes tedious, repetitive, and too random. Also, if you are looking for a good story or narrative, look elsewhere.

Eindruck nach 4. Partie: Das 3D-Gelände macht echt was her und erhöht Spielspaß und Immersion. App-Unterstützung wieder ein Stück weiterentwickelt seit VdW und HdR. Neben dem reinen Abenteurern hat man nun dazwischen Stadtaufenthalte mit Ereignissen und kann in der Stadt craften und einkaufen. Artwork (an die Helden musste ich mich gewöhnen, aber inzwischen bin ich froh,dass nicht einfach wieder Artwork recycelt wurde) gefällt mir sehr gut. In der App hat jeder Schauplatz seinen eigenen Hintergrund. Neben den Helden kommen auch noch NPCs ins Spiel, die ein tolles Artwork haben. Die Intro-Sequenz ist toll vertont und illustriert. Ebenso gab es zu Ende des 1. Abenteuers überraschend nochmal eine schöne Zwischensequenz. Misses im Kampf sind nicht möglich, das verhindert Frustmomente im Spiel. Die Gegner haben dafür relativ viel Lebenspunkte, was dazu führt, dass die Gegner länger auf dem Feld stehen und nicht nach 1-2 Hits schon wieder abgeräumt werden. Den Schwierigkeitsgrad (hab auf normal gespielt) empfand ich als angenehm fordernd. Kein Spaziergang, aber auch nicht unschaffbar. Das Schadenssystem mit leichten und schweren Verletzungen ist elegant gelöst. Insgesamt hat man wenig Komponenten (Marker, Karten usw.). Ich finde das angenehm entschlackt. Außerdem mag ich es, dass es nur die Standard-Kartengröße gibt und keine kleinen Karten. Die Box finde ich Hammer! Kann überhaupt nicht nachvollziehen, wenn sich jemand beschwert, es würde eine halbleere Box verkauft. Wenn man das 3D-Zeug aufgebaut hat, ist die Kiste ja nicht mehr leer. Viel ätzender wäre doch, wenn man nicht alles in der Box unterkriegen würde. Das System mit der Box in der Box finde ich geradezu genial und die Miniaturen sind in schönen Trays sicher verpackt. Es gibt Haupt- und Nebenquests. Direkt nach dem 1. Abenteuer hat man die Wahl zwischen zwei verschiedenen Quests. Das fühlt sich nach mehr Freiheit an als z.B. bei HdR. Zusammenbau der 3D-Teile hat problemlos geklappt und war nicht so nervig wie befürchtet. Qualität der Marker, Karten, Minis ist einfach nur top! Für die Spielplanteile hätte ich mir etwas mehr Kreativität gewünscht. Wenn man sich die Teile anschaut, wirkt auf den ersten Blick alles einfach nur sehr grau in braun in dunkelgrün - warum nicht mal ein Dungeoncrawler mit einem etwas farbenfroheren Look? Oder mal ein anderes Setting als das immergleiche Dungeon. Auch ein paar mehr Details auf den Bodenplanteilen hätten nicht geschadet (Skelett, Blutflecken, Runen etc.). Wenn man den Spielplan dann während des Spielens aufbaut, macht das Ganze wie oben geschrieben aber schon was her und mir gefällt auch die Idee mit den Wasser/Lava/usw.-Unterlegteilen sehr gut. Für die Heldenbögen hätte ich mir dickere Pappe gewünscht, auch wenns vom Spiel her nicht zwangsweise notwendig ist.

Digan lo que digan... esto es Descent 3

Jugando no es tan diferente del 2 (de hecho diria que se diferencia mas el 2 del 1 que el 3 del 2), pero en elementos clave si es bastante diferente. y lo que es importante: se siente como una experiencia nueva.

La caja "base" se denomina "Acto 1" y se alarga durante 16 escenarios. Se juega completa y absolutamente mediante app. de hecho no hay modo asimetrico. solo se puede jugar hasta 4 jugadores cooperativo usando la aplicacion. Y no es solo porque la app te dice lo que tienes que montar de escenario y en que momento (por cierto, vuelve el descubrimiento de escenario segun avanzas, una de las cosas que se echaba de menos en la 2da edicion) y porque controla el movimiento de los enemigos y su vida asi como los eventos de final de ronda (si, aqui hay "mimitos", a lo juego de lovecraft, y dan un cariñito que no veas), de viaje previo al escenario, y de final de escenario cuando toca, sino tambien porque controla en gran medida el inventario de los jugadores. especialmente cierta parte del inventario que no se ve y no esta presente en la mesa de juego.

wait.... what?¿?

si. en este juego ademas del inventario que puedes ver (2 armas que puedes llevar encima y que tienes que ir alternando, equipo en plan armadura, escudo, anillo/talisman, y algunas pociones), hay un inventario conjunto del equipo, consistente en oro, recursos y experiencia, del cual solo queda constancia en la app, y que se utiliza en las tiendas entre misiones para comprar y mejorar el equipo de los heroes, y para activar ciertas mejoras del mismo

en otras palabras: que le han metido mecanica de looteo y compra de equipo con ese loot. no es que este mal implementado ni mucho menos... pero es curioso, porque es una linea de encuentro entre juego de mesa, juego de rol y videojuego que uno la verdad es que no se la esperaba.

el otro gran cambio, y este si es completamente visible en la mesa, son los niveles y escenografia 3D, con pisos encima de pisos (hasta cierto punto) y ciertos elementos de escenografia con los que se puede interactuar (buscar en estanterias y mesas de trabajo, saltar encima de mesas de comedor, usar de parapeto, trepar a arboles, bajar a pozos... sin duda el gran puntazo de esta nueva edicion.

otro punto nuevo que tiene claros y oscuros son los personajes. en el juego se lleva a 6 personajes nuevos, originales para esta edicion (no son personajes ni del 1 ni del 2 ni de ningun otro juego de terrinoth) lo curioso es que el juego es para 4 jugadores maximo pero el grupo que se lleva en el juego es de los 6 personajes. ¿como se hace eso? pues al empezar cada nuevo escenario se puede elegir que 4 personajes se incorporan a la partida pudiendo elegir cualquier jugador a cualquier personaje. el inventario se guarda de un escenario al siguiente y la experiencia que se adquiere suma a todo el grupo incluidos los 2 personajes que no se incorporaron, con lo cual en cualquier nuevo escenario, los jugadores pueden elegir con libertad con que personaje jugar, y cambiar de personaje de un escenario al siguiente si les da la gana (aunque todos mantuvimos mas o menos al mismo personaje toda o casi toda la campaña, de hecho el que mas cambie de personaje, fui yo).

esa es la parte buena del asunto. la no tan buena es que los personajes tienen de carisma lo justito, y en mi opinion, el arte del juego no ayuda. han cambiado el diseño artistico que venian llevando en practicamente todos los juegos de la saga de terrinoth por un nuevo arte que... sere sincero. a mi no me entra. no es "terrible" pero me parece bastante poco interesante con respecto al anterior, lo que en mi opinion es un minipunto negativo.

en el manejo hay cambios sustanciales. no en lo basico (se sigue manejando 2 acciones con movimiento interrumpible, tirada de dados para los ataques y pruebas, etc). ahora la iniciativa es automatica, la lleva la app aunque los jugadores pueden seguir eligiendo en que orden juegan, los enemigos se activaran a criterio de la aplicacion. donde si hay cambio importante es en el manejo de la fatiga, muy diferente a los anteriores descent, y el manejo de armas. los personajes tienen 2 armas en la misma carta y giras la carta para cambiar de arma. tambien cambian ligeramente las acciones (por ejemplo ahora ciertas acciones como abrir puertas consumen movimiento, no accion)... en general requiere cambiar un poco el chip, y no es mal sistema. a mi particularmente me gusta un poco mas el de la 2ed, pero este no es ni mucho menos malo.

por contra el diseño de enemigos es tan bueno como siempre, el manejo con la app esta muy bien depurado con respecto a los antecesores (descent 2ed, mansiones 2ed, ESDLA viajes...), el diseño de objetos y armas, aunque tambien me gusta mas el de los anteriores descent, es suficiente (aunque se echa de menos mas variedad de armas) y las fases de intermision en el pueblo ponen una buena guinda.

en general el desarrollo narrativo es de notable alto. la historia es bastante arquetipica (de hecho... SPOILER ATENCION SPOILER SI SIGUES LEYENDO A PARTIR DE AQUI TE VAS A COMER UN SPOILER ¿este juego es precuela del descent 2ed?... porque aqui en la ciudad te encuentras con uno de los villanos del descent 2ed (zacareth) y aqui es... uno de los NPC de la ciudad. (no recuerdo si es capitan de la guardia o algo asi. es importante pero no recuerdo los detalles), de hecho segun se va desenredando la trama, este personaje en concreto va derivando, hasta que en los ultimos escenarios hay que enfrentarse con el en determinado momento y despues de eso, huye... pero no me termina de quedar claro si esto es precuela o es "linea del tiempo alternativa" o que coños FIN DEL SPOILER)

ademas durante el desarrollo de la campaña te vas encontrando con bastantes personajes (heroes) de los anteriores descent y otros juegos de terrinoth, y eso le da una nota de colorcito guay al juego.

y si, esto es un acto I y se supone que habra un acto II, y el final del juego AQUI VIENE OTRO SPOILERACO ATENCION SPOILER PARA QUE LUEGO DIGAN QUE NO AVISO, AQUI VIENE SPOILER ... pues viene a ser un "concluirá" que ademas la cosa viene terminando mas o menos como venia empezando pero mas enredada... pero de algun modo la cosa queda "bien" desde el punto de vista de los heroes... y no queda claro que haran con ellos en el siguiente acto, si manejaremos a los mismos personajes, si llevaremos a otros, si podremos elegir... se nota que lo dejan todo abierto a la espera de la opinion de los jugadores para tomar la decision definitiva en el diseño del siguiente juego.

de hecho este juego salio en 2021, estamos a finales de 2023 (han pasado mas de 2 años) y ni ha salido acto II, ni expansion ninguna, ni se sabe planes concretos ni de una cosa ni de la otra... y FFG quedo muy tocada en los ultimos tiempos y especialmente desde el confinamiento de 2020. esta la cosa en el aire.

edit. en 2024 se publicó el Acto II. como no lo he jugado y no me he puesto a mirar reviews, no se si son personajes nuevos o no y como avanza la historia.

mi valoracion final es que es un excelente nuevo capitulo de descent. no es una esfera 100% perfecta, pero es una bonita esfera brillante.

Dungeon Crawler with app integration. Successor to Descent. There is a lot of cardboard terrain. Setting up and down the terrain is a bit tedious. App dominates the game, feels more like a digital game than a board game.

I like:
+ Card and resource (token and fatigue) management. Played cards get flipped (cards are double-sided). Cards can be charged with tokens. Multple cards can be used to build combos.
+ Dice have multiple symbols on a side (similar to Sword and Sorcery or Galaxy Defenders). Number of successes can be increased by playing tokens.
+ Heroes play differently. However, some play more interesting than others.
+ Dynamic maneuvering and terrain levels with different effects.
+ Fast pace gameplay.
+ Monsters have different stats plus active and passive abilities. Monsters may also manipulate other monsters. Scenarios may change monster tactics and behavior.
+ Scenarios: some with events with twists, encounters, small puzzles, and boss fights.
+ Character progression based on feats. Some feats are only available in certain scenarios.
+ Experience points are shared among players.
+ Difficulty levels. The game should be played on warfare otherwise the game is too easy and tactics become trivial.
+ Escalation: monsters get stronger over time (time pressure with warfare).

Neutrals:
# App required which handles most of the bookkeeping.
# Rather generic setting and boring story.
# Town phase.
# 3D cardboard terrain with multiple height levels and components (similar to Chronicles of Drunagor).
# Simple to manage, predictable AI.
# Rudimentary looting / equipment.
# Luck of the roll. Dice-based combat.
# Fail forward system (avoids exploiting the game that players grind all feats).

I do not like:
- Set-up (3D terrain). The composite board is somewhat unstable and must be handled with care.
- Difficulty does not always scale well with different player counts (can be patched in the App).
- Context change: It is a weird game. I'm not sure if I am playing a board game or a video game, since I have to switch back and forth regularly. The advantage is that the app takes care of bookkeeping and referencing encounters. Still, I wonder why they didn't develop the game completely as an app? I could then move my heroes directly in the app and the app could roll dies for me as well...
The app I would like to see would be one that reads the status of the board to control the monsters and events like a real game master.

See also:
* Chronicles of Drunagor: 3D terrain, cube management, motivating character progression, simple dice-based combat, generic fantasy.
* Sword and Sorcery: Ancient Chronicles: much more fiddly, a lot of bookkeeping, and rules heavy, overall slower gameplay, similar good scenario design, dynamic tactical combat with more depth, high difficulty, generic fantasy.
* Altar Quest: generated dungeons, resource management.
* The Bad Karmas and The Curse of the Zodiac: boss battler with full app integration and additional electronics to track physical game elements.

Overall really enjoyed playing through a 2 player campaign with my husband, but it was somewhat demoralizing that we lost so badly in the final scenario that it seemed like there was no way we could beat it, and to never have gotten a chance to level up the characters very much.
Now I'm playing through a 4 player campaign with my kids, and we're having a blast! The story is a huge hit with them, and they love reading their character's lines! They also love finding out which of their weapon effects triggered on each attack! Of course the terrain, etc., is so cool looking and tons of fun, too!

It's a high production value playset, with an overly simplistic board game attached. I have a lot of respect for designers that are trying to replicate the classic D&D experience without a GM. This is just mind-numbingly linear; all style, no substance.

The table presence is good, but all that terrain has very little gameplay value - AND it inflates the cost of the game. I really wanted to see multiple heights on the map make a tangible difference, but it doesn't. You can interact with terrain, but only in the most simplistic way (loot/objective). Shoving terrain, flipping tables, jump attacks from higher levels - none are present. I don't mind how the app takes some bookkeeping away, but this integration is quite heavy. You are basically being dictated a scenario. The app does more than the players do! Agency and depth of decision space is puddle-thin. Descent LotD paints a lovely fantasy canvas, and then denies players the agency to actually play around in the space.

I have not subtracted any points from my score for the art style, nor the presence of the app. The app is actually well designed. All of my focus was on whether this game was fun, and how it stood in comparison to similar dungeon crawls. For a fraction of the price, you can get your gaming table any version of Zombicide, or Massive Darkness 2 which both have similar levels of complexity, and can even play in a campaign style.

I really enjoyed Descent 2e, and I also enjoyed its app integration for how it added co-op modes and variable scenario styles. FFG is adamant that LotD is not Descent 3e, but I fail to see how it isn't. It's a spinoff trilogy (apparently), while the core inspiration product languishes without reprints or a product that plays to the established audience.

I do not begrudge anyone that has a blast with this playset. I do resent that FFG pushed this product as a spinoff series, yet discontinued the original line. This pushes the more board-gamey audience to their competition, rather than letting both groups run parallel or intersect with each other.

I approached Descent Legends of the Dark with... caution.
I read and listened a lot about it before deciding to acquire a copy, but I wasn’t sure it would suit my tastes.
It did, in a surprisingly positive way.

First and foremost: the app. It works marvelously, like no other before. It truly builds upon the shoulders of those used for Mansions of Madness and Journeys. It’s smooth, it keeps track of everything, it’s wonderfully integrated with the game. It creates the first working paperboard/digital game hybrid, allowing for effects (like buffing and various modifiers) that wouldn’t reasonably be trackable without the app. Of course, if one is a paperboard purist, should steer away.

Second: the 3D terrain. Far for being a(n expensive) gimmick, it’s finely integrated with the game flow and truly contributes to the gaming experience. Another positive surprise.

The gameplay itself is enjoyable, smooth, and the focus remains on the board, with the app acting as a game master and aid in the background.
The mechanics do work, and the game is an enjoyable tactical puzzle with exploration. The crafting between sessions is compelling and adds a dimension only digital games could offer until yesterday.

The whole art and presentation is amazing, and I really like the new direction taken (but I disliked the previous aesthetics of Terrinoth).
The miniatures are CMON quality and way above the previous FFG standard.

The game is far not perfect, though.
The dialogues feel very “meh” and could’ve easily been made much better and really interesting. The campaign as a whole? To be evaluated.

The price? Before buying it felt too much. Now that I tried the game, I am not so sure anymore. An app this good costs a lot, and can’t recoup money through a bazillion sales... so it must be factored in the box price.
175€ MSRP, in retrospective, is probably fine.

Have been playing through the campaign for a while now, with four of us playing. Must say, I really really like this game. As the forever DM for our group, this to me is the closest I can get to playing D&D as a player with no one having to be the DM, provided you accept you're playing an on rails story.

The story is good, provided you don't mind the overly sweet and good nature of the characters portrayed. Don't play this game if you want to be the bad guy or an anti hero.

The main points I would stress before playing this game, as it won't be for everyone, is:
* You will need to allocate a lot of time to play this. We have been finding each session (playing one actual quest and completing all the available narrative quests and taking care of the crafting stuff) takes about five hours.
* You will need to find players that don't mind having to deal with LOTS of dialog and narrative story. Personally I loved it but if you're after a game that goes straight into actual play you will be frustrated.
* You will need a LARGE table. The play area that this covers once you start exploring and laying out the 3D terrain, and all the player cards etc, is very large.

Good points:
* Story is well done
* Exploration is fun and engaging
* Combat is easy to perform but hard to master. What seems like a simple system with limited options is all about individual combos and timing (card flips) and team combos and timing, and managing your stress. When you get this right it's awesome. When you get this wrong, especially in the beginning when you're still learning, you will feel underpowered.
* Miniatures are fantastic and well worth the time to paint
* 3D board looks great on a table
* The app is easy to use and allows you to focus on the tactics and spend most of your time talking about which order to play that round, who's doing what, who's helping who, and how best to deal with the situation. The app just makes this easier, and doesn't require you to navigate silly menus to get things done. You spend most of the time looking at the table and board, discussing what to do and how to do it, and just use the app to input it and find the result.

Bad points: (and why I am not giving this 10/10)
* No voice narration, apart from the intro and a limited number of short cut scenes. If there ever was a game that demanded a proper voice acted narration, especially for all the character dialog, this is it. I can not understand how this was not included in the app. Heck, I would pay $15 for a DLC to the app for a fully voiced option. It forces you to have one person read out all the text on the screen, which is not an ideal situation, or have everyone sit around the iPad screen trying to read it.
* No animated graphics of the characters. You will spend A LOT OF TIME looking at the characters on the app, during narrative and dialog scenes. The character image NEVER changes. Again this is a really disappointing decision considering how story based this game is. They could have done some simple, and minimal animation, especially with facial expressions.
* Very minimal cut scenes. There is one in the beginning and an occasional one during the campaign but it really is lacking. Which is a shame because when you do get a cut scene, they are well done and really show what could have been.

Conclusion
With the right group of people this game is a lot of fun and well worth a play.

8/17/21 UPDATE: After a couple more missions I can say I am THOROUGHLY enjoying this. I Keep comparing it to it's previous brethren Mansions of Madness 2nd and Journeys in Middle Earth and I gotta say I think I prefer this game more than Journeys now. Although still like it about the same as Mansions. Which is to say I'm loving it. upping the rating to a 9.

Original review:

Initial rating based on the first mission and city phase and all around package, rating may go up or down after repeated plays. It's an enjoyable game! I really like the terrain elements and the underlays add a neat little effect and look to the game as well. The combat is pretty straight forward with you only rolling a single die and then tallying up successes and determining if you want to use fatigue to gain more successes AND if you can use any other abilities. Then you input your success total into the app and it calculates the rest. Nothing super complicated but also it is engaging since you have determinations to make with the fatigue usage.

The included rulebook is great and explains everything really well. Add the app to that and it really does help with learning the game during the first mission. The app has a glossary and search bar so you can just type in whatever keyword you have a question about and it will find it for you. Super helpful.

The components are mostly excellent with great card quality and the cardboard terrain looks really good. I love the fun different little terrain features such as the cauldron and shelves. Most of them feel very sturdy and have a nice weight to them as well. The plastic minis are superb, very much Games Workshop quality in the details. There are a decent amount of minis too, more than I initially thought were packaged with the game so you have a nice variety of enemies to come into contact with. I also like the neat little colored pegs you place below the base of the enemies to differentiate then in the app, a nice touch.

Now, for the things I don't like. Really don't like all the back and forth dialog in the app. I've only been playing the game solo as 2-3 characters (first mission with 2 and just started the second with 3) and I can already tell this is going to be an issue if I ever want to play with a larger group. Trying to read all the different rando characters that pop up to talk to each other while playing on a tablet or phone is just not going to happen. Would suck the fun right out and be awkward as hell to hold up the device so everyone could see who is saying what. Now, if casting to a tv it wouldn't be AS bad I don't think.

The story so far is pretty same ol same ol. Granted I have only seen a fraction of it so I'm not holding the overall story hostage here BUT the written dialog is pretty bad. It's bad enough that it would be a pain to deal with a group but also, it just isn't good dialog. The bit when you first arrive to the city after the first mission was soooo boring. I read through it all and could predict everything already before the end, AND it seems like it goes on forever! I think if this was all voice acted it would be better for group play for SURE. But not sure that could save it from the tediousness of it.

The price. Again, only 1 mission down with city bits but I'm just not seeing the value here. This will of course be a super opinion that will differ from person to person but yeahhhhh. I paid $140 and think it's wayyyy overpriced for what you get, app included. The most recent comparison I can make is FF's own Lord of the Rings Journey's in Middle Earth. App based and TONS of cards and interesting stuff included, lots and lots of tiles and less than half the price of this game. THE ONLY thing this game has, over that one, is the 3d terrain. Granted, it is pretty cool I won't deny.....but for an extra $60? Not worth it imo. Btw I'm taking these prices from online retailers, not Fantasy Flights retail price, which would put LoTR at $99 and DLotD at $175. BUT, it DOES look neat on the table. One of the most unique games I have for table presence now.

Overall:

Likes - I really enjoy the game aspects, the "dungeons" and even the city stuff is fun. The terrain is also really cool and the minis and components are top notch.

Neutral - The artwork is fine. I mean, art is art is art. The critics for art vary as much as the art itself for any piece and this isn't any different. I don't hate it but I don't love it.

Dislikes - The dialog is very bland and not a good fit for group play. The price is also much more than I felt the package is worth.

Giving it an 8....for now

Okay. A bit of backstory might be in order. My buddy and I played the first edition of Descent: Journeys in the Dark at GenCon SoCal when it was demoed by FFG back in 2005. I bought a large tackle box and got all the minis organized in it to assist with gameplay. We really enjoyed it.

When Descent: Legends of the Dark was released, I was hoping that it would be backwards compatible with Journeys in the Dark, similar to how Mansions of Madness: Second Edition worked with the first edition parts. I was so disappointed that it wasn’t compatible that I shunned the game. Earlier this year, FFG announced a 30% off sale. That was enough for us. We bought it at our FLGS and took it home to try out. From that point on, we played it literally every free moment we had. We were disappointed on the days we had to work late and wouldn’t get to play. We played it all the way to the end, and were thoroughly hooked. Is it the same old Descent? Nope. Not really. There are some similarities, but it is an entirely different game. The app is 100% necessary, but that didn’t bother us. Is it perfect? Nope. Not at all. Was it really fun and rewarding? Absolutely! We can’t wait for the expansions to come out, and would thoroughly recommend it.

Update #1:

I hit the 10-play mark! My kids like the game, and it hits the table occasionally at cons and game nights. I may actually hit 20 plays before death. So sue me.

For those hoping to improve balance issues, we always use the following variants: (1) threat costs on spawn cards are per figure, with the overlord having the option to spawn fewer than the maximum # of figures - although any master figures are always spawned last, and (2) killing the same hero twice in a row results in the overlord receiving half the number of conquest tokens, rounded down.

Update #2: (many years later)

Revisited 1E by finally cracking open the Quest Compendium during Nostalgiafest, New Year's Eve 2020.

The Compendium is an honest reminder of how screwed up 1st edition actually was. We selected the scenario with the smallest map (dueling giant/dragon), and our session still took 3 hours - and that included variants and on-the-spot house rules to salvage the experience by making it coherent and reasonably balanced.

Prior to playing, we wondered whether it might eventually be worthwhile to take our unpunched Sea of Blood for a spin. After the Compendium trip down memory lane, the answer is easy: decidedly not.

1E is best forgotten, and I've now given myself permission to pack up the Road to Legend campaign we abandoned a decade ago. Good times, bad times, you know I had my share.

One player takes on the role of the overlord controlling the monsters, and a team of up to four players take on the role of the heroes. The game can be quite long, but compelling in a number of ways that I don't often see in other games of this genre. There is some character customization, but the process happens very quickly as opposed to the tech tree slog of Descent 2. Additionally, as the players progress, the map gets revealed gradually, and most maps have a secret puzzle of sorts that the players need to work out in order to win. Additionally, since each level is a one-off, over the course of a single map, players go from having a feeling of being low level scrubs into being high level masters across a single session as they collect better and better gear.

That being said, the game can at times be frustrating. It could work out that several hours into a session, the players lose the game to a puzzle they didn't have the answer to. It could also be that players happen to get multiple cards together that each removes the overlord's action tokens making the next few turns a hero-steamroller rather than a proper back and forth experience.

In the late 80's and early 90's, games like HeroQuest and Dragon Strike sought to distill the dungeon crawl experience provided by D&D into a board game. These games largely succeeded and still hold up today, trading openness and flexibility for easy rules and minimal prep work. But this lack of prep and creativity also left the ersatz Dungeon Master with little more to do than facilitate the experience for the "real" players. (Fittingly, the new version of HeroQuest offloads this administrivia to an app.) Enter Fantasy Flight Games and Kevin Wilson in the early 2000's, who combined this one-versus-all dungeon crawl paradigm with a tactical minis game. Suddenly, the players weren't simply discovering pre-set traps and treasures, they were actively competing against a human adversary. The battle of wits had begun.

The rules of Descent are nearly self-explanatory to someone who has played any type of dungeon crawl or minis game. On your turn, you move and attack. Roll dice for damage, subtract armor, deal wounds according to the difference. But that simplicity belies the emergent complexity that comes from the vast array of scenarios, modular map tiles, dozens of monsters, scores of characters, and stacks on stacks of items.

In some ways, this is D&D as a board game. But in other ways it is decidedly not. Yes, the theme is the same, combat is very similar, but this is not a game about creativity and problem solving. This is a game of brutal tactical combat that can lead to a TPK in the first room if the players aren't careful and the overlord does their job. The overlord is not a referee, not your friend, and is playing a totally different game outside of the tactics on the board itself.

Descent is a very long "weekend-only" sort of game (4+ hours), but it hits all the right notes for me. The length is a necessity to feel the progress of leveling up. As your hero goes from store items to copper treasures to silver treasures before finally picking up those gold level treasures for the final boss fight, you will feel a real sense of accomplishment. You don't appreciate the real power of a gold-level weapon until you've spent an hour using a silver-level weapon. Descent as a design grants itself space to breathe.

The success of Descent led to a second edition and then a third edition. But neither of these fully captures the essence of what made first edition so unique. The length of the game didn't need to be shorter, that detracts from the experience of leveling. The overlord's job cannot simply be offloaded to an app without making the joy of beating the scenario feel hollow. And you absolutely cannot play this as an ongoing campaign without unbalancing the entire experience. Descent's first edition was lightning in a bottle. No publisher could possibly succeed with a design like this in today's market. People clamor for campaigns, apps, and solo play. But Descent is unapologetically a lengthy, multiplayer, single-session affair and it's the better game for it. Nothing has ever captured my imagination and obsession quite like it.

This is a really fun game with beautiful miniatures, but unfortunately, it has too many flaws that reduce the fun and the points I can give to the game.

First, it is a game with tons of minis, cards and tokens. For a game with that many components, especially at that cost, I expect some way to help me stay organized. However, nops, nothing there: no ziploc bags, no playtic trays, no cardboard organizing help, simply nothing. Even though I raided the kitchen for freezing bags, it takes too much time to organize the components before starting the setup. My gaming group isn't willing to waste that much time. If course, I could buy some foam organizers, but that leads to the second point...

Second, I don't like the box. It is cheap, thin cardboard, and while the box is huge, it is too small for the content. So even if would buy foam organizers, the is no room for them. The big miniatures make the matter worse: You have to assemble them, but in their assembled state, they take far too much space. Thus there is no real way to paint them and keep them assembled, unless I replace the boxes.

Third, the cards: I don't know how exactly, but from the beginning, the cards were kind of sticky, like someone handled whem with really messy hands. I could, of course, sleeve them up, but as I mentioned in my second point, the box is already far too small, sleeved cards simply won't fit. Also, I don't get the reason why the buyable equiptment cards are double sided, with two identical sides. A simple backside for all equipment cards you can purchase would help to get cards sorted.

Fourth, the miniatures: They are beautiful, but...
The hero miniatures are very small, I simply couldn't paint them without magnifying glasses. Compared to them, the monsters are huge, and as I said before, some have to be assembled and are then too big, so while the dragon and demon look great, I can't paint them unless I replace the box with an even bigger one.

Finally, this is an overlord game. Per se that isn't bad, but there is a high risk that either side doesn't have fun. In descent, that is a big problem. Either the overlord plays his position well and gives the heroes a really hard time, or he lacks to give them a b etter chance, which unfortunately makes the game quite b oring for him. So far, in neither game we played both sides got to enjoy the game at the same time.

So what does that mean for me? Most likely, we won't play the game again. Instead, the miniatures will get assembled, painted and put into a vitrine. Actually sad, since the game had a lot of potential.

Very fun dungeon crawl game that's only drawback is playing time. But even playing time can be fairly variable depending on the scenario and the number of players/heroes. The rules aren't overly complicated for a game like this to the extent that it is pretty easy to get a new player up to speed quickly with what they need to know to function at a basic level and then just introduce more specific rules as the situations come up. The stock scenarios have good variety with each tending to introduce something unique (monsters, tactics etc.). There are also a lot of well done, interesting fan created scenarios on the Fantasy Flight website.

While there are a fair amount of rules this is a game that can be picked up quicker than you might expect. I'd recommend the more experienced player play as the overlord if you want the game to flow along at a nice pace. For new overlords out there be sure to play a couple of solo games prior to running a group of heroes through a scenario, especially if they will be new players. This will help you get the rules down well enough that the game shouldn't bog down too much. You'll want to be able to explain each players options for each turn at least for the 1st room or so.

There are a large number of expansions available for the game including a book of new scenarios. That combined with the fan created scenarios on FFG's website gives the game a huge replay factor. I'd count the Well of Darkness expansion as a must have since it provides several interesting monsters that work well with less experienced players. Weak monsters that still have the ability to hurt you are great for scaling adventures for different numbers of players and for players of varying levels of experience. The addition of expansions that introduce campaign play (Road to Legends and Sea of Blood) takes the game to another level. If you want to play the game a lot then these expansions offer an easy way to accomplish this.

The first dungeon crawling game I ever truly loved. Honestly in some ways, it's still my favorite.

The Pros:

-Playing just one scenario is truly satisfying and gives you a complete dungeon crawling experience WITH PROGRESSION. This is something no dungeon crawler since, even Descent 2.0, has managed to get right. The escalation as both sides grow in power feels epic. This is what drew me to the game in the first place and what makes it work for those of us who don't have the time to devote to regularly play an RPG.
-Fatigue is an excellent mechanic. Being able to strategically spend some limited resource just to get an extra square of movement or activate a cool ability or add a power die is great.
-Surges are also a cool mechanic. Adds more fun and variation to rolls.
-Playing as the Overlord is fun!
-Characters are varied and interesting.

The Cons:

-Can be lengthy. This is one of the few games I will sit down and devote 2-3 hours to, but now that I've played so many games of it that's less appealing.
-The balance is pretty fucked in the base game. Don't expect to win if you're the Overlord - your monsters suck too much. Except in a couple scenarios where the Heroes don't have a chance. Ugh.
-There's a couple things that are a little fiddly. Things like the different types of actions (move, run, especially readying) are unintuitive.

Game progression is out of whack. The first part of the game feels just right. The heroes must work together, and there is a real sense of danger. The game tilts as the heroes gain treasures. This is a real problem. The toughest monsters are no match for the toughest treasures. End game often has the heroes waltzing into a room, using an uber-item, and watching dragons and giants disintegrate.

For the overlord to win, he must delay the heroes in order to cycle through the deck and remove conquest tokens. This results in heroes fighting wave after wave of weak spawned monsters. The monsters have no hope of killing the heroes after they obtain silver and gold armor. So, battles become incredibly repetitive and tedious for both the overlord and heroes.

As overlord, I often find myself NOT spawning creature after hours of repetitive fighting, just to get the game over with. I still must sit through the rest of it just to get to the inevitable ending where the heroes finally reach a room full of dragons and creatures that might actually pose a threat. But alas, they really don't pose a threat because by the time the heroes get that far they have such powerful uber items that they just waltz into the final room, use their, "Rune of immediate disintegration of all creatures ever imagined within three solar systems" and game over.

The 2nd edition eliminates all the negatives from this first edition, keeps the good stuff, and adds some more good stuff.

For those who have fond memories of HeroQuest from their youth, this game is like HeroQuest on steroids. Suffers from overly long playtimes (6-8 hours or more, unless you play it all the time and remember all of the rules, official rulings, FAQs, and errata off the top of your head). Suffers also from FFG's obvious lack of thorough play-testing (particularly when expansions are added on). Suffers also from fairly cheesy storylines. Also anti-climatic in that by the time the heroes reach the end of the quest, they are so buffed as to be able to take out the largest dragon with one swipe.

The components are awesome, though, and the sheer amount of stuff that the game allows for is great (yes, we've got rules if you are stunned! or dazed! or poisoned! or are walking through mud! or lava! or on ice! or if you are standing on top of some mushrooms!). I prefer the art direction here to the second edition, where it became a bit too cartoony/anime for my taste (in addition to having some of the cooler elements of the game removed in the dumbing down of it all).

I have hopes that I'll get another chance to play this when my kid is older and when I have a dedicated game room that I can shut the cats out of so that we can play this in little pieces over a number of evenings.

An airing of grievances:

1) Takes 3-4 hours to barrel through a full scenario, not including the time it takes to set up and break down.

2) There's no sense of drama or mounting tension. Adventures always start out tough on the players, and once they grab silver/gold items it's a cakewalk from there on out. The end game seems to drag on endlessly as the mists of story and atmosphere dissipate, revealing a clunky hack-and-slash dice-off.

3) No control over character advancement. Characters don't actually improve; they just loot more powerful swag. Goodies are drawn randomly from various Treasure Decks which often leads to situations where characters will draw completely useless items (i.e. melee fighters drawing Runes), thereby not advancing their power level and making further reaches of the dungeons even more of a grind.

4) LOS spawning system is very, very irritating. Example: Our party once spent forty-five minutes of real time clearing the baddies out of a room with a single door only to walk through that doorway, lose LOS into that room, and then watch in horror as hordes of skeletons marched out of it the following turn. This makes no sense and guts any sense of accomplishment you might get from smashing bad guys.

For a game that tries to do so much, it's disheartening to see it fall short. I've read that the expansions improve on the base game quite a bit, but until the dude in our group who owns Descents picks any of them up, I've got to stick this rating. For the time you've got to put in to make this work, I'd rather play D&D.

We went through a full campaign of 1st ed back when. I've always enjoyed it, but it did have a few rough patches.

Teleporting back to town and going shopping in the middle of the adventure was king of strange and broke up the flow a bit.
The most bizarre part, though, was the monster spawning system. As the OL accumulated 'threat', he could use it to bring in reinforcements, which he could then move immediately on his turn. But, he could only place them in out-of-the-way corners where the heroes had no line-of-sight. So, you were in constant danger of being ambushed by packs of monsters who would appear out of nowhere. You might think this would increase tension, and it kind of did, but mostly it lead to this repetitive gaming of the system where you try and position your heroes around the room so that they can see all the nooks and crannies. And if you ever missed one, boom! a bunch of goblins, or spiders, or blood apes start chewing on you. This system warped the entire way the game was played. Instead of sticking together as a team, you were always fanning out to cover all the angles.

1st ed was always a bit too complex for its own good. It was generally good complexity, but no denying that the deluge of cards, chits, and minis made it tough to manage. I think things like the hand of hero special power cards (introduced in expansions) were kind of overkill.

Laying out the dungeon speeds play but here are a few ideas if you want to lay out the board as you play:
* Lay out the dungeon in advance, before the players come. Then put each room in labeled baggies. Label each baggie by Area number. You can include the miniatures and tokens in the baggies.
* Lay out part of the dungeon. Take a break after every two or so battles (they can get long!) and lay out the next two or so areas during the break.

Also:
* Buy a plano box (a plastic box with small areas) to hold the bits. I think a 15-section box works fine.
* Download "The Rescue" from the FFG site. It's a good introductory adventure. The first adventure in the Quest book is long and uses as many miniatures as it can from the set. IMO, You don't need really need to do that in your first game of Descent.

This is one of those dungeon crawling games. Yes, I know. Each of "those" games has a different feel to it, some work better, some not so well. What this one has going for itself is that it has really, really nice components, and that rolling the many coloured dice is fun. I also like that the heroes are quite diverse, have quite a few tactical and equipment options, and I like that the dungeon master has quite the selection of mean stuff up his sleeve - which he cannot necessarily play as he would like it.

It's a hack-and-slay dungeon crawl. It's far from bad at that, but it's also not the most exciting implementation of it. The rule for (teleporting into town from the dungeon) and buying stuff seems a tad unrealistic. Also, the fact that the dungeon master's best action - respawning monsters in unobserved spots of the dungeon - can be severely restricted by heroes who have famililars (and know how to use them to that end), seems quite unbalanced.

What always gnaws at me whenever I play one of these games is the question why I don't rather play a real RPG. If the game were real quick, it wouldn't matter that much, but it strives to be as facetted as possible for the hero players, which ends up being quite time consuming, while the pay off is insubstantial. I would recommend this one specifically for people in their early teens who might use it as kick off into playing RPGs.

I used to play this game a lot. One of my very first 'bigger' games. It looks cool with a those minis, dungeon map and everything.
The beginning feels good, really thematic. It is a nice dungeon crawl flair with exploration feeling. The heroes are eager to discover new rooms, enemies, treasure.

But it wears off pretty soon (after ~60 minutes of playing, not counting setup). Tasks becomes repetitive: Try and get to the new room, slay monsters, try to be faster than the newly spawned monsters. Dungeon layout is often designed so you have to run back and forth (get key from there, move back etc.). While this might be fun once, twice or thrice is not. There are major turning points whenever the heroes get a new item tier (silver, gold). If the heroes got their gold gear, the dungeon master can pretty much throw away all cards that are not buffed by permanent boosting cards. But you can also decide to play these cards. It will make the game last longer but not more fun (fun in this games depends on the master being not a dick...).
The boss fights are always luck driven. Who rolls better. After hours of playing, this is frustrating.

If you're the one owning the game, you will end up being the master most of the time. Owning the game isn't that much fun.
I would like to test the second edition though.

Descent takes the players for a potentially epic adventure of monster slaying and looting. The game feeds the most basic human cravings for killing your enemies and getting richer.

Descent is also a very ambitious venture trying to simulate an action role playing game in a boardgame format. It takes quite a lot of effort to manage all the rules, unique items, character builds, spells, events etc. Throw in an expansion or two and you find yourself amidst mountains of plastic and cardboard. All this translates into a very consuming gameplay for something that should be fast and jampacked with action on an instinct.

Here the role of the dungeon master (usually the owner of the game) is crucial. He has to keep the players from analysing their moves too much. He is also the most important person at the table for the story telling and immersion. If you find yourself just pushing plastic and rolling dice instead of imagining yourself running in a dungeon with a sword in your hand, you know that you are missing the best part.

With the right group, Descent can be great fun. Play on a gut feeling and forget analyies. Clinch fists and throw yourself into an adventure.

The crux of the problem with Descent was how the Overlord would activate all his guys at once and pick off one hero (often strolling by others) until he was knocked out. Then repeat. This was THE way for the OL to play every scenario as it worked. And the downtime waiting for him to maximize his 10+ dudes and cards was annoying. It felt imbalanced in terms of both power and fun.

SW: IA uses group activations that fix that balance of power and downtime beautifully. Now, the Imperial player can only activate a subset of his forces. This may be 1-2 powerful guys or 3-4 Average Joe Stormtroopers. The result is more interesting choices for the Imperial player and a more balanced back-and-forth among all the players.

To further imbalance the fun factor, the OL gets to level up way more than the heroes. After a session, the OL gets "experience income" (Conquest points) and purchases upgrades, not the heroes. SW: IA fixes this by both sides getting to purchase skill and/or weapon upgrades after a session but with the winning side getting more. How simple of a fix is that?

The result of all this is the OL and the heroes have very different experiences. The OL gets to play cards, play a wide variety of monsters, and make a lot of different decisions about using them each turn, and generally get to spend more Conquest tokens. The heroes plod along with a few dice rolls and only occasionally have enough Conquest to purchase a skill upgrade (and even here several have been nerf'd for the RTL expansion).

All in all, I'd much rather have the OL's experience for 6 hours than a hero's. My prediction was that this was the best of breed for its genre at one point but another game will come along at some point and make this obsolete by addressing the flaws identified above. Little did I know that, per my prediction, SW: IA would come along and fix the flaws I identified above.

I played a few campaigns of D2E (Shadow Rune, Labyrinth of Ruin & Shadow of Nerekhall) prior to playing the original D1E with a campaign (Road to Legend). While I like both games, at their cores D1E and D2E are fundamentally different games.

D1E plays more like a tactical dungeon crawl with an overarching storyline (i.e. go to a dungeon and get treasure, then go to town to heal and buy stuff, and ultimately go kill the final boss). D2E is more like a lite role playing game in which completing the objectives often trumps defeating enemies (i.e. go investigate what's going on around the battlefield and fight enemies if need be, but complete your mission before the bad guys complete theirs). Ironically, D2E is more linear in storyline (the winner of one quest determines which quest will be played next), whereas D1E offers a little more freedom as to where your heroes can go next.

Overall, I like both systems for the unique niches they each offer, but I wouldn't necessarily own both games. I would recommend a Descent edition based strictly on whether you are looking for a more classic dungeon crawl style game (D1E) or a lite RPG (D2E). Personally, I already own a few dungeon games, so I'm happy to own D2E vice D1E.
