Several plays in, the game works pretty well. I enjoyed it enormously and look forward to future play-throughs. The production values are incredible and the gameplay strikes a nice balance between tactics and pure hack-n-slash dice rolling. It has the sentiment of D&D's lineage but the intuitive design and streamlining of modern board-gaming. If only that intuitive elegance extended to the rulebook and balancing rather than just the components and mechanics--Descent is no better and no worse in this sense than Arkham Horror or any other Fantasy Flight endeavor.

Balance is wonky so far. The first two-thirds of the In the Dark were a cakewalk for the heroes. The final third saw almost all of their conquest tokens dissolved, but more through my effective use of threat and a REALLY well timed Dark Charm than anything in the dungeon--the final boss monster was taken down very quickly and the heroes were one-shotting all of my other most powerful monsters.

I've been digging through the fan-made Cataclysm series with much more success, and I will eventually work up to building my own dungeons. I also have yet to try being a hero. Despite my quibbles, if every game went about like my first run of In the Dark, I would consider my money well spent. And with better vanilla dungeons and some of the fan work out there, things are only improving.

[Played 48 times]
The core rules (mostly taken from "Doom") are decent, but would have needed a better development and much more playtesting (e.g. costs of the cards, Golden Items, etc.).
The scenarios are not very engaging (unbalanced and lacking any sort of flavour).

Being used to the GW titles (HQ, AHQ and especially WHQ), it lacks more variety of enemies, a "campaign mode" and a "random dungeon generator" (you'll need to design your scenarios, investing time and hoping to make them well).
I also miss a "magic system" worthy of this name (magic is just a different kind of ranged attack; it's as if the only known spell is "Magic Missile"... and ANY character may cast it! Despite the name, they're fireweapons, not magic).
There is a lot of randomness, but also tactical choices.

It has a more "German" approach to the dungeon crawling genre than the GW titles (e.g. optimization, resource management, simple story arc, extremely abstract town, etc.).
It also lacks much of the "dungeon crawling" feeling: you're a commando trying to rush in, grab the goodies and kill the enemies before they can react and crush you; it doesn't feel like exploring, discovering, alternating battles and lulls, etc.

Long.

For a game that is supposed to last hours, this was less fiddly than I expected. Then again, I was the newbie running a hero, and I didn't have the burden of all the rule subtleties. What do I like? I like the cooperative aspect of working with other heroes. I like that heroes play differently. I like that line of sight matters, and the range/charge/damage dice are pretty cool.

Despite a large amount of initial skepticism, I have to acknowledge this is a well-produced adventure game. The adventures are great and the special powers are well done.

While not innovative, FF did a great job assimilating mechanisms from a bunch of different old Games Workshop games. The GW dice system saves a lot of charts and hassle once you get used to it. The thematically hokey runes or glyphs or whatever allow for mid-game powering up and prevent player elimination. Best of all is the wholesale porting over of the one-vs-many system from Fury of Dracula, in which the 'Overlord' moving the bad guys has his own challenges to face and resources to manage. All of these put Descent head and shoulders above most similar titles.

Alarmingly absent is any form of campaign system, which will be a huge sticking point with most players who are attracted to creating storylines or history and enriching the experience, and I predict some backlash beacause of this. Errata aside [yet again FF is guilty of a shameful lack of playtesting and pre-press editing], Descent is a worthwhile investment if you want to have one-night-stands of dungeoncrawling.

With the second edition of this on the way, I figured I'd write out my first review on BGG for one of my favorite games in my collection.

This game looks like a dungeon crawler but plays more like you're manipulating a swords-and-sworcery wielding SWAT team. Running and gunning without a plan will allow the overlord to swat down your group without breaking a sweat. Tactical movement - covering angles, staying close together, planning targets - is essential. Combat is dice-rolling, and with all the randomness that dice entail. The unpredictable element just forces you to play more strategically and throws a monkey wrench into your well-laid-out-plan quite often.

I love the asymmetrical nature of the gameplay. Playing as an adventurer turns the game into a tense race towards the end, as lingering anywhere too long will get you killed as surely as forging ahead too quickly. And in contrast, playing as the overlord is an experience not dissimilar from squashing ants with your thumb. Chipping away at the adventurers, timing your attacks and traps, is excellent fun. Most often, however, it comes down to a single strong attack and some unlucky rolls from the adventurers and it's game over. It's very similar to the Diablo series - the weak monsters will barely scratch you, while the stronger ones will punish you mercilessly, killing you multiple times.

With all the rules-mongering and strategic placement going on, however, the atmosphere of the game suffers somewhat. It feels odd to have traditionally stupid monsters act in perfect harmony to out-flank adventurers. Another problem is that in order for the overlord to win, he has to kill the adventurers - any of them - enough times to deplete their pool of tokens. What this leads to is the optimal strategy for overlord is to simply gun for the weakest character, over and over. Every monster, every trap, every spell will target the same adventurer, and every time that character is brought down the adventurers creep closer to game over. The game then becomes no fun for the adventurers. When the overlord isn't using such cheap tactics, however, and is evenly matched with the players, the balance is generally excellent.

The modular board, while adding plenty of replayability, is same-y enough that you feel like you're running through different variations of the same dungeon. Some more variation in the tiles would be nice - but I believe that the expansions fix this problem.

The length of the game can be somewhat overwhelming, and it is complex enough that you have to refer back to the rules often. I'd call it D&D-lite, but it's really not that much lighter in rules - the experience is just more streamlined. The pacing is good, however, and the constant escalation of both player and overlord abilities makes it so that there's plenty going on to sustain interest. Adventurers are constantly getting better and better loot, and the overlord stockpiles enough tokens to pull more and more dangerous tricks out of his/her hat.

It's such a monstrous game - it requires more table space and time than any other I own. But I've had some spectacular sessions of this game, and when everything clicks it's a great game of combat-heavy strategic dungeon crawling.

Aah, Descent. If only it didn't take so much time ... but then, if it didn't, it would miss half the chrome that makes it so splendid to look at. All these great monsters and dungeon tiles and floor tiles and tokens and counters and cards and bits and pieces and chits ... it's a great view to behold.

The gameplay is pretty good, too, although meanwhile I'm attracted to ... slightly less over-the-top chrome. The main disadvantage is that setup takes a long while, and then playing the game can take a long while as well due to both AP and the GM (well, OL) having to pick all the right monsters and cards and effect tokens when they're needed. Requires a well-organized game box.

The game does get better with more expansions, the main sad thing about these is that they're all meant to be playable with only the base game and one expansion ... consequently, there are precious few places (even with RtL and SoB) where monsters and pieces from all the expansions are needed together. In fact, bar the Quest Companion, I don't think I recall one official scenario with bits from all the expansions.

Which is a bit of a pity.

Anyway, if you're looking for a dungeon crawl and have plenty of time to spare, this is the game you want. Despite sometimes gaping imbalances (mostly fixed by the various FAQ though) and long playing time, Descent is a very awesome experience overall, with mechanics that exactly match the theme's requirements for furious and savage action.

If you want to bling up the game, I recommend the cardstock Battle System's Dungeon Set for the ruins terrain. It's not cheap, so buy it for your miniature games as well (yes, you can use the Descent mini's for other games, such as Song of Blades and Heroes). Archon and other miniature companies have various scatter terrain as well as crates and barrels you can use as Search tokens.

If you can pick it up at a low price at a flea market or trade, sure, go ahead!

Frustrating that there are minis included for characters, for monster groups, but not for bosses. Boss monster minis are sold separately.

I wish hero players could invest points into multiple professions. There's so much content in this game, it feels a little overwhelming that you can play the same class and have a near infinite character/skilltree combinations to pick from. For a player like me who enjoys exploring game systems, locking a character into one tree of skills for however many sessions it takes to beat a campaign feels overly restrictive.

I wore on this game as I wore myself out of 1 vs many games, and dungeon crawl games generally. When I do crawl, I've been more interested in playing fully co-op games with less dice luck. Part of the disconnect for Descent 2 in particular is that most games are more of a race to the end and less of a crawl. Often monsters just serve to delay and distract the heroes rather than being something to overcome. The balance of the game is also such that it's not uncommon for players to take down monsters before they get a single activation, which leads to situations that look like they should feel epic being very dull.

There are a wealth of expansions to increase the different heroes, archetypes, monsters, etc. This is the third generation of this system (Doom, Descent 1st ed, this) and the system grew again with Imperial Assault - in fact, a couple of the solo systems use a similar turn order as IA. At any rate, it is a lot of fun. FFG has done a great job in making Campaigns (though the original base set campaign is not very good, the others are good and the base set was replaced by Heirs of Blood in other editions - for those with the original, you can purchase the hardbound HoB campaign book.

I just finished playing a full campaign, my first dive into a dungeon crawler board game. I played the whole thing solo because, unfortunately, I don't have any friends willing to devote the time. And ya know, it was both frustrating and fun. I loved the overall theme and mechanics of the game, and doing battle was always an exciting experience. Watching my characters level up, acquiring new gear and skills, was as rewarding as it should be.

However the balance felt very off. The overlord seemed OP in the beginning and, being unreasonably on the side of the heroes, I got irritated at how often they lost. Some of the encounters seemed ridiculously rigged where the heroes had to get somewhere on the map before the overlord could complete an objective, but it seemed like there simply wasn't enough time to travel, loot, and attack so the overlord was just destined to win. HOWEVER, I didn't realize for the first few encounters that there's actually an addendum to the rules online that balances the game more in the heroes' favor if playing with only 2 heroes... which I was. Then later on, the heroes seemed OP and seemed to not even be challenged. This could have been because of my next point though.

Managing the game solo is near impossible. For me at least. There were so many things to take into account, actions that could be performed during attacks or other actions and movements, and I know I failed both the heroes and overlord on multiple occasions because I forgot about a card or item or spell. The game wasn't designed for solo play though so this isn't necessarily a criticism of the game, just a warning if you want to try to play solo.

Overall though, fantastic entry into the genre. The components are high quality, the variation in characters, items, spells, and so on is great. The tension between the overlord and the heroes is really cool and would undoubtedly be fun with more folks playing. Yeah, I'd totally recommend this game.

Rating lowered, as the many-against-overlord mechanic is finally starting to grate. When monster actions are 100% dictated by an omniscient player, monsters always perform the perfect move/attack for any given situation. Not fun.

The other problem is many monster abilities don't matter, since the single best power a monster can possess is the ability to block exits. Since all monsters have this ability, all monsters will always be annoying. In terms of game design, that's not a good thing.

So, introducing a degree of randomness into monster actions (cf. Gloomhaven) would have been a good idea. Though now I'm less inclined to purchase additional expansions, so all the better for me and my pocketbook.

This appears to be the second coming of a game that I wanted to play a lot of in my youth but I was never able to get to the table (HeroQuest). I have always been interested in this fantasy dungeon theme and spent countless hours in games like the Diablo series. While probably only playing HeroQuest once or twice as a kid, this was one of the first games that I saw when I was getting in to the hobby that I truly wanted to get. It also looked to be a step up from HeroQuest and was something that I could really get in to with a group in a campaign.

Well... I have only played it once (July 2013) and, while it was good to get that under my belt as I'm more familiar with the mechanics, it seems to be relegated to collect dust in my collection... the same way its predecessor had.

It is unfortunate because I feel that the game itself (at this point) is mechanically solid and is something that I would really enjoy. The problem is that, after being able to play it at all, it would benefit from people that like to role play a bit or get more vocal during the game (myself included). The introduction of Imperial Assault (a more favorable theme to many it seems) would appear to have put the final nail in the coffin for this game but, for some reason, I don't think that I'll be parting with it any time soon.

More streamlined and generally better than the first Descent. Cool miniatures. Actually playing the game is fun, but setup can take really long. You need a dungeon master who is well prepared and (optimally) sets up the game in advance.

I found out that I'm not a player who enjoys campaign style games. The reason being that you need to play the game with the same group of people. I played the game quite a few times with 3 players and managed to get a level 8 character. But every time you play with a different group of players, you have to start all over again. Especially when you have new players, you end up playing the same scenarios multiple times and I didn't find this exciting at all.

Another problem with the game I had was that while I generally really like when you're able to level up, I didn't really find the powers themselves that great. I never had the feeling that I want to buy them all but don't have enough experience points. Most of them are pretty mediocre so saving up was always an easy choice.

Lastly, I absolutely hate the 'X' on the blue die. The blue die doesn't deal that much damage to begin with and having a critical miss side that cancels out all your other dice is infuriating. This means 1/6 of all your rolls will be misses and this isn't fun to me. They could have made it a '0' side, which would have been bad as well but you could still make the roll if you got lucky. Alternatively, they could have used a critical hit side as a counterbalance. This would have made the game more random but possibly more exciting.

In conclusion, I think it ultimately comes down to having the same group to play with regularely so you can really enjoy the campaign and all of the expansions. Because I think when you can minimize setup through proper preparation and have a fun crowd it overshadows the other downsides of the game.

Did a lot of really good things compared to the first edition:

1. More efficient on space/components. Fewer heroes that have more customization with cards. Fewer monster types, but still covering all the bases. Fewer dice. Fits in a reasonable box.

2. Gender parity among heroes and less male-gazy art.

3. Simplified, better action-selection system.

4. The missions often had more interesting goals (on paper)

But they also removed everything that made the first fun:

1. They relegated gold and items to between missions instead of during a mission. No longer can you run to town in the middle of a fight to gamble for a crazy good new item. Maybe that's less realistic, but we're already in Terrinoth, and we're here to have fun.

2. The missions are smaller (and sometimes come in multiple parts). A single cohesive dungeon was more fun to delve into.

3. The Overlord has more fun cards, and the goal of depleting the conquest tokens often works better than the new mission objectives.

4. Having dead heroes respawn in town and have to come back is more fun than them just spending an action to stand up (or have a buddy give them a quick pep talk).

This is one game where I prefer the big, janky, rough mess of a game that had so much charm. The second edition had the fun streamlined out of it.

In the 1 vs many, the game feels much more like a tactical combat and race to objective game, where one player is the Overlord and the rest of the players a set of heroes. The game is played in a campaign format divided into quests. Each quest has a determined objective known by all players (all information is open and read at the beginning), and the first to finish it will win that quest. This makes the game much more tense (and fun!).

So far, we've played 2 incomplete campaigns of Descent 2nd, as well as the full co-op campaign. In general, I like it more than the 1st edition, but it has introduced new problems as much as it's fixed things.

So, the good: there's been a crapload of simplification. This has hit pretty much everywhere. Special skills and abilities are gone, replaced with a new class system. The whole separation between town & dungeon (teleporting between them) has been done away with. Threat and special spawning is gone, though the overlord's deck and its customization remains. The campaign's been trimmed down, so you no longer wander about freely on this huge map, but instead proceed along a branching storyline, hitting specific story missions and some side ones. The overlord similarly doesn't have to worry about sieging towns and moving his lieutenants, but just winning the missions he's fighting (and still upgrading his guys). I could go on, but they've streamlined so much.

There's new ideas, too! Your characters have a special ability and an archetype, and you then select a specific class from within that archetype. The class determines what kinds of things your guy will be doing. For instance: If you're a blue (support) type, you could be an alchemist tossing potions at people, or a bard buffing your team with passive songs, or a more traditional cleric-type healer. If you're a yellow (caster) type, you could become a necromancer and move your skeleton figure around attacking things, or you could be a geomancer who kind of does similarly but with summoned stones, or the more classic runemaster who just blasts things with magic. Of course, only so many of these classes are in the base game, so if you want more choices, you'll need to invest in the expansions.
Once you've picked your class, that sets up your base ability that you tend to build off of, as well as starting equipment. As you level up, you get exp, which you can spend to unlock more abilities (there are a couple each of 1-, 2-, and 3-cost skills). Some of them make your base skill stronger in some way, others give you new attacks and such.

The campaign is now built into the game, instead of being an expansion add-on, which is a big change.

Now the not-so-good. There are just a couple things from the old version that I miss. Being able to use the special orders was situational, but often very powerful. Now the ability to react during the enemy's turn (or even defend) is gone.

With the above changes has come one regarding hero deaths. Instead of respawning back in town, and the overlord being rewarded with points, your figure is KOed on the space it was occupying. You can take your entire next turn to stand back up, or an adjacent friend can take one action to revive you. This is all fine. However, when you stand back up, you roll 2 red dice and get back that much HP & stamina. This is usually around 5 HP (as low as 3 or as much as 6), and 1 stamina (if you're lucky). That's fine in the early game, but woefully inadequate later on. Instead of threat or points, the overlord gets to draw a card when he KOs someone. So, in later missions, if a weaker or weakened hero is ever even slightly exposed, they can get mobbed with enemies and killed in short order. Then, they're left with no option but to stand back up, get killed, stand back up, over and over. This is really not fun, nor is it good design.
Which leads me on to the next point about balance. Some of the hero classes I talked about above seem crappy, but are actually quite useful in practice (the bard, for instance). Others seem crappy because they are. There's a big difference in power between some of the class types.
As noted earlier, the overlord has deck specializations he can go into, and these have similar disparities. Traps seem pretty lackluster, while the weapon mastery (I forget what it's really called) has some crazy combos in it. For instance, you can put a couple of cards in your deck that add extra damage to your monsters' attack rolls. S, our overlord, quickly noticed that these return to your hand if you spend a surge during the attack, and there's another card that adds a surge to your attack.. So, after a few turns of drawing (the OL's deck is only 20 cards), he can begin spamming this card that gives every monster attack 2 extra dmg, and he'll never lose it unless he gets a series of spectacularly bad die rolls. 2 may not sound like much, but trust me, its hard to stay alive under that kind of assault.

Oh, and while I'm thinking about it, there's some really perverse incentives created by the monster spawning system. The old one had you running around trying to cover all the sight lines, while the new one has defined spawn points. But the old one also had a cost to respawn things, while the new one gives the OL one every turn, for free. So in a bizarre way, you don't always want to kill the monsters. If it's your last character's turn, you've just come into this new area and none of the monsters in it have died yet, plus everyone else has just spent time moving/healing or tried to attack but only wounded things, there's zero point in you trying to kill something. If you do, it'll just come back to life at the end of the round, at full health. If you can't wipe all of them out in one go, it might be better to wound/incapacitate and try it next turn. This is especially true if the monster group is one of the larger, tougher ones, and doubly so if you're killing off a red one. (Monster groups have 1 or more white basic type and a red one with better stats. The OL gets to bring back any one thing he wants, so he'll always choose the red one of the strongest group he's got.) I really feel like there should be some kind of cooldown on these things, like each individual figure has to sit out a turn before respawning, or a red one costs more to bring back than a white. Conversely, perhaps the OL should get some compensation if the heroes haven't killed anything and he's entitled to a respawn, but everything's still on the map.

They've completely messed with the way that missions work, and how they're balanced. In some ways this is an improvement, since you always have story-specific goals and it's not just a grind-fest of trying to get as many hero kills as possible while delaying their advance as long as possible. However, they've replaced the effective timer that was threat and monster spawning (the longer you took, the more you'd have to fight) with these artificial timers. I wouldn't mind as much, except every single mission has one. It's always "you have 3 turns to get across the bridge", or "you have to save this guy before he's eaten by zombies", or "you've got to make it to the treasure before the villain does". There's always some type of race, even if the timer isn't fixed and explicit. Worse, it's clear that some of these weren't very well-considered. Time and again, we've run into situations where the overlord can accomplish his goal easily, whether by playing a card that gets him an extra move or simply by virtue of the scenario design. Now, the heroes can move to block these efforts (in some cases), or exert themselves to try and win in a hurry, but they have to know what they're doing. Going into a scenario blind, with just the instructions from the manual, it's really tough to anticipate these twists and win.
Worse, some of them are completely luck-based. There are quite a number where you have to find a needle in a haystack, or at least the right token out of a facedown set of 6, or the right room of 3 possible places something might be hidden. If you get lucky and it's in the first place you look, you're set up to win, but if it's in the last place, you're pretty much screwed.
Other scenarios revolve around making attribute tests to do things, and if you've got the wrong mix of heroes or just get unlucky in your rolls, you can forget about winning.
Now, I will say that there are some of these that we've looked at and said "this is impossible", but it's turned out to be very close. So maybe there are times when my judgement of the balance is off. Or perhaps we just got lucky to make it that far. There have also been scenarios where we've felt the same way and it's turned out exactly as we predicted, an easy waltz to the win for the overlord with nothing we could do to stop it.
The final point I'll make is that most of the missions are designed in 2 parts. In the first, you're introduced to the adventure and make it into the area to confront the first challenge. Whichever side wins the first half doesn't get a real reward, instead they get a bonus or penalty when it comes to the 2nd half of the mission. The first halves may also be the most skewed, in my experience. So if you can't beat the odds in the 1st part, you'll be facing even steeper ones in the 2nd.

We have had successful, contested, interesting campaigns despite these issues. But we have also had at least one that turned into a downward spiral for the heroes. If the overlord wins, he's that much more likely to keep winning. And although both sides get Exp (&/or money) regardless of the outcome, the winner will get more, and be in a stronger position next time. So, I think if the OL plays to win and is cutthroat about it, and the heroes don't know the missions in advance, you can easily slip into that death funnel without realizing it.

I wanted one Dungeon-Crawler to explore the game style a bit more, so this was my pick. I had Gloomhaven earlier but the kids were too daunted by the complexity, so I sold it.

We are late to this one though with Descent 3 on the way, so this review may be a bit skewed by the fact that there isn't much point in buying any expansions for it at this point (June 2021).

For a dungeon-crawler, this is a decent choice. The app-assistance makes it possible for all players to be characters, not needing a dungeon master. Personally, I appreciate that the app is a few years old now but I do think it could have been done a bit better. The way the messaging works between master and minion units is a bit confusing and repetitive and it's not always totally clear what the monsters are going to do and how often and when (just my own opinion). The app does make the game go faster though, keeping the action higher, and less tedious to track things like gold. One part I'm confused about is how we track items that are found from search tokens, like helms, weapons etc... The app doesn't know that we have those items, and as such, we cannot trade/equip/sell them.

I'm painting the minis, and that has been fun. Sorastro (Youtube) has an excellent series to give you some good tips on painting the minis. With any game involving minis, I find that the game is much more enjoyable with the minis painted, but if you don't have a painting enthusiast in your home, it may detract a bit from the game.

Overall, our 12 year old daughter has fallen in love with the game and the adventures we have are one of her favourite things to do on a Sunday morning on the screened in porch. It's a great way to bond with her and the narrative is helping expand her vocabulary and reading, so that's a bonus. I will say though that some of the verbage in the narratives is a bit out there... LOL!

The combat system is decent, and seems stable with the exception of the confusion around the app (see above). I think we would get a lot more out of the game had we purchased it 3 years ago, but it was a great first step into dungeon-crawlers.

Descent 2nd Edition is a pretty awful and vastly over hyped reboot. It looks a bit prettier with nicer looking models, but in terms of substance its dumber and shallower, lacking all the charm and charisma of its predecessor.

It might be faster to play, set up and break down again, but its killed all the decision making, fun and depth in the process. I personally never had a problem with Descent 1st being too long. If I actually manage to get a gaming group together then there will usually be a several hour slot for playing a scenario or two anyway! In its defence, Descent 2nd sets up a scenario in about 5-15 minutes and usually plays in about 15-55 minutes.

Its biggest move is from straight dungeon crawling to scenario based missions. It should be more interesting but it actually makes 2nd more prone to balance problems then the original.

Scenarios are weighted very unevenly- some the heroes will have almost no chance to win, some the keeper. The scenarios often have a timed element limiting heroes choices. In the two campaigns I played through heroes learnt that rather then move and explore freely thry should ignore treasure and monsters and run through to the end of the dungeon as it would be the only way to make it in time. This is not fun (and is a trend that continued to be wrong in Imperial Assault).

It also suffers from the same Hero development overkill problem that 1st Edition does, where by the time the Heroes reach the end of the campaign they are SO strong they can one hit kill almost anything unless they miss. This is even made worse in this version due to huge sets of crazy skill combos making them virtually untouchable, game breaking gods!

As the Overlord they've also rubbed out the dynamic ability to deck build and spend/build threat, leaving you with few effective choices. After a point there is little to spend OL experience on, as only a handful of cards will have a use depending upon your opponents.

I feel overall that those looking for a rich and in depth Dungeon Crawler are best to stick with the original edition or look elsewhere- once Descent was all we had for board game dungeon crawling, although this is not the case anymore.

There was some elements from this version that I actually kind of liked (no special actions, more controlled spawning, no glyphs, recovery rolls). Think if they had just made some adjustments like this to Descent 1st but kept all the juicy complexity it would have been alright. I like throwing 6 dice and having to assign surges!

I play this game a lot with my (as of writing this) 6 year old son. We play a very modified version that does not use the overlord, the app for solo/full co-op, or the various automated Overlord/Monster AI variants out there. We play it with me controlling the monsters almost as a DM would in a game of D&D. We have a lot of fun with it, even if its not necessarily the way the game is intended to be played.

The game itself is a classic fantasy dungeon crawl with some decent minis and and some pretty nice artwork on both the cards and the map tiles. On your turn you will take two actions: Move, attack, interact with objects, etc. The combat in this game is surprisingly fun and pretty simple to grasp. attacker rolls their attack dice and the defender rolls their defense dice. The number of hearts rolled is how much damage is dealt, and the number of shields rolled is how much is defender. Subtract the number of shields from the number of hearts, and that's how much damage the defender takes. This is usually easy to work with numbers like 3 hearts and 1 shield or 5 hearts and 2 shields, so it never feels overly "Mathy" and certainly never needs any numbers to be written down to figure out how much damage is dealt. There are some more special things here and there with ranged combat and surge abilities, but it never is overly complicated and turn to turn the game plays pretty quickly.

Setup can be a bit of a slog, but only because there are so many map tiles. Compared to something like Gloomhaven, it setups up rather quickly. Every player gathers there character card, mini, item cards and any special tokens, you set out the condition cards and the health/stamina tokens, pick a quest, gather the map tiles and place the doors and search tokens, and your off! It is more involved than folding out a board and shuffling some cards, but the game experience is more than worth the setup time.

This game belongs on the shelf of every fantasy dungeon crawl fan.

A few plays in, seems like a decent system. I'm somewhat worried about scenario balance so far, though.

I think the game system is pretty good. At least, it inspires me to write custom quests. However, the quests that come in the box are too swingy. Masquerade Ball, for example, is either a cake-walk for the overlord (if they win the first encounter), or an early victory for the heroes (if the overlord has some bad rolls). This could be fixed with house-rules, but as written it's too luck-dependent.

Most of the quests are just a race, with the heroes and Overlord running to their respective win-conditions. There are rarely interesting decisions to make. Each turn is just move and attack, move and attack, with dice determining the outcome. The line-of-sight rules make tactical positioning near impossible.

The story is thin, and role-playing opportunities are sparse. Quests within an Act can be played in any order, so story-line continuity only happens between acts. I tried hard to find the fun in this, but the system fights against fun, seemingly at every opportunity.

NOTES:

* Hero death is insignificant; they spring back up on the next turn
* Monsters can be wiped out before the Overlord even gets to use them
* Quests are unbalanced - it always feels like one side had no chance to win
* Quests are usually a race between the Heroes and the Overlord
* The Overlord's quest goal is often unrelated to the heroes, so both sides tend to avoid each other
* Reinforcements are predictable (usually one per turn) and weak
* Overlord card effects feel weak and insignificant
* Overlord cards are difficult to remember (there are 15 cards in the deck)
* Quest information is public, encouraging players to game the system instead of role-play
* Monsters completely block hero movement
* Line of sight is convoluted
* Figures can miss an attack (1 in 6 chance), which is anticlimactic
* Movement around corners when a monster is present feels unfair
* Large monster movement ("shrinking") feels silly and unfair
* Fatigue-movement feels unfair
* Heroes choose the quest order, so there's no chance for a linear story progression
* There isn't much story to follow anyway - the flavor text for each quest is sparse
* Travel is unrewarding and nearly flavorless

What do you get when little tactics, entirely dependent on luck, merge with infinite respawning heroes, often unlimited enemies, no exploration, no loot, and a barely realized character development system? It's a remarkable testament to the designer's skill that from this horrible sludge of ingredients a functional game was even created.

Descent is a Dungeon Struggler game where players struggle to find a reason why they are not playing Gloomhaven, Shadow of Brimstone, Sword and Sorcery, Kingdom Death:Monster or the deeply superior Road to Legend app-fueled version of the game. The game starts with the overlord picking monsters with fat butts that can block doors, the only strategy he will ever need, and players deciding if they want to play a scenario designed for their victory or the overlord's (this may have improved in newer releases which no longer include the awful Shadow Rune campaign).

After this initial setup phase nothing interesting happens for a hour or two as each side tries to accomplish their objective in a war of accounting and attrition, where each immortal and indestructible side tries to slow down the other. At the end of the game one of the sides wins in something that didn't involve fun fantasy combat, if the players win they will get to buy new items, buy skills and determine where the next game will be set, if the overlord wings he will get a new card. Maybe.

As a owner of the game you do have some extra meta-game choices: as you will be forced to be the overlord forever, you may choose to exploit the fact that the game makes you overpowered at the beginning (and have the other players hate the game on the first night), or play dumb and let the players get away with mistakes, making them untouchable demigods and dropping the campaign at the 3rd or 4th game. The choice is yours.

I think my general problem with games like this is that they’re taking the least interesting part of a role-playing game (the combat system) and turning that into the entire game. Even just looking at combat, in a full role-playing game, the interesting thing is when players think outside of the box and do something unforseen to take advantage of the environment or use an ability in a novel way. You lose all of that in these stripped-down dungeon crawlers with some pasted on story at the beginning and end of each mission.

Mechanically, this game is ok. Each character we’ve played so far does feel different and you will do much better if you use each character’s strengths and play off of each others’ abilities. Some of the rules are very fiddly though and could be streamlined. There are some balance problems with some missions and some monsters being much easier/harder than others. It would be nice if there was some mechanism to balance a mission in-progress to make it closer throughout. Instead, most of the mechanisms serve to make the winners stronger.

This game shares a common problem with many co-op games. It can easily devolve into one of the hero players quarterbacking all of the hero turns. Over time, as the heroes level up, it can get harder to hold all of the info for every hero in one person’s head, but it’s certainly do-able.

規則:
*選擇任務，組建地圖，一個玩家當城主，其他當英雄，搜索卡洗勻放置，狀態卡疊起放一旁
*每個英雄玩家拿一個啟動卡跟英雄標記，選擇一個英雄那對應腳色版(至少兩英雄)，每人拿一個類別牌組對應其英雄類別，然後跟據此拿起始裝備跟技能，放置英雄模型在起始地點
*城主玩家跟據任務選擇怪物跟對應卡牌，然後跟據任務做起始設置，洗勻15張基本地主卡，抽等同英雄張數
*遊戲進行數輪，每輪先進行英雄階段，順位玩家自選，每個英雄行動階段全部結束換城主階段
*英雄行動階段
1.起始 結算效果卡，可啟動回合開始效果卡，並重置使用卡
2.裝備 可更換裝備，不使用的蓋著放，最多兩手加一個裝甲跟兩個其他，沒有標示的沒限制
3.行動 可執行兩個行動，且每個行動執行完才能換下一個，可選如下
>移動 獲得對應英雄的移動點數(可一次花掉兩的行動來獲得兩倍點數)，每移動相鄰一格花一點，特定地形會多花點數，不能通過模型或障礙物，可對角移動或通過友方模型，移動中間可做其他行動後再繼續移動，英雄可以透過獲得疲勞標記來增加一點移動點移動(不選擇移動行動也可以)，疲勞標記最多上限等於英雄耐力值，移動到出入口要一點
*進入水要花兩點，進入坑洞受到兩點傷害並停止移動，且只能做爬出行動(移動到相鄰格)，熔岩經過扣一血，停留就死亡，英雄標記是放在相鄰非熔岩格
>攻擊 使用裝備武器，近戰目標要相鄰，遠距要有視線，有五個步驟如下
A.宣告使用武器跟目標，收集對應骰，赤手攻擊丟一顆藍骰
B.雙方丟骰，多個被打則分別丟防禦骰
*骰面結果 愛心代表傷害或是補血，盾牌代表防禦點數，X代表失誤，有出現就不結算，數字代表距離
C.遠距攻擊則距離結果要夠，從相鄰格計算到目標格，可對角，骰結果加總數字要超過或等於，否則就算失誤
*視線從要算的格任意角落連到目標格任意角落，只要不要被障礙檔掉即可
D.攻擊方可花骰到的能量使用用來攻擊的卡上技能，英雄最多可花一閃電來移除一個疲勞標記
E.超過防禦的傷害放到敵人身上
*擴散攻擊會打到隊友，每個防禦玩家丟骰結算，但是攻擊只丟一次且距離只算主要目標，穿刺則無視對應點數的防禦點，可疊加，到達則是可對兩格內的做近戰攻擊，一樣要在視線內
*怪物沒血就移除，英雄被擊倒時，馬上放滿疲勞標記跟傷害標記，模型移除改放標記，棄掉狀態卡，城主抽一張卡，該格視為空格，且下輪只能有一個行動點，如果被捕血也會馬上站起
*帶有狀態的攻擊至少要造成一點才會有效果，英雄拿卡，怪物拿標記，每種狀態上限1
>使用技能 使用要橫置卡的技能，下方有疲勞花費的就要花
>休息 放置英雄標記在啟動卡上，回合結束要翻面時取回標記跟返還所有疲勞標記
>搜索 相鄰搜索標記的可執行，翻面該標記棄掉，不是特殊的就抽裝備卡頂牌，特殊的跟據任務拿
>站起 被擊倒的可執行，丟兩紅骰，回復顯示的愛心數血量，疲勞移除等同閃電數，模型放回標記處，啟動卡蓋著
>甦醒一個英雄 對相鄰被擊倒的英雄執行，同上
*遊戲中對角都視為相鄰
>開關門 開了放一旁，關了放回
>特殊 可能會橫置卡牌來行動或是拾取相鄰格目標標記，也可丟棄在相鄰格

It cleans up a lot of Descent 1st Edition, but in the process, loses a lot of the charm as well. This is a major problem that plagues most 2nd edition FFG games I've played. The 1st editions are often everything and the kitchen sink which can be fun, but needs to be fine tuned by the players. In a completely enclosed environment, it's fine, but with countless games coming out, that task is nearly impossible to create a game that you'll enjoy and isn't over-encumbered with cruft in the limited amount of time you have.

The 2nd edition games often go in the entirely different direction and overcorrect. They often feel too bland because of that. The tampering they did with this makes it feel too much like a tactical skirmish game instead of an RPG. It often feels like a race to grab the objective tokens while being constantly flooded with monsters.

There is also the persistent issue of having 1 vs. All in that the 1 can have a horrible time if the players are absolutely trashing the monsters and obstacles in their way. Same goes for the players if they feel overwhelmed and frustrated by the flood of monsters. These types of games balance a very fine line and often don't work because of that. Unfortunately that means 1 out of every 3 games is enjoyable/great and the others leave one side frustrated and unsatisfied.

Realistically, this only gets above a 5 with the Road to Legend expansion app. It completely abstracts the games DM out and makes it an enjoyable co-op instead. I've since sold it, but playing this on TTS has been fun, but is still a slog at times.

My group and I played a yearlong Descent v1 campaign using Road to Legend. I went from loving the game to loathing it. The big problem with Descent v1 was how the Overlord would activate all his guys at once and pick off one guy (often strolling by others; ta ta!) until he was knocked out. Then repeat. This was THE way for the OL to play every scenario as it worked. And the downtime waiting for him to maximize his 10+ dudes and cards was annoying. It felt imbalanced in terms of both power and fun. Throw in lots of rules ambiguities and the fun got sucked out, and we simply ended things prematurely because nobody was having fun.

Then SW:IA comes along and, as wary as I am, I'm convinced to try it -- and lo and behold, I find it fixes just about everything I hated about Descent. The one-at-a-time monster group activation vs all-at-once is brilliant so turns go much more quickly and things feel much more balanced (no more monster parade of suffering 12 attacks before your next turn). We meet monthly for a 1vMany campaign. So, when Descent v2 was announced, one of my friends picks up and we start playing a coop campaign using the app. I’m in love again!

But something is bothering me about these games. I leave my sessions fried after 4+ hours of parsing out permutations of movements and actions to find the best one because the result always comes down to the dice anyway. I don’t feel that the player agency is commensurate with the effort required. You can figure out the best order of moves all you want, but the dice will determine the story told.

Furthermore, the key to the game is not exploring a dungeon but racing to get to the next phase of the mission. You don’t clear a room and loot the chest, you just kill what’s in the way and keep moving. The app has a built-in timer that lets you know you’re not progressing as quickly as you should and penalizes you for going too slow (we always go too slowly). It’s antithetical to how I want the experience to be. I want a dungeon crawl where I get to immerse myself in a story, explore a dungeon, and kill a bunch of monsters, not race to reach objective points.

This is the streamlined version of descent 1st ed. On paper it makes a lot of improvement, reducing the gameyness and craziness of the first edition. The campaign system is also not virtually broken, like Road to Legend.

Despite all this, it is a disappointment. While individually the changes improve some of the feel of the game, they also drastically reduce the depth. The best part of the first edition of descent was the very challenging tactical conundrum present to both sides. How do you over come them? Was often an opaque and difficult question.

This edition, so far, feels much less difficult the Grok, the overlord has far less options and less decisions in the game. He lacks terrifying powers and difficult decisions that he used to have. The players are similar (and there are some cool features, like classes) to the old edition, but as the powers are more restrained, it is less about maximising gamey effects. While this improves the feel it reduces the depth.

On the upside the campaign appears to be a lot better and descent 2nd ed probably works in that regard, but it lacks the interest in the individual mission, so overall, fun, but a disappointment.

Though its predecessor was apparently a beast to play, Descent 2.0 has very intuitive rules once you get over all the small print in the rules booklet. It’s the ne plus ultra of dungeon crawlers: nice components, including great monster miniatures, a unique way of using dice, and a fun campaign system that has just enough complexity to make it interesting. One player plays the Dark Overlord, the rest individual warriors, mages, priests or rogues. I suggest watching a good “how to play” video first (e.g. like Rodney Smith’s), then looking up specific rules as needed. Other than the small print in the rules (a problem with a lot of Fantasy Flight games), my only real criticisms are (a) the uselessness of the cardboard insert, which prevents all the components fitting in the box (I cut it up and used the pieces to make two smaller boxes that fit everything in it nicely), and (b) the somewhat anti-thematic “no hero death” rule, which admittedly avoids player elimination. Instead of the fear of death motivating players, it’s time: each encounter makes the heroes act quickly before the Overlord achieves his objective.

I’ve grown tired of the dungeon crawls as they all feel the same: if you want to sweep a dungeon, just play an RPG, which is their home turf.

So, even Descent - which is still one of the older and better around, mainly thanks to its "one versus many" mechanism - scaled back in my rating: it’s solid and fun when played once on a while but it still has all the drawbacks any dungeon crawl has.

So much fun. Each person is a different class with different abilities; there is a campaign that consists of several quests; you can level up your character to gain new abilities; you can find treasure during missions; you can buy and sell equipment; each scenario has different objectives. Just great.

My rating is also based on the system as a whole, not just the base game. The base game is okay, but when you add some of the expansions you have a ton of variety in heroes, monsters, items, quests, and classes.

Road to Legend update: After many, many games of Descent, I have to say that the one-vs-all nature of the game is its biggest drawback. It tends to create frustration: either the overlord is getting crushed and has a table full of other players who are all celebrating his defeat, or the overlord gets the advantage and gleefully attacks the disgruntled players.

Road to Legend turning the game into a pure co-op is brilliant. It works great and is very similar to Mansions of Madness 2.0, where the app just tells you how to set everything up and it keeps up with a few things, but it doesn't get in the way or take over the game.

The app keeping up with heroes' gold and xp is takes away all of the bookkeeping that you had to do previously. The town section is great because it gives you some real choices between quests now: take time to refresh the shop to hope for better items, go on some sidequests, or do special activities to gain more gold or xp.

My only complaint with the app is that sometimes things aren't very clear. If you put out a unique monster, the app will still act as though you have put out both master and minion versions of the monster. This initially created quite a bit of confusion. Also some of the directions aren't completely clear. In one mission each hero's specific gear was spread around the map. If you find someone else's gear then they immediately equip it even if they're not nearby. It seems like the intent was for each player to recover their own gear, but the app didn't say so.

Overall I'm loving the game with the Road to Legend app. The app itself is mostly great, and the game is even better as a pure co-op.

If you have played Gloomhaven and are dying for an expansion, this game may be for you. This is not a hack and slash dungeon crawler adventure. It tries to be a euro engine builder.

The designers reached beyond their limits in an atempt to create the ultimate tactical, puzzle, RPG, townbuilding game. They felt the need to add more but often for little value.

For instance, instead of picking up coins, you pick up raw materials like metal and wood to "craft" items. But you can just craft any item, sell it, then buy materials to craft what you want. So it is a meaningless process that bloats a simple system of just looting universal currency. Additionally, you use 90% of your materials just to upgrade the town, which can only be done once per session, so ultimately you don't care what you pick up as loot because it will go in the communal supply.

Similarly, missions are now not just kill all enemies, but they are loads of convoluted rules that dictate how you are going to play. In gloomhaven the objective was the same in name, kill all enemies. But you were free to devise your own strategies for how to do it. Do you tank, kite them with high and low initiative, etc. That was the fun of the game.

At its heart, the card based hand managment is built around a hack and slash dungeon crawler backbone. Cards are about attacking, tanking, controlling enemies, and healing. So when a mission says ignor all those things and do x, all your level ups and items can be entriely useless. For a unique mission to break the mold once in a while could be a breath of fresh air. But when every mission is so full of specific rules and objectives that it essentially tells you how to play your hand for you, I feel the joy sucked away.

I fear the designers lost track of what made Gloomhaven great and went down tangents that in many instances dirrectly interfere with the strong suits of the base structural system.

This game is okay, and I would play it if invited, but I don't see myself ever replaying the campaign, unlike gloomhaven.

Compared to Gloomhaven:

Pros:
- More Complex Characters. Fantastic design, tough to play, very enjoyable.
- More Complex Scenarios. A shocker at first, but after a while I started to really, really appreciate the added complexity.

Cons:
- Pennycounting. I'm sorry but no, managing 10 resources in this game is a total chore. We spent hours discussing imaginary redisigns to make the system better, and quite frankly, the most enjoyable ones were the ones that simply shafted it.
- Riddles. We really did give them a shot. We did. Nope, straight to the solutions now. Nothing to enjoy here.
- Terrible use of the Campaign system. Complex Characters + Complex Missions + Big Outpost phase means you will max at one scenario per session. Add a not so strong story that is broken into different weak narratives, and even if you play once per week you will pretty soon forget why you are fighting and stop caring. The narrative should have been organized into many JotL size chunks for such complexity to work.

Pros & Cons:
- Various new system ideas, tied to the buildings. I loved some, mehed others, and thought some didn't really work. I wish I could publicly say which ones I thought were better, but it has to be hidden behind spoilers which is another bad design choice. Frosthaven is a bag of experimentation for the system, in many ways, I just hope the correct feedback reaches the developer.

Not Improved (and dissapointingly so):
- Immersion. The setting is still generic meh high fantasy. It's so high, you cannot be surprised by anything happening on it - I wouldn't blink even if alliens invaded at this point with all its sillyness. The story is so disconnected from the gameplay, you just don't care. No matter what you do, Frosthaven is gonna grow, your mercs are gonna retire, and boring things will keep happening - It's just an excuse to play a different scenario. And the storytelling is also disjointed, by the time you reach a mission you really don't remember what led you there. Even the payed audio app didn't help much, I found the performances very annoying and almost impossible to understand most of the time due to ridiculous accents combined with loud background noise.
I'm grumping a bit here, perhaps it really didn't help that the previous campaign game we played was Oathsworn: Into the Deepwood - which was a fantastic experience, immersion wise.

Overall it’s 2 steps up, 4 steps down from the original. Let’s hope the future of the series is more inspired.

Frosthaven, the sequel to Gloomhaven, delivers much of the same engaging gameplay, now expanded with deeper city development and crafting systems. It’s a solid and ambitious follow-up—but it doesn’t quite capture the groundbreaking magic of the original.

Scenarios tend to take noticeably more time to play, not just because of their internal complexity, but also due to the expanded city phase that wraps around them. The city phase, with its frequent attacks, upkeep, and administrative steps, often feels more like a tedious chore than a rewarding mechanic. While thematically fitting, it can slow the overall pacing and bog down momentum between scenarios.

The gold and resource economy feels much tighter—or slower—than in Gloomhaven. Saving gold for personal purchases is genuinely difficult, as most resources are immediately funneled into fixing the city or meeting retirement goals. This may be a deliberate design choice, but in practice it can feel restrictive, making many items and enchantments seem largely out of reach for much of the campaign.

The scenarios themselves—and especially the new characters—are on average more complex, often layering in additional rules. For some players, this added depth will be a welcome challenge. For others, it may feel like the game demands one too many mental gymnastics sessions per turn.

Unfortunately, the story and backstory remain muddled. Much like in Gloomhaven, it’s often unclear what is really happening in the larger narrative or what should be prioritized next. This is likely a side effect of the semi–open world structure and emphasis on exploration, but it undercuts the sense of an epic, cohesive storyline. Given how central narrative progression is meant to be, it’s disappointing to see that this aspect still isn’t fully realized.

Still, if you’re a fan of Gloomhaven and ready for a heavier, more systems-driven experience, Frosthaven offers plenty to chew on—even if it sometimes asks for more patience than its predecessor.

5 is frankly a generous rating for this. As someone who played through all of Gloomhaven and Forgotten Circles and greatly enjoyed them, I am playing Frosthaven basically out of sunk-cost and massive social inertia. Under no circumstances would I ever recommend it to any other person or group.

I cannot believe Cephalofair put all that money, labor-hours, and effort into producing this onerous, groaning, time-wasting update to the formula. It's like they thought the core fun of the game was spending hours on bookkeeping, moving decks around between organizer slots, and resolving pointless phase and event after pointless phase and event. The entire outpost phase is a bust, but it isn't just a bust, it's an enormously time-consuming bust. The entire outpost attack system is a bust, but it isn't just a bust, it's a bust with a dozen subsystems feeding into it that you manage and progress through for genuinely no reason with genuinely no risk or reward.

When you combine that with the color palette of the game, you have to conclude that design and development was done sadistically, as a prank on the players. Every map component is just ice-colored. When setting up a scenario, you find several ice-colored map tiles from among the other ice-colored map tiles, and populate them with important and mechanically distinct overlay tiles which are also just all ice-colored. It's absolutely insane that this enormous box full of environmental art is just all one color and one tone and virtually indistinguishable.

In the last scenario we did, I set up an ice-colored initial room, with genuinely indistinguishable ice-colored obstacles, ice-colored difficult terrain, and ice-colored... ice. The difference between these was the key mechanic of the scenario. They are almost identical and on an identical background. Almost all the components are that same color. The only reason you can tell they're different in the set-up booklet is that they give them different (colorful!) borders to denote their mechanics -- borders which the physical components don't have. We had to replace them with improvised materials just to be able to do the scenario at all. They're shipping these fifty-pound boxes around, and we're storing them in our houses, and all the components are identical! What is the goddamned point of this wardrobe's worth of identical cardboard that we're supposed to pretend look different!

Then we skipped the outpost phase, so we'll have to do it at the beginning of the next scenario. Everything has to happen in a specific order with consequential timing and resource input/output, so we can't resolve the easy stuff, do some of it async, etc. We just have overdue paperwork. Oh, you want to think about buying some of the thousand items in stacks? Well, it technically has to happen specifically in the middle of the outpost phase, not the beginning or end. So, we'll all chill out for an hour while you figure out the specific resources you have and items that are available exactly right now, and then we can move forward with the next stage of our paperwork. We can't even fudge it because we need to know the resources you've spent for the next phase. Oh, you're leveling up right now? Well, you have to finish that before we can move on to the next paperwork stage, so you better do that right now. No, you can't participate in our figuring out how we're going to spend our common resources which also specifically affect you and your build, because we have to do both in this phase and so it'd take twice as long if we wait for you to level up. And you better not even think about both leveling up and purchasing items. It's already 12:30 AM.

It is just such a complete downgrade to Gloomhaven. And they talked so much about the development experience online. They bragged about how much work and effort and testing went into it. I remember one of the specific points was that they made sure player characters rarely ever see level 9, to make it more special. Oh yeah, you wouldn't want the players of your three-year game to ever get a payoff. After all, you guys did plenty of level 9 content in pick-up playtesting. Seems boring after that, I bet. No, better to pace it such that my six-month journey to collect fourteen tally marks on my character sheet is just all setup, and then I start right over.

Speaking of which, Frosthaven is tightly designed around everyone racing to retire their characters as quickly as possible, and never overstaying. That feels natural and obvious to me -- I want to retire characters, unlock more stuff, meta-progress, etc. However, that's not how everyone wants to play the game. Frosthaven discussion forums are absolutely filled with groups complaining that they're practically soft-locked and the game systems don't work, because people in their group like their characters -- which is also natural. Gloomhaven supported these personal playstyles. Frosthaven does not: You have to bully all your players to always be retiring. One of our players wanted to malinger on a character. It would have broken our game. We had to insist that he not. In Gloomhaven it would have been fine, he could have fun his own way.

If someone came to me saying they finished Jaws of the Lion and Gloomhaven and Forgotten Circles, and were absolutely craving more, needed more -- I would tell them to get Crimson Scales, the standalone fan expansion. No one should play this game. No one should even have to store this game.

What if the issue with Gloomhaven was that it wasn't big or complicated enough? It sounds ridiculous to think (and it is), but Frosthaven reaches into uncharted waters of potential by daring to dream bigger and more ambitiously than ever before. If Jaws of the Lion improved on base Gloomhaven by ruthlessly streamlining the clunkier parts out of the game and reducing it to just the hits, Frosthaven is counterintuitively attempting to do the exact opposite. Somehow, it works. Mostly. This game is a monster. Brilliant in mechanics (it's still the Gloomhaven system), with more interesting character classes and more branching paths and scenarios, it also just has so, so much overhead. A summer/winter cycle, an upgradable town, crafting mechanics, road and town events, assaults on Frosthaven, the list of new mechanics stretches out to the distant horizon. I personally have trouble remembering how the game works if I can't get it onto the table frequently, which hampers it in my opinion. I think I would absolutely love this game if I could play it every week, but alas my friends don't live close enough to make that happen. As it is, I still like the game a great deal, and plan on playing it as often as I can.

Aug 2023: Gloomhaven But More! More classes, more items, more missions -- my group played through Gloomhaven and was very excited to get more.

One odd thing I'm noticing is that every scenario has a Gimmick; not just that layouts and monster placement are unique or challenging, but that the scenario has a special rule that is a Gimmick. We don't just go down a hole and clean out all the skelemen -- there's a spawner or slow poison or we have to play cards upside-down or something.

For our group it also seems that literally every mission is balanced to take the maximum amount of effort. We win, but we win with one turn or less of cards remaining. That's fun once in a while...but not EVERY single time.

Dec 2025: The missions continued that way for two more years and we got sick of it. We're house-ruling our way to the end of the "plot" as fast as we can. Frosthaven made some decisions about narrative and game balance that are very much not what our group wanted.

Was finally able to give this game a try on 6 DEC 2025. Four player game, and this was the first time 3 of us played. As we had all played Gloomhaven previously, the learning curve was pretty flat.

Talk about a box full of goodies! 30+ lbs of cards, counters and map boards!

It is similar (combat) yet different from it's predecessor. Some of the icons have changed, but after a few turns, it becomes fairly straight forward.

It's no longer gold/coins you loot, but it could be other resources you can use in town. The idea to craft/build up the Town is very a very interesting game within the game.

The characters were similar, yet different. I had the opportunity to try the Drifter, who has quite a few persistent cards and the ability to move the token backwards, so you can tailor your approach to the scenario/mission at hand.

All in all, an interesting game, but I would recommend players learn with Gloomhaven first.

The tactical combat with all the monsters and different abilities remain fantastic, but to me, this game is just a little too ambitious for its own good, which is why I think Gloomhaven is better.
The outpost phase has just too much going on: events, possibly (annoying and tedious) attacks, going through all the buildings and their boni, unlocking all kinds of extra stuff that add rules, options and things you are prone to eventually forget. Crafting is nice in theory, but when you get to the more complex items, it's painful and tedious to find out what exactly is needed to get the item.
Worst of all is the puzzle book, which not only has some badly thought out puzzles, but is inexplicably required to eventually progress in the game. And for one of the puzzles, you need to build a certain building early in the campaign; if you don't (like me and my wife), you will be stuck for quite a while through no fault of your own. In order to solve all these puzzles, you have to take notes extensively - or re-read dozens of text snippets you eventually gained in the campaign. Making this thing mandatory to finish the campaign is just awful.

Regarding the actual gameplay, many scenarios have lots of extra rules, making gameplay slower and more tedious. Also, the number of scenarios that don't work as well with just 2 players seems to have increased since Gloomhaven. Some characters are also so specialized that they don't work well in all scenarios. The complexity balance is also weird, why are there two starting classes that are considered to be in the highest complexity tier?

It's still a lot of fun, but if there is a third big -haven game, I'd prefer scaling it back a little to the likeness of the original Gloomhaven.

Taylor's 100 point rating:

Enjoyment - 20/20 - This has been one of the most fun, if not thee most fun, game I've ever played. I love combat, the scenarios, the world and everything there is to unlock. I enjoy playing this game solo, or with friends and I love unlocked new classes and new content so frequently.

Replayability - 14/15 - Although this is a campaign game, there are so many scenarios and game nights to be played in a single campaign, and there are now lots of tools to help track and play multiple campaigns. The only reason this didn't get a 15 is because you do need to use external resources to restart a campaign.

Game Mechanics - 15/15 - Frosthaven took the mechanics I already knew and loved from Gloomhaven and took it to the next level. I love building and upgrading the town of Frosthaven, I love the way combat works with the dual card system, and I love how unique each class is.

Theme/Artwork - 15/15 - The theme and story telling in Frosthaven is amazing. It truly feels like you’ve been immersed in this fridged wasteland with monsters and enemies. I love all of the art work and this is one of the most thematic games I’ve ever played.

Gameflow/Pace - 9/10 - I wanted to give this metric a 10, but I couldn’t without feeling like a fan boy. The flow and pacing isn’t perfect, and there are a few times when you’re waiting on a friend, or listening to a part of the story that doesn’t interest you, but these moments are few and far between.

Flexibility - 7/10 - The reason this doesn’t get a 10, is because I wish I could play with more than 4 players and I dislike being required to run 2 characters in single player. The game is great from 1-4 players and has pros and cons at every player count, but that’s to be expected.

Production - 5/5 - This is the production gold standard. There are so many pieces to this game, and they’re all fantastic. Great quality, the minis have fantastic detail. I love everything about this game.

Effort To Play - 2/5 - People might be screaming I didn’t give this a 0, much less that I gave it a 2, but the reason for that is 2-fold. 1. The tools and apps that are available make this game much more manageable and requires much less setup. 2. This game has been really easy for me to setup before my party gets here which allows us to play 2 scenarios in a single night.

Accessibility - 4/5 - Again, people might want my head for how easy it is to get into this game, but my main reasoning is that I can carry the bulk of knowledge. I need to know a lot in order to play this game, but I love learning about nitty gritty rules, I just need to teach my friends how combat works and then the rest falls into place as it happens.

Total Score: 91/100

- The outpost-phase is too much of a hassle without any real benefit.
- Story arcs are locked behind outpost-events. So you have to wait and can't play through a storyline and have to start too many different stories, that aren't that interesting.
- 250€ and only 8 elite standees is a joke, especially when there is a scenario early on that starts with 9 elites (4P) and spawns elites every round and the game tells you to look for a substitue for these standees.
- crafting items was interesting at first until you unlock items that require other items and just list numbers as materials and you have to look through the whole pile of items to see what item you need.
- retiring your character feels unrewarding compared to gloomhaven. In gloomhaven you looked forward to a new character and imagined what mechanics fit the icon and anticapeted playing the new character. In frosthaven you get to open a numbered enveloped and unlock boring stuff for the outpost-phase.
- many characters require a setup turn to play ideal, so every turn 1 looks the same.
- scenarios are more complex and take longer and enemies are stronger so the game becomes more diffucult. Which in my opinion is less fun.
- summons were buffed and still (mostly) useless.
- everything on the map is blue/grey. There is very little diversity compared to gloomhaven.
- starting characters are very interesting and feel well balanced.
- I like the way how loot works in this game. But you could've just share your gold in gloomhaven instead of following a stupid rule that's no fun, but that's just my opinion.
* update after ~25 scenarios: too many characters use terraintiles and feel way underpowered.
- multiple print errors in the scenario book.
- some scenarios feel too diffuclt or borderline impossible with certain characters.

This game is a textbook example of how to not make a sequel

Details: The best parts are from gloomhaven, and everything that has been added on top is a bloated mess that adds hours to running the game.
The tiles not being books shows no learning from all the glowing reviews from jaws of the lion and listening to a vocal minority who say they will design scenarios and require unlimited freedom of map tiles to do that… maybe, but multiple map books would also allow for that,
The loot bloated into a loot deck, more shuffling, no more interesting (plus: I killed a sun demon, it dropped a pelt on the ground… pretty unthematic).
The puzzle book with puzzles that… aren’t interesting. I’d rather play the puzzle of the combat than a side project that doesn’t belong in this game.
The hundreds of standees but no organiser for them. The hundreds of terrain pieces but depending on the scenario will be different terrain, so instead of having a reminder on the token, you have to look back at the scenario book to see what kind of terrain it is - how did this make it through to final product?!
More status effects but they aren’t more meaningful and old overpowered effects are still there - looking at you stun - I could go on… but then this would become bloated too… you get the picture. More for the sake of more, with little or no thought as to why.
It’s just so bloated, and why not? Gloomhaven was as well (although not so much as frost) - it’s just that there are now alternative campaign games that are refined, have less set up, and the same level of satisfying coop dungeon crawling gameplay. Because other designers looked at gloomhaven and thought they could do it cleaner and more streamlined, and that would be the inovation as well as lead to more fun/less work. Personally I agree with this.
overall, This game feels like 2 steps forward, one step back. What a wasted opportunity to iterate in meaningful ways.
The main positive I have is that the game was clearly play tested more, so more of the classes are fun and engaging, but there were plenty of good classes in gloomhaven, so you could skip the less interesting ones.
Don’t get me wrong, I still have a good time playing this half of the time, but I’m rolling my eyes at the ridiculous bloat the rest. Thank god for the free community made app making this easier to play (the fact that the official one is paid for is laughable, compared with smaller budget campaign games who make free companion apps).

Comments: Frosthaven is a thematic strategy game about cooperation, card driven actions, variable players powers, scenarios, campaign, hand management and deck building. The ideia is that players will use their characters cards to move, fight, loot, and many other effects, exclusive for the class of said characters. Each scenario has its own win condition and maybe some extra losing conditions; and all scenarios are connected in an overarching campaign. In this campaign, heroes can and likely will retire, and the player is able to use different ones. Furthermore, players can develop the town of Frosthaven, have events there and in the road, plus by items, craft items, and more. Frosthaven has a lot going on.

There are two things people coming from Gloomhaven will notice right away: first is the new design of cards, in which icons where chosen instead of text - only more complex cards have text in them. It was a real struggle to get used to them, at least the game gives you 1 billion scenarios for them to become a second nature. The second thing is how power down basically everything on the heroes side were: rare are the instances of Disarm and Stun; Invisibility no longer serves to block; most items were basically cut in half (+1 movement instead of +2; Advantage for a single attack, not a full attack action, etc). Most summons are quite weak still, but at least most are also not a lost card.

Two of my main issues still remain: the loot being individual (at least you can spend part of these to improved Frosthaven, if you want); which makes little thematic sense to me. The second being that is simply way, way too long to finish a campaign. There was no need to do that in Gloomhaven, but at least one could learn (and Childres sort of did), and instead of making another 80-100 scenarios campaign, would be much better (for me) to have four 20 scenarios campaign - considering 20 scenarios is already more than most scenario-driven games have. But, but... what about the evolution and retirement? Well, again, most games manage to have the evolution with less scenarios, and retirement could remain alongside gaining new options once a campaign is finished (for instance, people you helped in the 1st campaing, can now move into Frosthaven and become an adventurer there as well).

Frosthaven did introduced paths of stories: which could be considered as mini-campaigns insided the larger one. But they don't really work this way, as most of them you can do from start to finish - you enter into mandatory stops for a number of weeks (inside game time; which happen for story-driven reasons), before being able to return. Which is fine and dandy if you play solo or in two, leaving the game on the table, playing most nights. But for a group like ours, which is 4p, meeting once a week, to play a single scenario, that weeks in game stop is a full-on weeks on real time stop, that leads to us forgetting what that whole thread was all about: we have an outline ideia of what was going on, but we then tend to miss a lot on the theme involved, making the campaign, while not lacking in the written story, lacking in cohesion and sense; which, in turn, makes us care less and less - a not ideal situation in a thematic game.

The hefty time cost of playing a full campaign demands too much. Sure, people who play solo and are dedicated to a single game, maybe won't mind using months in a single game. But my group, as mentioned, plays a single time a week. Since we have always the same folks, we opt to concentrate in campaign games - which are too hard (even with the plebe amount of around 9-15 scenarios) to play with occasional groups. For us, a campaign of Frosthaven will take us nearly 2 years to finish! Smaller-ish campaigns would allow for more natural stop points (as we still want to try other games, and not create a queue with a 2 years waiting period) without hurting a bigger story - the current way of having several story threads going don't help in this matter.

Contrary to my expectations, I found it slightly worse than Gloomhaven. Still a great game, don’t get me wrong, but at times managing it felt exhausting.
I’m probably in the minority who didn’t find Gloomhaven’s scenarios that repetitive. Sure, the goal was more often than not to kill everything, but, to me, the variety of monsters, environments, and classes made them all feel engaging.
Frosthaven tried to fix this "flaw" by diversifying the various scenarios, but that increased rules complexity and play time, sometimes by a lot, and I can't really say I prefer this solution.
The new town phase only made things worse by adding unnecessary complexity and dragging out the playtime of a single session far too much.
Combined, these two new "features" worsened the overall experience, and I hope the next installment opts for a more streamlined approach. From what I heard, Gloomhaven 2e seems like a good compromise between the "barebone" structure of the original game and the overcomplicated version of Frosthaven.
I liked most classes and they all felt unique; the plot is still somewhat generic, but the setting is cool and it's not like I'm playing a boardgame expecting a narrative masterpiece; the books that replace the tiles should be included in these games by default, as I can’t imagine having to set everything up on top of the playtime issues discussed above; I didn't like how the puzzle book was implemented.
Still have lots of sidequests to complete - having so much to do after the main quest sure is nice.
