I played through Gloomhaven twice (yes, I bought two copies and played through them with different groups). I was so excited for Frosthaven, but after a few sessions I was EXHAUSTED. There’s so much more setup and tear down, and Frosthaven does this “outpost phase” in between scenarios where you go to town and deal with a bunch of bs and more setup/teardown. It’s so much to track. Then, doing scenarios feels like even more of a chore because you have to bounce around the scenario books like a “choose your own adventure”, spending 20-30min digging through and trying to figure out what is linked with what. At one point, I got so lost and nobody in my group could figure out what was linked with a certain scenario in the book because it was missing a reference link, so the scenario just ended with no context. Also, the scenarios themselves are much more complex with MUCH more to track (I remember one in particular being an elevator mission where map tiles were inaccessible, deadly, or changed advantage/disadvantage based on the round you were in). Did not make any sense for a board game to do that. The game practically requires a DM, or someone who is willing to spend all the time explaining what to do and taking the hour to set everything up (and then the extra hour to take everything down).

Overall, FH as a board game is not good and is not worth all the effort. I’m sure it’ll be great in a digital format but jesus, it is an absolute mess in physical form.

Before i start, if you are looking at this review wandering which *haven to buy as you haven't played any, stop reading anything else and buy Jaws of the Lion. It's the one you want.

Frosthaven is what everyone that played and finished a campaign of Gloomhaven wanted, but not in the way they wanted it. Context: My group has played and finished absolutely everything Gloomhaven. We're talking games, expansions, fan campaigns and semiofficial scenarios, as well as full fan campaigns. We have poured 3000-4000 hours into this game system. So, that said, what about Frosthaven which we've mostly completed throughout?

Frosthaven has a huge amount of fluff on top of a structure that didn't need it, crafting that requires flow charts to understand, a base building system which works narratively but ends up being very uninteresting gameplay wise and adds extra logistics on top of a 3-4h dungeon session. Classes that are more complex and dense to play but that feel much too hard to play well, for the same benefits you'd get playing a classic Gloomhaven class moderately well.

I've been struggling to find enjoyment in some classes and you need to play them for about 12-16 scenarios to complete the personal scenarios... about 30-60 hours. Some feel very complicated for no real upside, others just don't feel good to play, if you played the original Gloomhaven, the triangle class is the closest to the experience of Frosthaven.

The town phase has promise, but if you're even moderately successful you'll never see any of the supposed narrative story engine happening. There generally won't be any highs and lows in fighting off baddies in the Winter season or any rush to prepare the town in the safe Summer season. The various shops and places seem somewhat random as to when they appear given how they're unlocked and we've felt we've wanted some much earlier than we got them doled out. In the end, all this does is tack on 30 minutes to a game that didn't need it.

The scenario system having a chart mode is really useful but also it misses the point of WHY anyone wanted to 'chart' the scenarios in Gloomhaven to begin with... you'll go into a scenario, if you play even 3-4 times a month, you can have NO clue what it's about, as the last time you've done the chain was four months ago. The flowchart doesn't adress that problem of needing a 'previously on'. The game allows you to go very wide in a quite sandboxy way, and you can get lost in a ton of misc scenarios and chains and chains which are LOCKED behind just.. playing other scenarios/waiting for them to tick down. The game still fails to provide a consistent narrative experience as much or harder than even Gloomhaven did. There's argueably one main 'act 1' and one 'act 2' main quest chain, which each have exclusionary 'choice' scenarios, and one very long chain that takes you all across the game, and that's sort of it. There are of course some other smaller 2-3 quest chains but it all feels somehow less but also more. There are enough scenarios, just that they kind of fail to provide some of the really organic narrative developments that Gloomhaven could do.

Scenarios themselves now seem to each have half a page of 'special rules' you need to read for them. Very few end up with a simple 'kill all the dudes' or 'loot the thing' or 'push two levers'. Each scenario has you relearning new mechanics, which often are described quite mechanically, and we'd be trying to figure out what the designer was intending to happen in the mission to be able to interpret how the rules would work. There's floating driftwood used as barges, sometimes working one way, othertimes another way, there's various pillars doing various effects in various ways or moving around the map or having special mechanics, monsters spawning in in different configurations at different spots on the map on odd or even or both types of rounds and some don't spawn past a round while others spawn indefinitely... it all felt very tiresome by the half game mark. Opening a scenario and seeing a big purple text block was just frustrating when maybe we just wanted to focus on the tactical challenge instead of figuring out how to play tiles that are elevator levels going up or down as you climb up a shaft.

Frosthaven is Gloomhaven turned to 12, not to 11, just overcharging it and making everything run stronger, but 12, going past overcharging right into blowing out the engine. It may be the right amount for some people, but i feel for some it might leave them entirely behind and cold.

I don't regret my time with Frosthaven, i just wish that now that we've 'gone big' we'll teeter back to a more condensed and focused experience with whatever's new. I really consider Jaws of the Lion struck a perfect balance of a moderate but heavy experience and not overstaying its welcome, as well as a better narrative by having the players be guided more thoroughly. Gloomhaven could also get long in the teeth and had its own batch of issues (fixed in 2nd edition mostly). But i wouldn't recommend Frosthaven to anyone else but people that have gone HARD and played all of the Gloomhaven games already.

(Scroll down for two later-gameplay edits to this review that dropped it from an 8 down to a 5 for us; hopefully it doesn’t go lower before we make it to the end.)

We’re on year two of playing this. For the most part, we're still enjoying it. For the majority of the combat mechanics, character cards (enhancement), and the like, it improves on most of the things we struggled with in Gloomhaven—notable exception: Oozes, which still ruin scenarios on a regular basis—but a few of the changes left us scratching our heads.

The biggest wins are in the characters, who feel a bit more balanced than Gloomhaven, and their thematics. We originally enjoyed how unlocking characters is story-based, not retirement based (with the retirement bonus turning to buildings for the Outpost)—but that lost its charm a year or so into playing when we still hadn’t unlocked half the new characters.

The setting feels more "alive," and having a stake in our own settlement helped grounding us more than in Gloomhaven. The loot system of using a deck, and crafting, has us more invested in picking up loot than before, as well—looting is way better than just coins.

Alas, crafting started off weak and slow and it might be our character choices, and potions were even worse. It’s the equivalent of RNG, but our journey through unlocking potions (which is entirely random based on the ingredients you manage to loot) was absolutely painful. It took forever for us to end up with a healing potion (and we were unlocking whatever we could, just never had the right combos).

The encounter cards split into season and road/outpost make for a more immersive experience, and while we've only bumped into a couple of scenarios where we've hit a wall (again, Oozes are still broken, and we're houseruling them twice over: waiting for both their shuffle cards to come up before shuffling them, and just copying damage on new spawned split oozes). We’ve also started playing on "Easy" which still feels difficult depending on our quartet of characters (the "closest character gets pummelled by massive number of attacks on round one" problem).

On the downside, the iconography on the cards is sometimes less intuitive (push and pull, for example), and multiple tiles are so close to each other it's frustrating looking for the right ones (cave "door"?). The time-per-session is was raised by the extra steps of the Outpost phase, which isn't inherently bad, exactly, but does sort of put a tedium tone to things after finishing a scenario, so we decided to skip it one session and then began playing with the Outpost Session as our starting point, and then playing a Scenario and stopping once we’ve finished the scenario (so, basically, we "finish" the previous scenario before we start a new one, then leave the Outpost Phase to be handled again next time).

One really sore point is—as we're playing with four players—the incomprehensible limit of two of each craftable item, especially the potions, which meant only two of the four of us can have any type of item. We're making them with ingredients we find ourselves. How can we only make two of each? It makes zero sense (and yes, I get the real-world reason: it would mean more cards) but I’d rather have had less options but enough cards to actually equip four players.

Added to this is the frustration of playing a new character after retirement with the slower scale of levelling via Prosperity—when our first character retired, the other three characters were level four, but even at Prosperity 3, my retired character meant I'm had to play a level one character, who routinely got one-hit-knocked out/required discards due to low hit points. Gloomhaven allowed characters to start at a level equal to or lower than the Prosperity level, but Frosthaven slows that down to half the Prosperity (rounded up) which meant starting at level 2 didn't happen until Prosperity 4… which was a long time coming.

Finally, "masteries" are obnoxious. If you've got a player who loves the challenge of trying to earn their masteries, prepare to have a frustrating experience of their character making very sub-optimal choices while they try to earn that extra checkmark doing things that make little-to-no sense. It's like an extra-frustrating Battle Goal, only far more tedious to watch unfold.

Edit to add: Bumping this down from 8 to 7 to 6. Having now played through the game for two years in real world, and entering year three of the game (we just started our third Summer), our four-player group has hit consensus that the "problem" of Frosthaven is mostly in how much more complicated everything feels on a scenario basis—far less "Defeat all enemies" (which wasn’t a broken situation) and quite a few more "here are the scenario goals" (which feels like fixing something that wasn’t broken).

It's by no means as bad as Forgotten Circles was, but—for example—Scenario 71 where there are *seven* enemy types, three of which use one battle deck while fighting the other four as well as the players, during an escourt mission, with summons happening on odd and even rounds and... Each round of combat took ages to figure out. If we hadn't had one of the unlocked classes with a particularly good one-two combination of cards to grant movements to allies, it would have taken at least another hour to play, we estimate, and could easily have ended for naught in a failure. Basically, when we see "Complexity Three" rank for a scenario, we find ourselves groaning in anticipation of much less fun, and a lot more "okay, wait, what happens this round?"

Further Edit to add: We’re on our third year of playing this, and we’re at the point now where we’re skipping it as many weeks as we’re playing it, because we have to be very much in the mood for the frustration that comes with so many of the scenarios, and add to that the puzzle book and… honestly? If it weren’t for people online, our entire group would have just given up. The puzzle book is *awful*, and it gatekeeps the story from concluding. Paths are locked until you use the puzzle book. Don’t like badly designed (and error-inclusive) puzzles? Then you’re done with Frosthaven unless you go seek out spoilers online. Worse, and especially if you—like us—generally only play, say, a scenario a week or every other week or so, these puzzles become even more unsolveable. As a not-so-random example, the clue you need for the solutions to one of the puzzles is in the concluding text of a scenario we played *two years ago*. Why would we remember that? The puzzle book alone has tanked this experience for us—its inclusion might be great for people who like escape room style puzzles, but if you don’t and were enjoying Gloomhaven and Jaws of the Lion, surprise! Frosthaven includes impenetrable puzzles now.

Frosthaven – A Long-Distance Group Review (Spoiler Warning!)

After five years since we wrapped up Gloomhaven, our group, now scattered across the globe, reconnected through Tabletop Simulator to tackle Frosthaven. Over the course of 74 sessions, we experienced all the highs and lows this massive game had to offer. Here are my personal thoughts, shaped by both nostalgia and hundreds of hours of gameplay.

We played entirely online using the excellent Frosthaven Workshop Mod, and while this definitely changed how we experienced the game, it also made it possible—something I'm incredibly thankful for.

⭐ What We Loved
+ Character Mechanics:
The new character classes felt distinct and fresh, with minimal overlap with the original Gloomhaven cast. It was a blessing that none of them relied on annoying obstacle manipulation gimmicks.

+ Loot Deck Mechanic:
Huge upgrade! No more just grabbing coins—each loot token was a surprise. Blueprints, items, resources... even if many items turned out to be mediocre, the loot deck brought variety and occasional excitement. The ability to manipulate the deck via upgrades or special scenarios was a great touch.

+ Rule Changes (Summons & Rolling):
The quality-of-life improvements here were spot on. Summons are much more balanced and usable. We’d happily adopt these rules in any future Gloomhaven-style game.

+ Road & Outpost Events:
Massive variety. Even after 74 sessions, we hadn't seen half the events. That’s amazing for replayability and made our campaign feel truly unique. Very few events repeated, and many led to side quests or unique unlocks.

+ Settlement Building & Upgrades:
Upgrading Frosthaven gave us a real sense of progression. Even when some upgrades were just resource sinks, they still felt meaningful. Planning our build path was fun and added a meta-strategy layer to the game.

+ Reworked Character Sheets:
Progression was far more personalized. No more cookie-cutter builds—each sheet encouraged different playstyles.

+ Challenges:
Fun and creative scenario tweaks. While the final reward was underwhelming, the path to completing them added extra flavor and variety to our sessions.

? What Didn’t Work For Us
– Puzzle Book:
Overengineered and frustrating. We enjoy puzzles, but this felt more like homework than fun. Having to remember obscure flavor text across multiple sessions, especially with a rotating player base, made it worse. Most puzzles weren’t intuitive or engaging enough to justify the effort. Optional side content? Great. But forcing it into the main progression? Not ideal.

– Trials (Especially With Errata):
Due to misreading the rules (and the errata not helping), we did these incorrectly, which soured the experience. Even correctly done, we didn’t enjoy them. Rewards were weak and the scenarios just didn’t feel worth the time. It might be more bearable in person, but we doubt it.

– Underused Mechanics:
Town guard upgrades were almost irrelevant in our playthrough. Most defense events were phased out due to story progression by the time our guards were maxed out.

– Pets:
Cool idea, poor execution. We caught pets but never used them except in the final boss battle—mostly for thematic reasons. They didn’t provide meaningful impact. We'd prefer them as part of crafting recipes rather than single-use items.

– Character Retirement Balance:
The swing here is huge. Some life goals were fulfilled in 2 scenarios, others took 25. While retirement often felt natural, the inconsistency caused frustration and sometimes delayed the fun of exploring new classes.

– Weak Item Design (Especially Two-Handed):
Most two-handers felt underwhelming. Many items in general seemed to exist just for specific builds or RP flavor. The core vendor/craftsman unlocks were usually sufficient to complete the game.

– Character Balance:
Some characters like Blinkblade, Trapper, and Drifter felt overtuned—almost to the point of spoiling the fun. Others, like Lurker and Bannerspear, were a chore to play in our group composition. They weren’t necessarily weak, just... not fun.

– A Few Scenario Difficulty Spikes:
The game is mostly well-balanced, but we hit two scenarios that felt off—too punishing for the level they were tuned for. It made us question the playtesting at times.

– Resource Micromanagement:
Managing resources started out engaging but turned into busywork in the late game. Hoarding materials became more about stockpiling gold, and it lost its strategic charm.

? Final Thoughts
Yes, we had frustrations. Some parts felt like chores, and a few systems didn’t land. But across ~300 hours, there were countless “skin of our teeth” victories, laughs, and tense moments. For a group not too invested in the story but deeply into cooperative tactics, Frosthaven delivered.

We didn’t feel the urge to replay failed scenarios—time zones and adult life made it hard enough to meet regularly. That likely impacted our experience, but we accepted it.

In the end, despite the flaws, we still rate Frosthaven 10/10. Why?

Because it gave us a way to connect, cooperate, and conquer across continents. And for that, we're deeply grateful.

We probably won't replay it on physical board anytime soon, but when the digital version drops, we’ll definitely take another look.

Thank you Lennart and Chambers

A better game mechanically, but If you're bored of gloomhaven this won't change your mind. Gloomhaven was ultimately broken once you got the hang of it, but the fun, like literally any rpg ever made, was in learning how to break it. Frosthaven has so thoroughly filed off all the exploitable edges that there's few exploits left to discover for yourself. This game feels like a job now.
It's the same problem rpg video games and even dnd now have, where they've been ruined by the Internet spilling their secrets. Instead of employing the man spamming class guides on the subreddit, they should have gagged him.

There's still conceptual darling classes like the geminate that are wildly OP once you realize the gimmick is not actually any kind of restriction.

Needs more wacky map effects, you should be building a rube Goldberg machine of scenario hazards and slippery ice and spike traps. The new balance seems to discourage you from cheesing the map layout, which is the most fun to be had in this combat system. Every other enemy seems to be flying now. In terms of visual clarity the map tiles are a huge step down from gloomhaven, what is ice/snow/bluestone is impossible to tell. What is hazardous/trap/difficult is extremely unclear and even the meaning of any piece of cardboard constantly changes between scenarios.

New chaff based loot mechanics remove the last bit of dopamine. Oh boy, a wooden plank for christmas.

Frosthaven is a behemoth of a game, in terms of physical size, game length, and complexity. But it's a good behemoth, like a friendly giant. You'll easily find yourself hooked (assuming that you like RPG dungeon crawlers) and coming back for more.

Frosthaven as a sequel continues the fun mechanics found in the original (Gloomhaven) and the prequel (Jaws of the Lion). The character progression is fun, the gameplay diversity is intriguing, and the combat is tight. Just when you start to get bored of your character, you're given the option to try another class. And the legacy-style unlockables add to the gameplay loop, since you're always striving to unlock that next milestone.

Frosthaven also has new mechanics. The "town" part is a mini game to itself, with you and your crew building up the titular outpost Frosthaven. It starts off minimal, but you soon grow attached building it up, as your combat prowess directly contributes to your restoration progress as you collect materials from monster loot. Althought this section can be tedious initially, it becomes very quick once you internalize the rules (or have a side table where you can leave it out always).

The story is quite good, focusing on Frosthaven's relationships with three different tribe species. Each has their own mini-story that you need to work through as a branch of the main campaign. There are plenty of side missions as well, some of them being one-offs and the others being a short 2-3 mission adventure.

Although the steep price ($250 USD MSRP) and the large size of the box may put some people off, I think this is a must-buy for anyone who's already tried Jaws of the Lion and liked it. It took my group over 2 years to finish a single campaign. The price to time value offsets any qualms I had with the original price tag.

I'm not finished with the campaign yet, but am far enough in (50 scenarios?) that I feel alright reviewing it.

If you like Gloomhaven, this offers that experience but deeper. More complex characters, interesting mechanics. It fixes some of the overpowered mechanics from Gloomhaven, creating a more balanced experience. Overall, I've had a lot of fun playing with my game group, and there have been many memorable moments. I enjoy the effort put into the story/event cards. The story still becomes hard to follow as you branch out into so many narratives, but it's much better than it was in Gloomhaven.

My main negatives are:
- At 4 players the games go a little too long. I used to be able to comfortably fit a 4-player game of Gloomhaven into a weeknight evening. But with Frosthaven's town setup phase + more complex scenario rules it becomes difficult, let alone if a character retires and someone has to make all the choices associated with a new character during the town phase. This has led to me doing some upkeep between sessions and trying to streamline our sessions. But it's still too long.

- You need at least one person who enjoys reading/consulting rules. I think Frosthaven has enough forgiveness for getting occasional rules wrong, and maybe more than that - but if you want to play correctly there are many rules to know, and edge cases come up fairly frequently for which I often consult online FAQs.

- [Spoiler?] The puzzle book... We are a group that enjoys puzzles, but the puzzles from the puzzle book are often just not good (too difficult/obscure/not following patterns they've established/requiring remembering information from a quest you did a long time ago; other times they are so easy that you overlook a stupid-feeling solution). Add onto that that these puzzles need to be solved to progress the game at certain points, and this is definitely a negative. It makes me wonder how they were playtested since there are so many examples of games (escape room games such as Exit, Unlock, etc) that do this well.

Overall though, I've found ways to manage the annoying parts of the game and the rest has provided so many hours of enjoyment!

Makes some significant changes to the base Gloomhaven system. The characters require a bit more time to figure out, as they have a learning curve, but many of them are REALLY satisfying (beartrap surprised me with its awesomeness).

I also like that you build up the fort of Frosthaven and that there are cards you reconcile; there’s a story there that builds up as you pick out the way the outpost grows. Relatedly, I like the new treasure system, too. (I admit I don’t see the point of the “Mastery” abilities unless on a replay you want to go the whole series as the same character.)

But, that said, what made me stop playing was just how constantly fiddly every scenario was. It was exhausting. I mean, they solved the “Forgotten Circles” issue of hiding the tiles from you at the start so you have to stop constantly and find them as you enter a new room, but there is constant upkeep and double-checking every single round of how and when new monsters come, who and what they attack, and how the rooms move around or checking the round number again and what effect that has, all while trying to figure out how to defeat the creatures you need to to complete the goal. It just felt like I was too busy running the map and the monsters than I was choosing my own strategy and cards.

Frosthaven meaningfully improves on many of the lackluster aspects of the original. The decent insert already pulls some weight (we still store map tiles and standees in other boxes).

The big areas of improvement are basically everything *not* to do with playing the scenarios themselves. The town system that replaces prosperity and Gloomhaven's stores is engaging, and ups the stakes for events. Events themselves are much more fun, and the new calendar means you've always got something to look forward to.

Events were also improved by the introduction of character traits; when faced with a choice in an event you can look to your character traits for an informed guess.

I'd say the new characters are more gimmicky in general. There's really interesting and cool new designs, but some of them go into a real lateral-thinking space. I can't really tell whether they are more complex to play/develop a build for than their Gloomhaven counterparts.

Some items were rebalanced -- in particular stamina potions. The breadth of new potions is fun. There's a bunch of new perks, including - if I'm not mistaken - triple tic mark perks.

Despite all these changes the core of GH doesn't change: it's still a table hog. You're still better off getting apps to track the campaign and monsters. Games still take hours. You will still bicker over misplays, loot and objectives.

It's still that tense, puzzle-y dungeon-crawler and campaign game that we all love.

Frosthaven is the sequel to Gloomhaven, and follows the formula very closely, where if you played and enjoyed one, you'll enjoy the other. Aside from some minor tweaked rules, it's basically just a giant, massive expansion.

There is a lot going on here. I won't touch heavily on the gameplay in-mission as it's basically identical to anything found in Gloomhaven. But they've done a better job avoiding spoilers due to how they broke up the book into 2. Most missions seem well balanced, as do the characters. But this game needs a Pro's and Con's list, so here goes.

PRO's

- Tight gameplay using the tested and true 2 card top and bottom action system
- Strong Character progression - levelling and perks through personal goals.
- Each character is unique, and unlocking a new character is the most exciting part of the game as it changes the gameplay drastically.
- Everything else not listed below

Con's
- The loot system - specifically the craftable loot. It's so difficult to reverse engineer what you need for crafting, it's often not worth the chase. While many of the loot pieces do offer interesting boons, often times they are far too situational to actually be used more than a simple starting card that has no fine print on it.
- The story - This is more of a neutral. I'm not quite done the story yet, but it's not that it's bad. It's well written etc. But there is just SO much going on, with branching paths, and choices to make. The choices are interesting, but so often we are looking at available missions, and we can't remember how we unlocked it, or any of the backstory to it, unless we just did the previous mission. Aside from making it more linear and thus less interesting, I don't know how they could have fixed this, so it is what it is.
- The PUZZLE BOOK. This is the worst tool/system/mechanic I've seen in any game to date. We were unable to solve any of them without hints (though we haven't completed it all yet, and probably could have got the 1st and 2nd one if we felt like spending the time). And even with full on answers for some, there is still no link as to how someone gets from A to B on any of the puzzles. If you've done a poorly done escape room before, it's like that, but 100x worse. Even with step by step instructions on HOW to do the puzzle, there is no connection. Just HORRIBLE.
- This game absolutely needs to be played with an app. I couldn't imagine anyone playing without, and how much of a slog it would be flipping and shuffling and ordering the cards and initiative each round. Honestly, they shouldn't even make the components, and just force you to use an app (ideally tablet sized as a phone is difficult to read)

Overall, though this game is excellent, and stands up as one of the best dungeon crawlers there is. If you liked Gloomhaven, this is more of that. If you didn't, you won't like this, as not much has changed. Personally it's my favorite series of dungeon crawlers as I love the tight mechanics and the character variance. Is it perfect? No. But you can bypass the bad parts enough to have a truly amazing experience.

EDIT: I had to come on (twice) and dock a 1 point from my review thanks to the puzzle book. I had written about how bad it is above. But it's just so much worse than that! We have finished the 3 main quest lines, and done many many side quests. Upon searching if we were done or not, we find out that you have to nearly complete the puzzle book to finish the main story... After looking up hints to solve the next puzzle, we know we need AT LEAST 10 more missions just to solve this ONE puzzle (of which there is again, no indication why the puzzle would have anything to do with the objectives we need to accomplish). And realistically, it would take many more than 10 missions due to the tiny tiny tiny chance of each mission actually furthing the "objective".

I don't know how anyone in development could possibly think this was a good decision. Honestly, it is the single worst mechanic I've seen in any board game. And sadly has soured my opinion of the game. Anyone reading this should just print the answers and automatically solve the puzzle once they reach the milestones needed. Thankfully someone has posted them online for this exact reason. Just brutal. BUT, the rest of the game is still excellent.

I waited until my 5th play to give my thoughts because I felt like this game needed it (I usually do this after my first play). Overall I am loving the game. It is basically just Gloomhaven 2.0, pretty much better in every way. If you like Gloomhaven you will obviously like this one, but if you didn't I don't think the changes are enough to sway you. I appreciate the improved story, added depth and extra components and mini games. I wasn't sure how I would like the city building phase after the first couple of games but we are starting to build up our town and it is awesome.

I like the potion system where you can combine ingredients to make stuff. The first time you make it it is a surprise but after you know what the recipe makes you can come back to the ones you like. The crafting system is also very cool, more ways to get gear than just coins.

The insert for the game is doing a decent job but I just purchased a dedicated insert and I think that will help a lot with getting the game to the table. I also pre-ordered the map tile books from the latest Kickstarter, they work like Jaws of the Lion, and I think that will be the single best improvement to the game over Gloomhaven. I am counting down the days until that comes!

Overall I am enjoying Frosthaven even more than Gloomhaven so far, both games are great but this is just one step above and feels like a more polished game. I do with the game were easier to play, every scenario is roughly 15-20 minutes of setup, 3 hours of gameplay and then another half hour of the town phase, rewards and loot etc... Then you have another 15 minutes to put the game away. It is quite a feat to play the game, and we are playing at a friends house which means I have to lug the 35 pound game over and set it up there. I think this would be way better to play in your own home and setup before people arrived but this is what we are stuck with. Looking forward to seeing all that the game has to offer.

Frosthaven is harder, more complicated, and has more stuff, but it's more tedious to play. Lots of issues with poor quality components, poorly explained rules, mistakes and errata, scenarios that feel designed for digital and play poorly with physical components, etc. It's a good game when it works, but it's not a great game. I had fun with it, a LOT of fun at times. I also had a lot of discussions, arguments, and frustrations with the unclear rules. Some of the classes are game-breakingly broken too, and had to be house ruled out of play as they are too tedious or too powerful. One or two of the classes felt like they fundamentally didn't work as a concept.

I loved the idea of the outpost phase, but I don't think it quite worked. Sticking things to the board is fun, seeing the outpost develop is great, but the payoff isn't - we were swimming in resources and rarely ever had an interesting decision to make, just more and more upkeep to deal with each scenario.

There's elements of greatness here, but all those elements are already in Gloomhaven. If I was to play either again, I'd be strongly pushing for Gloomhaven.

Probably the most disappointing experience of my adult life. We loved Gloomhaven so were really looking forward to this. Unfortunately the many flaws mean it has overall not been a fun experience.

The biggest issues are
1. The story is extremely poorly written to the point it essentially doesn't exist. The actual writing content is bad, like a 12 year old wrote it, the pacing is appalling. We find out about the big bad 3 scenarios from the end, which isn't even really an end. It doesn't have an ending.
2. It is designed for 4 players and is not well balanced if you have 2 players. Several scenarios we had to replay over on a lower level but could clearly tell with 4 players it would have been trivial, either because monster spawn hit points or movement didn't scale correctly with character count.
3. Special rules. I get it, kill all monsters got a bit dull in gloomhaven. But special rules for the sake of it often became like managing a small accounting firm.
4. Randomisation of events doesn't work well. We didn't have the first town guard upgrade until 3 scenarios from finishing and didn't have the trial deck until the last scenario. What's the point in having functions that you don't get to use unless replaying scenarios?

Frosthaven feels worse than Gloomhaven in almost every way.

The loot system was changed to add a lot more complexity and busy work setting up the loot deck for every scenario. Just have to sort and shuffle essentially ~5 decks every scenario.

The new town phase is a lot of busy work with more mediocre writing. Lots of steps and rules involved. This phase would have been a bit better if it were more streamlined to be quicker.

The overall writing/story is not good. Worse than Gloomhaven. Super generic groan inducing writing. When a choice is given, the better / more rewarding choice seems to be to always do the action that is more 'nice'. Promote peace an harmony among those who hate each other.

The strive for class balance has greatly increased, which kind of makes everyone feel just weak. A great thing about Gloomhaven was how you could find strategies or combinations of actions that made you feel rather OP if pulled off right. Now in Frosthaven, you feel like no matter how hard you try, there is not much you can do. Maybe this changes for a few of the locked classes I haven't seen yet.

Almost every scenario has Special Rules. No longer is it just about having fun playing the normal way. Scenarios now have to have some weird gimmick to limit how you play or hinder your actions. This ties back into the bad writing of the story in that the mechanics reinforce the idea that 'you must be this specific kind of person' (Scenario 55). And they don't even reward you for following in the exact spirit of the scenario. Instead you are essentially penalized. A lot of the fun has just been sucked out of playing.

I'm not sure how well the scenarios are really balanced as I've always played 2 player. Between the overbalanced classes, and maybe underbalanced gimmicky scenarios, the game feels quite a bit harder overall.

Speaking of rules, the overall set of basic rules have just been expanded upon to add a lot more complication.

The cardboard overlay tiles also have a lot more specific meanings/uses based on scenario, so you constantly have to keep checking and remembering what the tile means for the specific scenario you are running. They should have worked better to include more unique overlay tiles that are more visually distinct so it is easier to set up each scenario and easily know at a glance the meaning of each.

The first printing also has a lot of errors that make things confusing. There is a giant Errata you can go through and mark up lots of cards to make corrections. They should have provided free replacements of all the incorrect / missing content.

TLDR: Gloomhaven but with a lot more rules, busy work, worse writing, and less fun classes. Would be better as a video game.

It builds on a very strong foundation, being a direct successor to Gloomhaven. However, it is not as good as it's predecessor for a couple of reasons.

a) The characters you can play are less straightforward, requiring much more expertise. Hence, this game is clearly meant for (and marketed to) people that have played at least a full campaign of Gloomhaven and can't get enough. While the variation is still in there, the complexity rating of handling the characters shoots up as well, while the enjoyment of actually effecting the game remains the same. Luckily, it comes from a high base so playing those characters is still a joy even though a bit more fiddly.
b) There is a whole set of added game rules attached to it, allowing you to build your own town. While the idea is refreshing, it really doesn't add much to the game other than a whole lot of complexity.
c) Because of the outpost phase, playtime goes up as well, making it a little harder to fit into a single evening of play.
d) There is a crafting mechanism by which you loot stuff to create items. This however, is unbalanced as either some characters that are more suited for looting end up with everything, dooming the full party if they all wish to use that for themselves and their own items instead of the townbuilding part, or you have a group loot arrangement by which the whole crafting thing becomes a thing of periodically browsing to the item deck asking 'have we unlocked this already?' and negotiating an extra item for your character. Much less straightforward as just getting rewarded and looting coin and being able to shop. Again, added complexity which really doesn't add much.
e) The kickstarter was exceptionally lousy ran, where in update #92 (!) you HAD to react or get your game downgraded. No refunds, no explicit mailings urging you to make a choice, no nothing. This is so bad that this almost ruined the complete experience for me by itself.

Other than that, it still enjoys the same highlights of the excellent Gloomhaven: the slow unlock of the full game experience, the intricate cardplays and varied skirmish mode that follows from it. Sadly, even though it's a successor, it still suffers from that one minor flaw Gloomhaven has: too many missions where the objective is 'kill all'. They really missed an opportunity there.

As such, I feel this doesn't improve on its very, very good predecessor. It adds a lot of complexity and gains almost nothing compared to Gloomhaven other than perhaps potion crafting. Because of that, it's merely OK. Will never play this with beginners, only with experienced Gloomhaven players that really can't get enough and for such a group, it's fine. Other than that, you better get Gloomhaven from the shelf again or play something else.

Finally, for the way they ran their Kickstarter, will avoid any future Cephalofair KS campaigns like the plague. This is not included in the game rating but it is a warning should you feel inclined to pledge in any future campaign in the Gloom-/Frosthaven Universe.

Having owned it for over a year now (original KS backer), painted the miniatures, and played a whopping 45+ scenarios by myself and with several friends, I can safely say this is the crown jewel of big box board game fantasy roleplaying.

The scenarios are challenging and varied. The writing is top notch and the foreteller app brings a level of performance quality that has yet to be matched by other big box RPGs. The characters are all unique and continue the excellent class variety from Gloomhaven. Every class unlocked is a mouthwatering reward that will radically transform your play style and party synergy. While it is slightly more difficult than Gloomhaven, it's easy enough to adjust. While some may bristle at the expanded downtime phase of the Outpost that is new to Frosthaven, I love it. The loot system is much richer than the simple coins of GH, and you really can see your party transform the landscape of your Outpost as you play. It adds yet another layer to FH's rich narrative experience, with buildings expanding, stories unfolding, and time passing with a marked variety and interest that the downtime of GH simply lacked.

If you're a lover of fantasy or long form board game RPGs, you'll struggle to find something more deep, rewarding, and gorgeously produced. Just make sure to lift with your knees…

I want to love Frosthaven more that I do, and I struggle to know what I don't. Jaws of the Lion was great because we stuck with one charter throughout. They got stronger. The levels got harder. We became powerful and really grew to enjoy the charter and to learn their style of play. This led us to Gloomhaven, with even more charters to discover, from the straightforward, to the complex, but they all felt unique and fun.

Frosthaven seeks to build upon this, and in many points it succeeds, but in other instances it does not draw me in as much.

The town phase takes FOREVER. You do events, work buildings, buy buildings, put on new stickers, unlock new items. All of this is cool, but it is SOOO time consuming, Everything is costly and I feel like I am grinding through this constantly.

Because there are 175 scenarios and an endless supply of items, the game kind of stretches out how long it takes you to get to the really good stuff. Grinding out incremental wins for access to new items that are not game-changers or exciting feels a bit disappointing.

Positives
+ The narrative feels so much more coherent. With the layout of color-coded story lines, you know where you are and where the story is headed.
+ The story gets put on hold, with a calendar date, encouraging you to go explore other storylines and to experience other parts of the game.
+ New characters get unlocked fairly early, which give new options of play. Exciting to discover new characters in unexpected way.
+ Loot is varied and can be used for different things.
+Unlocking buildings and options reveals the game piece by piece. There is unity in paying for town things where everyone should be more likely to share their loot.

Negatives
- Upgrading characters takes longer and upgrading prosperity takes longer.
- Characters do not feel as powerful or as fun when compared to my favorite characters from Gloomhaven.
- Color pallet of overlay tokens are all blue, grey, and more grey. Hard to distinguish.
- Some scenarios have way too much enemy character management.
- Some scenarios feel way too long without necessarily being complex.
- Game does not feel as hard or as fun as previous iterations.
- Scenario setup is a bear. This includes tiles, loot deck, overlay tiles, etc, etc.

I think my son and I will continue to revisit the campaign and maybe discover characters that are more to our liking.

Played quite a number of scenarios and while the game is definitely fun, it does not seem to reach the fun we had with the original Gloomhaven.
What has improved over Gloomhaven:
- Summons: Summons are usually cards that are discarded after they get killed, not lost like in Gloomhaven. That makes the summons much better.

What's kind of annoying:
So the game is still strong but here's a list of things that bothered me or my group:
- The game does not seem playtested too well for four players. The characters rely more on summons, creating hazardous terrain or traps than in Gloomhaven, but usually there's hardly any room to place that stuff without severely annoying the other characters. While monsters and spawns are adapted to the player number, smaller corridors are not. So you have more characters more summons, more tiles and sometimes even more monster on the same map space.
- Low-level character design:
Banner Spears was nice from level 1 on, the Lurker was no fun until it was Level 4. You basically stand around and watch how the working characters win the scenario. Trapper is boring on the first two levels. It gets better from Level 3 on. In Gloomhaven, Brute seemed to be the only character which I didn't enjoy and I played 6 or 7 characters. But in Gloomhaven most of the characters started at a higher level due to the prosperity level ruling, which was changed in Frosthaven. I like the idea that characters start at lower levels, but not if they are just boring.
- Character design in general: The character design is different. Many characters are designed in a way that they have additional downtime. Beside the short or long rest, you regularly need rounds to buff yourself before rejoining the battle. This is often reduced at higher levels. That's a nice idea for a character, but several characters work that way in Frosthaven.
- Scenario design: The scenarios of Forgotten Circles had a typical design: You had a cool idea, and then you repeated it three of four times, so that it always felt that the scenario went for at least one iteration too long. In Gloomhaven, we did not feel that too often. In Frosthaven, we feel this more often.
- Puzzle book: The puzzle book is rather annoying. The puzzle book has definitely not been playtested. Give this book to five playtesting groups and you definitely have half of the groups solving the first puzzle wrong, because there are great other solutions that are also logical.
You decipher the language and number system of a machine race and it uses a more inconsistent system as us humans. A later riddle shows numbers in a decimal system. Have the machines suddenly learned our system? And to solve the puzzle I do not need the hint from the last deciphered section, but from a scenario that is hinted there that we played quite a time ago before even finding the puzzle book. In a computer game you might remember such places. In a board game you should have incorporated that in the scenarios (like placing a closed door on the table that cannot be opened).
I like puzzles, I played a lot of Exit games with my wife and we enjoyed these, but the puzzles in this book are not for the majority of players. The riddles can only be solved in order and basically you need all gaming material to solve the riddles and I'm not sure there are always hints which material you need. Perhaps I just overlooked that. So you need to look at the map, you items, the rooms in a scenario, scenario conclusions, ... for hints. This might be nice for the designers who have an overview of the game. For players, I don't know... It would even be better if you had just a collection of 20 puzzles and you try to solve these. But the order in which you have to solve them, just makes it worse. I don't know yet if you can just ignore the puzzles or if something comes as a conclusion that is worth the effort.
- Building cards: Building cards contain costs of the building on the next level. When you to decide which building to upgrade, you look at the cards which buildings can be upgraded. But wait, you also have to look at the Frosthaven map because Level 0 buildings are there and not in your card deck. I don't know how many times, we overlooked something, but this is really bugging me. Not severe, but annoying.
- The difficulty - a priori - at the beginning of the game is quite high. In comparison to Gloomhaven:
- Take away one or two additional hit points of a character's starting hit points.
- Add negative scenario effects more often.
- Puzzle a bit more or otherwise you will lose the scenarios.

Review written after 30+ scenarios played. For context, I gave Gloomhaven a 10 and Jaws of the Lion a 9. A common refrain in my group is that Frosthaven is about 20% too much. So I feel it's all the more appropriate to give Frosthaven an 8.

First, some quick pros. Characters are more complex, deep, and unique than in previous games. Scenarios are more varied and interesting. The story so far is more coherent than GH. Expanding the settlement is neat. Puzzles!

And now to counter each of those. Some characters are too niche and can be frustrating to pull off even basic competence. Scenarios often have large chunks of special rules, often leading to weird edge cases, and are almost universally too long. The story is still forgettable and now split up, so nothing really feels urgent. Settlement management is WAY too much upkeep, particularly after a long scenario. Puzzles are required and often very wonk.

To loop back and sum up, I think cutting about 20% of the length, complexity, and upkeep from FH would have led to a much more satisfying experience. If scenarios were 20% shorter (yes, I recognize the characters are tuned for a given length and this is not a trivial change), settlement phase had 20% less upkeep (actually, the settlement phase could probably be 50% less), if the characters were 20% less "clever," etc etc then this package would have been a home run. As it is, we're burning out of this campaign much faster than previous outings and will soon likely be taking a break, if not outright moving on.

Rating it a 3, but it's a very split rating.
The underlying mechanics are still good, and in fact have been slightly improved from Gloomhaven (which I gave a top rating to), making it a great tactical skirmishing RPG thing. The new character designs are often complex in unnecessary ways, and there is an over reliance on placing overlay tiles which makes it harder for many combinations of characters to play together due to competing over the resource of featureless hexes. In Gloomhaven we generally couldn't wait to play the new characters, but in Frosthaven that is a relatively rare feeling. My adult group hems and haws, not really finding them enticing, with one player reaching back to pilot a Gloomhaven class as none of the available options are interesting to her. At home with my children it's no better, one of them is playing her second Gloomhaven class in Frosthaven, and the other is planning to play a Gloomhaven class next, despite our having 5 unplayed unlocked classes. We have only 4 classes left to unlock at home, and I doubt that those last 4 will be much more enticing.

Story is slightly improved, the lore is a bit better.
The new method of unlocking characters is poorly done, and the new outpost phase is a slog that I'd skip given the chance. Splitting the resources/loot into several types of material and also many herbs introduces unnecessary variance in what your mercenaries might have; one group of mercenaries in my home game had an excess of hides but a continual lack of metal, while in another game at a friend's house we have very balanced material resources, but have one specific herb that we never seem to find. Why not just use coins and exchange them for need materials?
Two huge frustrations are the inability to tell a story with any foreshadowing, and the puzzles.
For the foreshadowing, I am referring to the plot, the character unlocks, and the events.
Events (road, outpost, etc.) Still mostly fall back on the Gloomhaven standard of "pick A or B, but you can't really tell which will be the good result"; some events now use the character traits on cards (e.g., strong, persuasive, etc.) And where this works it does feel better, like you have correctly interpreted the message (some foreshadowing, Yay!), but these events are not common, and sometimes use the "wrong" attribute. One example suggests that I've option might be to convince the NPC of your plan or something, which sounds clearly like the "persuasive" trait would be helpful, right? Wrong! Isaac expected you to threaten them, even though that isn't implied anywhere on the card, so the correct trait is "intimidating".
This lack of foreshadowing extends to many of the class unlocks, which may make sense in hindsight, but are otherwise random.
But by far the worst aspect of this game are the puzzles. The reaction to the puzzles in Gloomhaven was from what I saw largely negative, with people exasperated at having to do a crazy amount of sitting symbols in card art it hidden on the map to unlock a bonus, but at least it wasn't required. You could skip it and not really notice anything lacking from the game. In Frosthaven, Isaac doubles down on puzzles, making them a required part of the campaign. The puzzles are poorly designed for the most part, the best of these being a simple cypher to decode. Others are as nonsensical as the puzzles in Gloomhaven, with no built in hints. Having introduced the calendar, Isaac could have added a hint system overtop of the puzzles (add xxx.x to the calendar in 3 weeks, this is a hint on the puzzle you just started) but instead there is nothing to advance things. A game like pandemic legacy does this repeatedly - if you don't have the previous bit solved and wouldn't be able to advance, plot events catch you up.

The puzzles are frustrating, I'm trying to avoid "spoiling" them, though it is very generous to assume that any appreciable portion of players will enjoy them. They ruin a game that was among the most enjoyable otherwise. I'm only about 2/3rds of the way through the puzzle book, but each one I find makes me more angry with the crappy puzzles we are meant to solve. I would not play this game again, and will likely not buy any follow up. I think Isaac developed a really neat game engine and is a good designer of mechanics, but is not a great story teller, and is a horrible puzzle designer. The fact that an escape room owner weighed in on Reddit about how badly these puzzles are done is exactly the point.

I think the design philosophy of this game can be summed up as: let's make players feel bad about their choices. Loved Gloomhaven and Jaws of the Lion, but after about 30 missions I think we're probably giving up on Frosthaven. Have tried it with 2, 3 and 4 players and all have serious problems, but the game is especially unfun as a two player game.

Many scenarios are poorly designed for two players. For example quite a few scenarios require splitting the party, either at setup or due to a need to reach multiple distant objectives in a limited time. That's fine if you're both playing fast-moving jack-of-all-trades characters (blinkblade/drifter) but what if you're not? Punishing players for choosing to play a fun-looking class is certainly a choice, but not a good one.

I agree with a lot of what others have said: difficulty is spikey and missions are often completely unfair due to certain specific OP monster cards (e.g. focused stabs has movement now!; summons that shuffle-in and are immediately redrawn after being played, etc.)

Other choices seem downright baffling, such as locking upgrades behind a specific personal quest.

That said, there are a some additions and changes from GH which I really liked: the stamina potion nerf-yes, it was broken; different winter/summer event decks; item upgrade chains; and the design and story of the new characters and monsters. Seriously, those shrikes are nightmare fuel. Well done.

Ulimately, I think what makes me want to put down this game is that the best part of the game, the rich story and dynamic world, are always kept just out of reach of the players. "Want to hear how the quest-line ends? Give it one more try and two hours later there's a 33% you might actually get to hear it. But probably, you won't. Better luck next game night. That is not fun.

We're playing at 4P, which may impact this rating. It feels like an awful lot of the characters in Frosthaven have very narrow abilities; either everything works out perfectly and you do something moderately cool, or something goes a little bit sideways and you take a move 2/attack 2 (at best), or skip altogether due to retaliate or enemy movement. We've found that this often either leads to unsatisfying play, or we have to spend a huge amount of time planning each turn, which makes the already long scenarios longer. The admin is also very high - after 17 scenarios, none of the city building feels "worth it," and we have one person in our group who spends significant time between each session organizing everything. Ultimately I can't help but recommend Gloomhaven or Jaws of the Lion instead.

This game feels like a parody of Gloomhaven. It has far more bookkeeping than Gloomhaven, more extraneous tokens and charts, and is dangerously close to jumping the shark. At this rate, I wouldn't be surprised if Brighthaven(or whatever Element+haven they go with next) adds astronomical charts, weather tables, stock markets and child rearing to the bloated rules.

Besides being a table hog and an organizational nightmare, the rules are once again poorly written. Clear evidence of this is the ever-expanding FAQ and Typo list. It's so bad that you basically are required to check the FAQ every session to make sure the current mission you're running isn't missing something vital or includes something you missed.

As a glaring example of this, there are Buildings which must be upgraded in the game on a regular basis to gain Prosperity for the town and aid in character progression. If you fail to notice that there are extra buildings in the initial deck of cards corresponding to ones printed on the map and nowhere else, you will have a difficult time with resources. Unfortunately, these are not mentioned in the rulebook at all.

I fully expect that a 2.0 version of Frosthaven will be released to much fanfare in a few years. They will correct and improve, much like they are apparently doing with Gloomhaven 2.0. If you are not a diehard 'Haven fan and can wait a few years, I'd suggest you hold for a 2.0 or at least a reprint that has some rules fixes added in.
